items.gloss_md: The tumour suppressor gene encoding p53, the most frequently mutated gene in human cancer.
items.body_md:
Full name *tumor protein p53*; located on 17p13.1. It encodes the transcription factor p53 (plus N-terminally truncated isoforms such as Δ40p53 and Δ133p53 from alternative promoters/splicing).

- Alterations: mutated in roughly half of all human cancers. Unlike most tumour suppressors, about 75% of mutations are missense changes in the DNA-binding domain, with hotspots R175, G245, R248, R249, R273 and R282; the second allele is usually lost (LOH). Many missense mutants act dominant-negative or gain-of-function.
- Frequencies: ~70% of PDAC, very common in high-grade serous ovarian cancer (nearly all), lung squamous cancer, triple-negative breast cancer; ~30% of HCC. R249S is the signature mutation of aflatoxin B1–associated HCC.
- Germline: Li-Fraumeni syndrome (sarcomas, early breast cancer, brain tumours, adrenocortical carcinoma, leukaemia).
- History: found in 1979 by several groups (Lane & Crawford, Linzer & Levine, DeLeo & Old) as a protein bound to SV40 large T antigen; first thought to be an oncogene because the cloned cDNAs were mutants; recognised as a tumour suppressor in 1989 (Vogelstein lab).
- Clinic: aberrant p53 IHC (strong diffuse overexpression or complete loss) is a surrogate for mutation; TP53 mutation predicts poor prognosis in AML/MDS and CLL; no approved drug restores mutant p53 yet.

attrs.mnemonic: p53 is the 'guardian of the genome' (David Lane, 1992) – picture a guard at gate 53 checking every cell for DNA damage before it may pass into S phase.
attrs.anecdote: p53 was named simply after its apparent molecular weight of 53 kDa on SDS gels – the real mass is ~43.7 kDa; its proline-rich region makes it run slowly. In 1993 Science named it 'Molecule of the Year'.

items.gloss_md: A tetrameric transcription factor that responds to DNA damage and oncogenic stress by inducing cell-cycle arrest, apoptosis or senescence.
items.body_md:
Tumour suppressor protein of 393 amino acids encoded by *TP53*. Domains: two N-terminal transactivation domains, a proline-rich region, the central DNA-binding domain (where most cancer mutations lie), a tetramerisation domain and a C-terminal regulatory domain.

- Activation: DNA damage activates ATM/ATR and CHK1/CHK2, which phosphorylate p53 (e.g. Ser15, Ser20) and block MDM2 binding; oncogene activation induces p14ARF, which sequesters MDM2.
- Regulation: in unstressed cells MDM2 ubiquitinates p53 for proteasomal degradation (half-life ~20 min); MDM2 is itself a p53 target (negative feedback loop).
- Targets: *CDKN1A* (p21, G1 arrest), *GADD45A*, *BAX*, *BBC3* (PUMA), *PMAIP1* (NOXA), *FAS*, *MDM2*.
- Mutant p53 escapes MDM2-mediated turnover and accumulates, which is why diffuse strong nuclear p53 staining in IHC indicates a missense mutation (whereas complete absence suggests a truncating mutation).
- Drug efforts: MDM2 inhibitors (idasanutlin etc.) for TP53-wild-type tumours; reactivators of mutant p53 (eprenetapopt/APR-246) remain experimental.

attrs.mnemonic: Three outcomes of p53 activation – 'Stop, Repair or Die': arrest (p21), DNA repair, apoptosis (PUMA/NOXA/BAX).

items.gloss_md: The most frequently mutated oncogene in human cancer, encoding the small GTPase K-Ras; mutated in >90% of PDAC.
items.body_md:
Named after the Kirsten rat sarcoma virus (Werner Kirsten, 1960s), whose oncogene v-Ki-ras is its retroviral homologue. Located on 12p12.1. Alternative splicing of the fourth exon yields two isoforms, KRAS4A and the predominant KRAS4B.

- Alterations: activating point mutations at codons 12, 13 and 61. KRAS mutations are found in >90% of PDAC (mainly G12D, then G12V and G12R; KRAS mutation is the initiating event already present in PanIN), ~40% of colorectal cancers and ~30% of lung adenocarcinomas (G12C, smoking-associated, ~13% of NSCLC).
- Clinic: KRAS (and NRAS) mutations predict lack of response to anti-EGFR antibodies (cetuximab, panitumumab) in colorectal cancer, so RAS testing is mandatory. After decades as 'undruggable', covalent KRAS G12C inhibitors sotorasib (approved 2021) and adagrasib were approved for NSCLC; G12D-selective and pan-RAS(ON) inhibitors such as daraxonrasib are in trials, including in PDAC.
- KRAS-wild-type PDAC (~5–10%) should be screened for actionable alternatives: NRG1, NTRK, ALK, ROS1 or RET fusions, BRAF alterations, MSI-high.
- Mutant KRAS can be detected in plasma ctDNA for monitoring.

attrs.mnemonic: '12-13-61' are the RAS hotspot codons – remember 'a dozen, a baker's dozen and 61'. And PDAC is the 'KRAS cancer': >90%.
attrs.anecdote: Called 'undruggable' for almost 40 years because its smooth surface and picomolar GTP affinity offered no pocket; Kevan Shokat's lab found the cryptic switch-II pocket of KRAS G12C in 2013, leading to sotorasib in 2021.

items.gloss_md: A small membrane-bound GTPase that acts as a binary on/off switch relaying growth-factor receptor signals to the MAPK and PI3K pathways.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *KRAS*; KRAS4B has 188 amino acids. The G domain contains the P-loop and the switch I/II regions that change conformation between GDP-bound (off) and GTP-bound (on) states; the C-terminal hypervariable region ends in a CAAX box that is farnesylated and, in KRAS4B, a polybasic lysine stretch that anchors it to the inner plasma membrane.

- Regulation: guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs, e.g. SOS1 recruited by GRB2 to activated receptor tyrosine kinases) load GTP; GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs, e.g. neurofibromin NF1) accelerate GTP hydrolysis.
- Oncogenic G12/G13 mutations sterically block GAP-mediated hydrolysis, Q61 mutations impair catalysis itself, so the protein stays GTP-bound.
- Effectors: RAF kinases (→ MEK → ERK), PI3K (p110), RalGDS, TIAM1.
- Drugs: sotorasib and adagrasib covalently bind Cys12 in the switch-II pocket of GDP-bound KRAS G12C, trapping it in the off state; SHP2 and SOS1 inhibitors act upstream.

attrs.mnemonic: RAS is a light switch: GEF = 'Get Exchange Fresh GTP' (on), GAP = 'GTPase Accelerating, Pulls the plug' (off).

items.gloss_md: A short-lived bHLH-leucine-zipper transcription factor that, with its partner MAX, amplifies the expression of growth, ribosome biogenesis and metabolic genes.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *MYC*; main isoform 439 amino acids. Domains: N-terminal transactivation domain containing MYC boxes (MB0–MBIV), central region, and C-terminal basic helix-loop-helix leucine zipper (bHLH-LZ).

- Mechanism: heterodimerises with MAX and binds E-box motifs (CACGTG); at high levels it invades low-affinity sites and acts as a general amplifier of active transcription. MXD/MNT–MAX dimers antagonise it.
- Functions: cell-cycle entry, ribosome biogenesis and protein synthesis, glycolysis and glutaminolysis, nucleotide synthesis; represses CDKN1A and CDKN2B via MIZ1; strong expression triggers apoptosis via p14ARF–p53, so MYC-driven tumours typically disable that checkpoint.
- Regulation: half-life ~20–30 min; ERK phosphorylates Ser62 (stabilising), which primes GSK3β phosphorylation of Thr58 and recognition by FBXW7 for proteasomal degradation. T58 mutations in Burkitt lymphoma stabilise it.
- IHC for MYC protein (≥40% nuclei) is used in lymphoma work-up.

attrs.mnemonic: MYC needs MAX: 'MYC alone does nothing – it always shops for MAXimum growth with MAX.'

items.gloss_md: A tumour suppressor locus on 9p21 encoding two different proteins, p16INK4a and p14ARF, that guard the Rb and p53 pathways; inactivated in >90% of PDAC.
items.body_md:
Located on 9p21.3 next to *CDKN2B* (p15INK4b) and *MTAP*. Two separate first exons (1α and 1β) spliced to shared exons 2–3, read in different frames, produce two unrelated proteins: p16INK4a (inhibits CDK4/6 → keeps Rb active) and p14ARF (p19Arf in mouse; inhibits MDM2 → stabilises p53).

- Alterations: homozygous deletion (often together with CDKN2B and MTAP), point mutation or promoter hypermethylation. One of the most frequently inactivated genes in cancer: PDAC (~95%, about 40% homozygous deletion), melanoma, glioblastoma, mesothelioma, squamous carcinomas, bladder cancer.
- Germline: familial melanoma / FAMMM syndrome (familial atypical multiple mole melanoma), which also confers a markedly increased PDAC risk (melanoma–pancreatic cancer syndrome).
- History: p16 was identified as a CDK4 inhibitor in 1993 (Serrano, Hannon & Beach) and as the 9p21 tumour suppressor MTS1 in 1994 (Kamb et al.).
- Clinic: homozygous CDKN2A deletion is a grading criterion in WHO CNS5 (IDH-mutant astrocytoma → grade 4); MTAP co-deletion creates a vulnerability to PRMT5 and MAT2A inhibitors (trials).

attrs.mnemonic: One gene, two proteins, two pathways: 'p16 guards Rb, p14 guards p53' – 16 > 14 just like Rb comes first (G1) before p53 checks.
attrs.anecdote: CDKN2A is a textbook rarity in the human genome: the same exon 2 is read in two different reading frames to make two unrelated proteins – hence the name ARF, 'alternative reading frame'.

items.gloss_md: A CDK4/6 inhibitor of the INK4 family that keeps Rb hypophosphorylated and enforces G1 arrest and senescence.
items.body_md:
Protein of 156 amino acids consisting of four ankyrin repeats, encoded by *CDKN2A* (exon 1α). INK4 = 'inhibitor of CDK4'; family members p15INK4b, p18INK4c, p19INK4d.

- Mechanism: binds CDK4 or CDK6 and prevents their association with D-type cyclins, so Rb stays hypophosphorylated and represses E2F; cells stop in G1.
- Senescence: p16 accumulates with age and in oncogene-induced senescence; it is a widely used senescence biomarker.
- Feedback: when Rb is inactivated (e.g. by HPV E7), p16 is strongly upregulated. Therefore diffuse 'block-type' p16 IHC is a surrogate marker for high-risk HPV in cervical lesions and oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma.
- Loss of p16 (deletion, mutation, methylation) occurs in most PDAC and permits unchecked CDK4/6 activity; CDK4/6 inhibitors (palbociclib, ribociclib, abemaciclib) pharmacologically mimic p16.

attrs.mnemonic: p16 = 'pharmacological palbociclib made by nature' – a natural CDK4/6 inhibitor.

items.gloss_md: The alternative-reading-frame product of CDKN2A that binds MDM2 and thereby stabilises p53 in response to oncogenic signalling.
items.body_md:
Protein of 132 amino acids (mouse orthologue p19Arf) encoded by exon 1β of *CDKN2A* spliced to exon 2 read in an alternative reading frame, so it shares no sequence with p16INK4a.

- Mechanism: binds MDM2 and sequesters it in the nucleolus / inhibits its E3 ligase activity, so p53 is stabilised and activated.
- Induction: by oncogenic signals rather than DNA damage – MYC, mutant RAS, E2F1 and adenovirus E1A induce ARF. This 'oncogene checkpoint' eliminates cells with hyperproliferative signalling.
- Because one deletion of *CDKN2A* removes both p16 and p14ARF, it disables the Rb and p53 tumour-suppressor pathways at the same time, which explains why 9p21 deletion is so strongly selected in cancer.
- Arf-null mice develop tumours early, showing that ARF is a tumour suppressor independently of p16.

attrs.mnemonic: ARF = 'Alarm for Runaway Factors' – it rings when MYC or RAS run away and sets p53 free from MDM2.

items.gloss_md: A tumour suppressor encoding the common mediator SMAD4 of TGF-β/BMP signalling; inactivated in about half of PDAC (originally called DPC4).
items.body_md:
Located on 18q21.2. Encodes SMAD4, the only common-partner SMAD (co-SMAD) of the TGF-β superfamily pathways.

- Alterations: homozygous deletion or mutation with loss of the other allele (18q loss). Inactivated in ~50–55% of PDAC (a late event in the PanIN progression), ~10–15% of colorectal cancers, and in other gastrointestinal cancers. In PDAC, SMAD4 loss has been associated with widespread metastatic rather than locally destructive disease (Iacobuzio-Donahue et al., 2009).
- Germline: juvenile polyposis syndrome (some families also have hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia).
- History: identified in 1996 by Hahn, Kern and colleagues as DPC4 ('deleted in pancreatic carcinoma, locus 4') through homozygous deletions on 18q in pancreatic cancer.
- Clinic: loss of nuclear SMAD4 by IHC is a useful diagnostic aid – it supports a pancreatobiliary primary in a metastasis of unknown origin and separates PDAC from reactive ducts (SMAD4 is retained in benign tissue). Not a drug target itself.

attrs.mnemonic: PDAC's 'big four' drivers: KRAS, TP53, CDKN2A, SMAD4 – 'Keep The Cancer Small' (K-T-C-S).
attrs.anecdote: SMAD is a fusion of the C. elegans gene sma ('small' worms) and Drosophila Mad ('Mothers against decapentaplegic') – a mutation in Mad made the mothers' embryos lose dpp signalling.

items.gloss_md: The co-SMAD transcriptional mediator that partners with receptor-phosphorylated SMADs to carry TGF-β and BMP signals into the nucleus.
items.body_md:
Protein of 552 amino acids encoded by *SMAD4*. Domains: N-terminal MH1 (DNA binding to SMAD-binding elements, GTCT/AGAC), a linker region, and C-terminal MH2 (protein–protein interaction, trimerisation).

- Pathway: ligand-bound TGF-β type II receptor phosphorylates the type I receptor (ALK5), which phosphorylates the receptor-regulated SMADs (R-SMADs) SMAD2/3 at their C-terminal SSXS motif (BMP pathway: SMAD1/5/8 via ALK1/2/3/6). Phosphorylated R-SMADs form trimers with SMAD4, enter the nucleus and, with cofactors, regulate transcription.
- Effects in epithelium: cytostasis (induction of p15INK4b and p21, repression of MYC) and apoptosis – the tumour-suppressive arm of TGF-β. Later in tumour progression TGF-β promotes EMT, fibrosis and immune suppression, partly SMAD4-independent.
- Inhibitory SMADs SMAD6/7 provide negative feedback.
- Clinic: IHC loss indicates gene inactivation (PDAC, colorectal, gastric).

attrs.mnemonic: R-SMADs are the 'Receptor' ones (2/3 for TGF-β, 1/5/8 for BMP), SMAD4 is the 'Co' – common partner of all; SMAD 6/7 are the 'Inhibitors' (I-SMADs).

items.gloss_md: An oncogene encoding the receptor tyrosine kinase EGFR, activated by mutation in lung adenocarcinoma and by amplification/EGFRvIII in glioblastoma; target of TKIs and antibodies.
items.body_md:
Located on 7p11.2. Also called *ERBB1* / *HER1*, the founding member of the ErbB family (with ERBB2/HER2, ERBB3, ERBB4).

- Alterations: activating kinase-domain mutations in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC; ~10–15% of Western and ~40–50% of East Asian lung adenocarcinomas, enriched in never-smokers) – mainly exon 19 deletions and L858R (exon 21); exon 20 insertions are resistant to classic TKIs. Acquired resistance: T790M gatekeeper mutation (to 1st/2nd-generation TKIs), C797S (to osimertinib), MET amplification. Glioblastoma: amplification and the EGFRvIII variant (in-frame deletion of exons 2–7, ligand-independent). Overexpression in head and neck and colorectal cancer.
- History: EGF and its receptor were discovered by Stanley Cohen (Nobel Prize 1986, with Rita Levi-Montalcini). Lung cancer mutations were reported in 2004 (Lynch, Paez, Pao).
- Drugs: TKIs gefitinib, erlotinib (1st generation), afatinib, dacomitinib (2nd), osimertinib (3rd); antibodies cetuximab and panitumumab (RAS-wild-type colorectal cancer, head and neck SCC); amivantamab (EGFR–MET bispecific, exon 20). In PDAC, erlotinib plus gemcitabine was approved (2005) but adds only ~2 weeks of survival.

attrs.mnemonic: Lung EGFR mutations: 'Delete 19, Leu-Arg 858' – the two classic sensitising ones; T790M is the 'Too-big gatekeeper' that blocks the drug.

items.gloss_md: A transmembrane receptor tyrosine kinase activated by EGF-family ligands that signals through RAS–MAPK, PI3K–AKT, PLCγ and STAT pathways.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *EGFR*; 1210 amino acids including signal peptide (~170 kDa glycoprotein). Extracellular domains I–IV (I and III bind ligand, II carries the dimerisation arm), a single transmembrane helix, the tyrosine kinase domain and a C-terminal tail with autophosphorylation sites.

- Ligands: EGF, TGF-α, amphiregulin, epiregulin, HB-EGF, betacellulin, epigen.
- Activation: ligand binding exposes the dimerisation arm → homo- or heterodimer (preferentially with HER2) → asymmetric kinase dimer → trans-autophosphorylation of tail tyrosines → docking of GRB2/SOS (RAS–MAPK), PI3K, PLCγ, STAT3/5.
- Termination: receptor endocytosis and CBL-mediated ubiquitination with lysosomal degradation.
- Drug targets: ATP-competitive TKIs (reversible: gefitinib, erlotinib; covalent to Cys797: afatinib, osimertinib) and extracellular antibodies (cetuximab, panitumumab). Typical side effect of EGFR blockade: acneiform rash (which correlates with response).

attrs.mnemonic: Rash = response: the more acneiform rash on cetuximab/erlotinib, the better the tumour usually responds.

items.gloss_md: An oncogene encoding the receptor tyrosine kinase HER2, amplified in ~15–20% of breast cancers and in gastric cancer; target of trastuzumab and related drugs.
items.body_md:
Located on 17q12 in an amplicon that also contains *GRB7*. Known as *HER2* (human) and *neu* (rat).

- Alterations: gene amplification with protein overexpression in ~15–20% of breast cancers and ~10–20% of gastric/gastro-oesophageal junction adenocarcinomas; also in biliary, bladder, colorectal cancers (rare in PDAC). Activating mutations and exon 20 insertions in NSCLC.
- History: rat neu was found in chemically induced neuroblastomas (Weinberg lab, 1984); human HER2 was cloned in 1985; Dennis Slamon showed in 1987 that HER2 amplification predicts poor prognosis in breast cancer.
- Testing (ASCO/CAP): IHC 0, 1+, 2+, 3+; 3+ = positive, 2+ = equivocal → ISH. 'HER2-low' (IHC 1+ or 2+/ISH-negative) became a treatable category with trastuzumab deruxtecan (DESTINY-Breast04, 2022).
- Drugs: trastuzumab (approved 1998), pertuzumab, antibody–drug conjugates trastuzumab emtansine (T-DM1) and trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd), TKIs lapatinib, neratinib, tucatinib. Cardiotoxicity is a typical side effect of trastuzumab.

attrs.mnemonic: HER2 lives on 17 – 'seventeen and amplified': the 17q12 amplicon.
attrs.anecdote: Trastuzumab's development story, with Dennis Slamon fighting for funding (partly from Revlon), was dramatised in the 2008 TV film 'Living Proof'.

items.gloss_md: An orphan receptor tyrosine kinase of the ErbB family that is the preferred dimerisation partner of the other ErbB receptors and a major breast cancer drug target.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *ERBB2*; 1255 amino acids, ~185 kDa. Same architecture as EGFR (extracellular domains I–IV, transmembrane helix, kinase domain, C-terminal tail).

- No known ligand: its extracellular domain is fixed in an extended, 'active' conformation with the dimerisation arm always exposed, so HER2 is the favoured heterodimer partner of EGFR, HER3 and HER4. The HER2–HER3 dimer is the most potent activator of PI3K–AKT (HER3 has six p85-binding sites but weak kinase activity).
- Overexpression (up to ~2 million receptors per cell) causes ligand-independent homodimerisation and constant signalling.
- Drug binding sites: trastuzumab binds domain IV (blocks shedding, induces ADCC), pertuzumab binds domain II (blocks dimerisation); combined they give dual blockade.
- Variants: p95HER2 (truncated, lacks the trastuzumab epitope, a resistance mechanism); the shed extracellular domain is measurable in serum.

attrs.mnemonic: Trastuzumab = 'Four', Pertuzumab = 'Pair': trastuzumab binds domain IV, pertuzumab blocks the pairing (dimerisation) domain II.

items.gloss_md: An oncogene encoding the MAP3 kinase B-Raf; the V600E mutation drives about half of melanomas and is a classic targeted-therapy biomarker.
items.body_md:
Located on 7q34. One of three RAF genes (*ARAF*, *BRAF*, *RAF1*/CRAF).

- Alterations: ~90% of BRAF mutations in melanoma are V600E (V600K second). Frequencies: ~50% of cutaneous melanomas, ~40–60% of papillary thyroid carcinomas, ~10% of colorectal cancers (serrated pathway, MSI/CIMP-high, poor prognosis in MSS), nearly all hairy cell leukaemias, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, ~2–4% of NSCLC, ~1–3% of PDAC (mostly KRAS-wild-type). Mutations are classified as class I (V600, active monomers), class II (RAS-independent dimers) and class III (kinase-impaired, RAS-dependent). KIAA1549–BRAF fusion in pilocytic astrocytoma.
- Diagnostic use: in MLH1-deficient colorectal cancer, BRAF V600E points to sporadic MLH1 promoter methylation and argues against Lynch syndrome.
- History: reported in 2002 by the Sanger Cancer Genome Project (Davies et al., Nature).
- Drugs: BRAF inhibitors vemurafenib (approved 2011), dabrafenib, encorafenib, always combined with MEK inhibitors (trametinib, cobimetinib, binimetinib); colorectal cancer: encorafenib + cetuximab. BRAF inhibitors paradoxically activate MAPK in BRAF-wild-type cells (dimers), causing cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas.

attrs.mnemonic: V600E: 'Valine 600 turned into glutamic acid (E) – E like Evil melanoma.'
attrs.anecdote: BRAF V600E was among the first major hits of the Sanger Institute's Cancer Genome Project – a systematic screen of kinases published in 2002, years before cheap next-generation sequencing.

items.gloss_md: A serine/threonine kinase (MAP3K) activated by RAS-GTP that phosphorylates MEK1/2 and thereby starts the ERK cascade.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *BRAF*; 766 amino acids. Three conserved regions: CR1 (RAS-binding domain and cysteine-rich domain), CR2 (Ser/Thr-rich hinge with a 14-3-3 binding site, S365) and CR3 (kinase domain with the activation segment containing T599/S602).

- Activation: RAS-GTP recruits RAF to the membrane, releasing autoinhibition; RAF forms homo- or heterodimers (BRAF–CRAF) and phosphorylates MEK1/2, which phosphorylate ERK1/2.
- B-Raf has the highest basal kinase activity of the three RAFs, which is why a single mutation is enough to make it oncogenic.
- V600E mimics phosphorylation of the activation loop, raising activity ~500-fold and allowing signalling as a RAS-independent monomer.
- Negative feedback: ERK phosphorylates SOS and RAF; when BRAF is inhibited this feedback is lost, a mechanism of resistance (e.g. EGFR reactivation in colorectal cancer, hence the encorafenib + cetuximab combination).

attrs.mnemonic: MAPK cascade order: RAS → RAF → MEK → ERK, 'Rats Run, Mice Eat Kernels' – or alphabetically R-R-M-E.

items.gloss_md: A tumour suppressor gene whose germline loss-of-function variants cause hereditary breast and ovarian cancer; its protein is central to homologous recombination repair.
items.body_md:
Located on 17q21.31; encodes BRCA1.

- Germline: heterozygous pathogenic variants cause hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome (HBOC; German HBOC = 'familiärer Brust- und Eierstockkrebs'), with lifetime risks of roughly 60–70% for breast and ~40% for ovarian cancer; modestly increased pancreatic and prostate cancer risk. Ashkenazi Jewish founder variants: c.68_69delAG (185delAG) and c.5266dupC (5382insC). Tumours lose the wild-type allele and typically are triple-negative/basal-like breast cancers or high-grade serous ovarian cancers.
- Somatic: inactivation by promoter hypermethylation in some ovarian and breast cancers.
- History: linkage to 17q21 shown in 1990 by Mary-Claire King's group; gene cloned in 1994 (Miki et al., Myriad Genetics). Myriad's patents were invalidated by the US Supreme Court in 2013 (AMP v. Myriad: naturally occurring DNA cannot be patented).
- Clinic: homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) makes tumours sensitive to platinum and PARP inhibitors (olaparib, niraparib, rucaparib, talazoparib); reversion mutations restore function and cause resistance. Risk-reducing mastectomy/salpingo-oophorectomy.

attrs.mnemonic: BRCA1 on 17, BRCA2 on 13: 'BRCA one-seven, BRCA two-three' – and BRCA2 (13) is the one also linked to pancreas and male breast cancer.
attrs.anecdote: Angelina Jolie's 2013 New York Times op-ed about her preventive mastectomy as a BRCA1 carrier caused a measurable worldwide surge in genetic testing ('Angelina effect'). Myriad's BRCA patents were struck down by the US Supreme Court the same year.

items.gloss_md: A large scaffold E3-ubiquitin-ligase protein that promotes homologous recombination by driving DNA end resection and recruiting PALB2–BRCA2–RAD51.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *BRCA1*; 1863 amino acids. Domains: N-terminal RING domain (heterodimer with BARD1, E3 ubiquitin ligase), central region with nuclear localisation signals and a coiled-coil that binds PALB2, and tandem C-terminal BRCT repeats that bind phosphorylated partners (ABRAXAS, BRIP1, CtIP).

- Homologous recombination (HR): at double-strand breaks in S/G2, BRCA1 counteracts 53BP1 to allow 5' end resection, then recruits PALB2 and BRCA2, which load RAD51 onto single-stranded DNA.
- Other functions: G2/M checkpoint, replication fork protection, transcriptional regulation, X-inactivation.
- Loss of BRCA1 shifts repair to error-prone pathways (NHEJ, microhomology-mediated end joining via POLθ), producing a typical genomic scar (HRD: large-scale transitions, LOH, telomeric allelic imbalance; mutational signature SBS3).
- Synthetic lethality: BRCA1-deficient cells die when PARP1 is inhibited (Bryant et al. and Farmer et al., 2005).

attrs.mnemonic: BRCA1 'opens the door' (end resection), BRCA2 'brings the RAD51 paint' – one before two.

items.gloss_md: A tumour suppressor gene whose germline variants cause hereditary breast, ovarian, prostate and pancreatic cancer; its protein loads RAD51 in homologous recombination.
items.body_md:
Located on 13q13.1; also called *FANCD1*.

- Germline: HBOC syndrome with lifetime breast cancer risk ~55–70%, ovarian ~15–25%, plus male breast cancer, aggressive prostate cancer and PDAC. Germline BRCA1/2 variants are found in roughly 5–7% of unselected PDAC patients (BRCA2 more often than BRCA1) and are the most common cause of familial pancreatic cancer. Ashkenazi founder variant c.5946delT (6174delT). Biallelic germline loss causes Fanconi anaemia (complementation group D1).
- History: mapped to 13q12–13 in 1994 and cloned in 1995 (Wooster et al., Stratton lab).
- Clinic: German guidelines recommend germline testing for all PDAC patients. BRCA-mutated PDAC responds well to platinum (FOLFIRINOX); olaparib maintenance after platinum in germline BRCA-mutated metastatic PDAC (POLO trial, approved 2019). PARP inhibitors are also used in breast, ovarian and prostate cancer.

attrs.mnemonic: BRCA2: 'the 2 that goes to the pancreas' – the BRCA gene most associated with PDAC and male breast cancer.
attrs.anecdote: Mike Stratton's team at the Institute of Cancer Research found BRCA2 in 1995 and patented it in the UK partly to keep it in the public domain, in deliberate contrast to Myriad's commercial BRCA1 patents.

items.gloss_md: A large DNA-repair mediator protein that loads the recombinase RAD51 onto single-stranded DNA during homologous recombination and protects stalled replication forks.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *BRCA2*; 3418 amino acids (~384 kDa). Key regions: N-terminal PALB2-binding site, eight BRC repeats in exon 11 that bind RAD51 monomers, a C-terminal DNA-binding domain with oligonucleotide-binding (OB) folds that binds ssDNA, and the C-terminal TR2 motif that stabilises RAD51 filaments (regulated by CDK phosphorylation).

- Function: recruited via PALB2 to BRCA1 at resected double-strand breaks; replaces RPA on 3' ssDNA overhangs with RAD51, forming the nucleoprotein filament that invades the homologous sister chromatid.
- Replication fork protection: prevents MRE11 nuclease degradation of nascent DNA at stalled forks.
- Deficiency yields the HRD phenotype: genomic instability, platinum and PARP inhibitor sensitivity, mutational signature SBS3.
- RAD51 foci assays on tumour tissue are used experimentally as functional HR readout.

attrs.mnemonic: BRCA2 has 8 BRC repeats – 'eight hands to carry RAD51'.

items.gloss_md: An oncogene encoding p110α, the catalytic subunit of class IA PI3K; one of the most frequently mutated oncogenes, especially in breast cancer.
items.body_md:
Located on 3q26.32 (the 3q gain region of squamous carcinomas).

- Alterations: hotspot mutations in the helical domain (E542K, E545K) and the kinase domain (H1047R). Found in ~30–40% of HR-positive breast cancers, ~15–20% of colorectal, frequent in endometrial, cervical and head and neck cancers; amplification in squamous cancers. Rare in PDAC. Mosaic (postzygotic) mutations cause the PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum (PROS, e.g. CLOVES syndrome).
- History: frequent cancer mutations reported in 2004 (Samuels et al., Science, Vogelstein/Velculescu labs).
- Drugs: alpelisib (p110α-selective, with fulvestrant in PIK3CA-mutant HR+/HER2- breast cancer, approved 2019; also for PROS), inavolisib (mutant-selective, 2024), and the AKT inhibitor capivasertib for PIK3CA/AKT1/PTEN-altered breast cancer. Typical on-target side effect: hyperglycaemia (insulin signalling uses PI3K).

attrs.mnemonic: PIK3CA hotspots: 'E542, E545 in the helix, H1047 at the kinase end' – helical 'E's and the kinase 'H'.

items.gloss_md: The catalytic subunit of class IA phosphoinositide 3-kinase that phosphorylates PIP2 to PIP3 at the plasma membrane, activating AKT.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *PIK3CA*; 1068 amino acids. Domains: adaptor-binding domain (ABD, binds the p85 regulatory subunit), Ras-binding domain, C2 domain, helical domain and the lipid kinase domain.

- Holoenzyme: an obligate heterodimer with a p85 regulatory subunit (p85α from *PIK3R1*), which stabilises p110α but also inhibits it. When receptor tyrosine kinases or IRS1 are phosphorylated on pYXXM motifs, the p85 SH2 domains bind them, relieving inhibition and bringing p110α to its lipid substrate.
- Reaction: PI(4,5)P2 → PI(3,4,5)P3; PIP3 recruits PH-domain proteins such as AKT and PDK1, leading to AKT activation and mTORC1 signalling (growth, glucose uptake, survival). PTEN reverses the reaction.
- Mutations: helical-domain mutations (E545K) disrupt the inhibitory contact with the p85 nSH2 domain; kinase-domain H1047R enhances membrane binding.
- Class IA isoforms: p110α (PIK3CA), p110β (PIK3CB), p110δ (PIK3CD, leukocytes; idelalisib target).

attrs.mnemonic: PI3K adds a phosphate at position 3 (PIP2 → PIP3); PTEN takes it off again – 'PI3K writes, PTEN erases'.

items.gloss_md: A tumour suppressor gene encoding the lipid phosphatase PTEN, the main antagonist of PI3K signalling; frequently lost in glioblastoma, endometrial and prostate cancer.
items.body_md:
Located on 10q23.31; formerly called *MMAC1* (mutated in multiple advanced cancers 1) and *TEP1*.

- Alterations: deletion, truncating or missense mutations and promoter methylation. Very frequent in endometrioid endometrial carcinoma, glioblastoma, prostate cancer (often with deletion), melanoma and breast cancer. PTEN is haploinsufficient: partial loss already promotes tumourigenesis ('continuum model').
- Germline: PTEN hamartoma tumour syndrome (PHTS), including Cowden syndrome (hamartomas, macrocephaly, high risk of breast, thyroid and endometrial cancer) and Bannayan–Riley–Ruvalcaba syndrome; also autism with macrocephaly.
- History: cloned in 1997 independently by Li et al. (Parsons lab) and Steck et al.
- Clinic: PTEN loss by IHC is a prognostic marker in prostate cancer and an eligibility marker for capivasertib (AKT inhibitor) in HR+ breast cancer; PTEN loss is associated with resistance to anti-HER2 therapy and to immunotherapy.

attrs.mnemonic: PTEN removes the phosphate from position 3: 'PTEN puts the brakes – P-TEN subtracts what PI3K added.'

items.gloss_md: A dual-specificity phosphatase that dephosphorylates PIP3 to PIP2, switching off PI3K–AKT signalling.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *PTEN*; 403 amino acids. Domains: N-terminal PIP2-binding motif, phosphatase domain with the catalytic CX5R signature (Cys124), C2 membrane-binding domain, and a C-terminal tail with phosphorylation sites and a PDZ-binding motif.

- Function: its main physiological substrate is the lipid PI(3,4,5)P3, which it converts to PI(4,5)P2 (3-phosphatase), terminating AKT recruitment and activation. It also dephosphorylates some proteins.
- Regulation: phosphorylation of the C-terminal tail (by CK2, GSK3) closes the protein into an inactive, stable conformation; ubiquitination by NEDD4-1 controls nuclear import and degradation; oxidation of Cys124 by reactive oxygen species inactivates it.
- Nuclear PTEN contributes to genome stability and chromosome integrity.
- PTEN-L, a longer translational isoform starting at an upstream CUG codon, is secreted and taken up by neighbouring cells.
- Loss of PTEN protein by IHC is used clinically as a surrogate for gene inactivation.

aliases: Phosphatidylinositol 3,4,5-trisphosphate 3-phosphatase and dual-specificity protein phosphatase PTEN
attrs.mnemonic: PIP2 ⇄ PIP3 is a tug of war: PI3K adds the 3-phosphate, PTEN takes it off again.

items.gloss_md: The first tumour suppressor gene cloned, encoding the cell-cycle gatekeeper pRb; its loss causes retinoblastoma and is near-universal in small cell lung cancer.
items.body_md:
Located on 13q14.2; encodes the retinoblastoma protein pRb.

- Knudson's two-hit hypothesis (1971): comparing bilateral, early, familial retinoblastoma with unilateral, later, sporadic cases, Alfred Knudson concluded that two mutational events are needed – one inherited in the germline in familial cases. RB1 was the gene that proved it.
- Alterations: biallelic inactivation by deletion, mutation or LOH in retinoblastoma, osteosarcoma (germline carriers have high sarcoma risk), small cell lung cancer (~90%, with TP53), and neuroendocrine transformation of EGFR-mutant lung or castration-resistant prostate cancers. In most other cancers the Rb pathway is disabled indirectly (CDKN2A loss, CCND1 or CDK4/6 amplification).
- Viral oncoproteins HPV E7, adenovirus E1A and SV40 large T bind and inactivate pRb.
- History: cloned in 1986 by Friend et al. (Weinberg and Dryja labs).
- Clinic: RB1 loss confers resistance to CDK4/6 inhibitors (which need functional Rb).

attrs.mnemonic: Two hits, two eyes: Knudson's two-hit hypothesis came from bilateral (two-eyed) hereditary retinoblastoma.
attrs.anecdote: Knudson worked out the two-hit model in 1971 purely statistically, from the age-at-diagnosis curves of 48 retinoblastoma cases – 15 years before the gene was cloned.

items.gloss_md: The retinoblastoma pocket protein that binds and represses E2F transcription factors in G1; its phosphorylation by CDKs releases cells into S phase.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *RB1*; 928 amino acids (~105–110 kDa). Belongs to the pocket protein family with p107 (RBL1) and p130 (RBL2). The central A/B 'pocket' binds the transactivation domain of E2F and LxCxE motifs of chromatin regulators and viral oncoproteins.

- G1 control: hypophosphorylated pRb binds E2F1–3/DP dimers and represses their target genes (cyclin E, CDC6, DHFR, thymidine kinase, MCMs) by blocking transactivation and recruiting HDACs, SWI/SNF and DNA methyltransferases.
- Release: cyclin D–CDK4/6 starts and cyclin E–CDK2 completes pRb hyperphosphorylation in late G1, releasing E2F; this marks the restriction point beyond which cells no longer need mitogens.
- Reset: PP1 phosphatase dephosphorylates pRb at mitotic exit.
- Also regulates senescence-associated heterochromatin and differentiation.

attrs.mnemonic: Rb = 'Red brake' at the G1/S crossing: phosphorylate it and the brake is released (E2F drives).

items.gloss_md: A tumour suppressor gene encoding the β-catenin destruction-complex scaffold APC; germline mutations cause familial adenomatous polyposis and somatic loss starts most colorectal cancers.
items.body_md:
Located on 5q22.2; the name stands for *adenomatous polyposis coli*.

- Germline: familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), autosomal dominant, hundreds to thousands of colorectal adenomas from adolescence and nearly 100% colorectal cancer risk without prophylactic colectomy; variants include attenuated FAP (mutations at the far 5' or 3' ends), Gardner syndrome (osteomas, desmoids) and Turcot syndrome (medulloblastoma). The I1307K variant in Ashkenazi Jews moderately increases risk.
- Somatic: truncating mutations in ~80% of sporadic colorectal cancers, clustered in the 'mutation cluster region' (codons ~1286–1513); APC loss is the first step ('gatekeeper') of Vogelstein's adenoma–carcinoma sequence. Also in gastric and some hepatoblastomas (FAP patients have increased hepatoblastoma risk).
- History: cloned in 1991 (Kinzler et al., Groden et al., Nishisho et al.).
- Clinic: genetic testing in polyposis; no targeted therapy; WNT pathway activation is a downstream feature.

attrs.mnemonic: Vogelstein sequence 'A-K-S-P': APC first (adenoma), then KRAS, then SMAD4/18q loss, then TP53 (carcinoma).
attrs.anecdote: Bert Vogelstein and Eric Fearon's 1990 model of stepwise colorectal carcinogenesis (APC → KRAS → 18q → TP53), often drawn as the 'Vogelgram', became the template for multistep cancer development.
attrs.full_name: APC regulator of WNT signaling pathway

items.gloss_md: A large scaffold protein of the β-catenin destruction complex that targets β-catenin for degradation and also binds microtubules.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *APC*; 2843 amino acids (~310 kDa). Regions: N-terminal oligomerisation domain, armadillo repeats, three 15-amino-acid and seven 20-amino-acid repeats that bind β-catenin, three SAMP repeats that bind AXIN, and a C-terminal basic domain binding microtubules and EB1.

- Wnt pathway: together with AXIN1/2, GSK3β and CK1α forms the destruction complex. CK1α phosphorylates β-catenin at Ser45, then GSK3β at Thr41, Ser37 and Ser33, creating a degron recognised by the E3 ligase β-TrCP → proteasomal degradation. APC helps shuttle and ubiquitinate β-catenin.
- Cancer-associated truncations remove the SAMP repeats and most 20-aa repeats, so β-catenin is no longer degraded, accumulates in the nucleus and activates TCF/LEF targets (MYC, CCND1, AXIN2, LGR5).
- Non-Wnt functions: microtubule stability, kinetochore attachment and chromosome segregation (APC loss contributes to chromosomal instability), cell migration.

attrs.mnemonic: Destruction complex = 'A-A-G-C': APC, AXIN, GSK3β, CK1α – together they mark β-catenin for the proteasome.

items.gloss_md: The founding anti-apoptotic oncogene, activated by the t(14;18) translocation in follicular lymphoma and targeted by venetoclax.
items.body_md:
Located on 18q21.33; name from *B-cell lymphoma 2*.

- Alterations: the t(14;18)(q32;q21) translocation places BCL2 under the immunoglobulin heavy-chain (IGH) enhancer in ~85–90% of follicular lymphomas and in a subset of diffuse large B-cell lymphomas ('double-hit' with MYC). In chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL), BCL2 is overexpressed largely because deletion of 13q14 removes the repressive microRNAs miR-15a/miR-16-1.
- History: cloned from the t(14;18) breakpoint in 1984–85 (Tsujimoto, Croce lab; Cleary & Sklar; Bakhshi, Korsmeyer). In 1988 Vaux, Cory and Adams showed that BCL2 promotes cell survival rather than proliferation – the first oncogene acting by blocking cell death, opening the field of apoptosis in cancer.
- Clinic: BCL2 IHC (with CD10) helps distinguish follicular lymphoma from reactive follicles. Venetoclax, a selective BH3 mimetic, was approved in 2016 for CLL (initially with del(17p)) and is used with azacitidine in AML; it can cause tumour lysis syndrome.

attrs.mnemonic: IGH on 14 is the 'loudspeaker' in both lymphoma translocations: t(8;14) turns up MYC (Burkitt, fast), t(14;18) turns up BCL2 (follicular, slow – cells just refuse to die).
attrs.anecdote: Venetoclax was designed by structure-based drug design (Abbvie/Genentech, Walter and Eliza Hall Institute in Melbourne – the same institute where BCL2's survival function was found in 1988).

items.gloss_md: The prototypic anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family protein that binds pro-apoptotic BH3 proteins and BAX/BAK to prevent mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilisation.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *BCL2*; 239 amino acids (BCL-2α isoform). Contains four BCL-2 homology domains (BH1–BH4) and a C-terminal transmembrane anchor inserting into the outer mitochondrial membrane, endoplasmic reticulum and nuclear envelope.

- Mechanism: BH1–BH3 form a hydrophobic groove that captures the BH3 α-helix of activator and sensitiser BH3-only proteins (BIM, PUMA, BAD, BID) and of activated BAX/BAK. This prevents BAX/BAK oligomerisation, mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilisation (MOMP), cytochrome c release and caspase activation – the intrinsic apoptosis pathway.
- Cells 'primed' for death have BCL-2 loaded with BIM; BH3 mimetics displace BIM and trigger rapid apoptosis (measurable by BH3 profiling).
- Venetoclax binds the BCL-2 groove with sub-nanomolar affinity and spares BCL-xL, avoiding the thrombocytopenia of the older dual inhibitor navitoclax.
- Also regulates ER calcium and autophagy (via Beclin-1 binding).

attrs.mnemonic: Anti-apoptotic 'guardians' are B-C-M: BCL-2, BCL-xL, MCL-1 (plus BCL-w, A1); pro-apoptotic effectors are BAX and BAK – 'BAX and BAK make holes in the mitochondrion's back'.

items.gloss_md: An oncogene encoding β-catenin; activating exon 3 mutations drive WNT signalling in about a quarter of hepatocellular carcinomas and in many other tumours.
items.body_md:
Located on 3p22.1; encodes β-catenin.

- Alterations: gain-of-function mutations or in-frame deletions in exon 3 affecting the N-terminal phosphodegron (D32, S33, G34, S37, T41, S45), which prevent recognition by the destruction complex. Frequencies: ~25–30% of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC; often co-occurring with TERT promoter mutations, mutually exclusive with AXIN1 mutations), the majority of hepatoblastomas, the β-catenin-activated subtype of hepatocellular adenoma (risk of malignant transformation, especially exon 3 S45-sparing deletions), >90% of solid pseudopapillary neoplasms of the pancreas, sporadic desmoid tumours (T41A, S45F), endometrioid endometrial and ovarian carcinomas, adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma.
- Liver pathology: CTNNB1-mutant HCC tends to be well differentiated, cholestatic, with diffuse glutamine synthetase (GLUL) IHC staining, and is often immune-excluded ('cold').
- Clinic: nuclear β-catenin IHC and diffuse glutamine synthetase serve as surrogate markers; no approved direct inhibitor.

attrs.mnemonic: Liver zonation: β-catenin is 'pericentral' – glutamine synthetase (a β-catenin target) is normally only in the hepatocytes around the central vein; diffuse GS staining = activated β-catenin.
attrs.anecdote: Its Drosophila homologue is 'armadillo' – fly embryos lacking it have a denticle lawn resembling the armour of an armadillo; hence β-catenin's 'armadillo repeats'.

items.gloss_md: A dual-function armadillo-repeat protein that links E-cadherin to the actin cytoskeleton at adherens junctions and acts as the nuclear co-activator of canonical WNT signalling.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *CTNNB1*; 781 amino acids. N-terminal region with the phosphodegron, 12 central armadillo repeats (binding E-cadherin, APC, AXIN, TCF/LEF) and a C-terminal transactivation domain.

- Adherens junctions: binds the cytoplasmic tail of E-cadherin and α-catenin.
- Wnt off: the destruction complex (APC, AXIN1/2, GSK3β, CK1α) phosphorylates the free cytoplasmic pool (S45, then T41/S37/S33) → β-TrCP ubiquitination → proteasome.
- Wnt on: Wnt ligand binds Frizzled and LRP5/6 → Dishevelled recruits AXIN to the receptor → destruction complex is inhibited → β-catenin accumulates, enters the nucleus, displaces Groucho/TLE from TCF/LEF (e.g. TCF7L2) and with CBP/p300, BCL9 and Pygo activates targets such as MYC, CCND1, AXIN2, LGR5, and in liver GLUL and other pericentral genes.
- Nuclear localisation by IHC indicates active WNT signalling (e.g. desmoid tumours, colorectal cancer).

attrs.mnemonic: Two jobs, two places: at the membrane it is 'glue' (E-cadherin), in the nucleus it is 'gas' (TCF co-activator).

items.gloss_md: The gene of the catalytic subunit of telomerase; TERT promoter mutations are the most frequent non-coding mutations in cancer and an early event in hepatocellular carcinoma.
items.body_md:
Located on 5p15.33 near the telomere of 5p. Normally silenced in most somatic cells; reactivated in ~85–90% of cancers.

- Alterations: two mutually exclusive promoter hotspots, C228T and C250T (−124 and −146 bp upstream of the start codon), create new binding sites for ETS transcription factors (GABPA) and reactivate transcription. Discovered in melanoma in 2013 (Huang et al.; Horn et al.). Very frequent in glioblastoma (IDH-wild-type), melanoma, urothelial carcinoma and HCC (~60%), where they appear already in cirrhotic dysplastic nodules; other mechanisms are TERT amplification, rearrangements, and HBV DNA integration into the TERT promoter in HCC.
- Cancers without telomerase use alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT), typically with ATRX/DAXX loss.
- Germline loss-of-function variants cause telomere biology disorders (dyskeratosis congenita, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, aplastic anaemia, cryptogenic cirrhosis).
- Clinic: in WHO CNS5, a TERT promoter mutation in an IDH-wild-type diffuse astrocytoma qualifies as glioblastoma. Imetelstat, an oligonucleotide telomerase inhibitor, was approved in 2024 for lower-risk myelodysplastic syndrome.

attrs.anecdote: Telomerase was discovered in 1984 by Carol Greider (a PhD student) and Elizabeth Blackburn in the ciliate Tetrahymena, which has ~40,000 tiny chromosomes; they shared the 2009 Nobel Prize with Jack Szostak.

items.gloss_md: The catalytic reverse-transcriptase subunit of telomerase, which adds TTAGGG repeats to chromosome ends using its RNA template TERC.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *TERT*; 1132 amino acids. Domains: TEN (telomerase essential N-terminal), TRBD (binds the telomerase RNA), the reverse transcriptase domain and the C-terminal extension (thumb).

- Holoenzyme: TERT plus the RNA component TERC (hTR, containing the template 3'-CAAUCCCAAUC-5'), dyskerin–NOP10–NHP2–GAR1 (H/ACA RNP that stabilises TERC) and TCAB1 (Cajal body localisation). The shelterin protein TPP1 recruits telomerase to telomeres.
- Function: extends the 3' G-rich overhang that DNA polymerase cannot fully replicate (end-replication problem), counteracting telomere shortening.
- Expression: high in germ cells, stem and progenitor cells, activated lymphocytes; absent in most differentiated somatic cells, so their telomeres shorten until they reach the Hayflick limit and enter senescence (or crisis).
- Cancer: TERT expression is limiting for telomerase activity and enables replicative immortality, a hallmark of cancer. TERT peptides were tested as cancer vaccines.

attrs.mnemonic: Telomerase brings its own template: TERT is the 'pen', TERC the 'stencil' with the TTAGGG pattern.

items.gloss_md: An oncogene encoding the ABL1 tyrosine kinase; fused to BCR on the Philadelphia chromosome in chronic myeloid leukaemia, the paradigm of targeted therapy with imatinib.
items.body_md:
Located on 9q34.12; homologue of v-abl of the Abelson murine leukaemia virus. Two isoforms (1a and 1b) arise from alternative first exons; 1b is N-myristoylated.

- Alterations: the reciprocal translocation t(9;22)(q34;q11) fuses BCR (22q11) upstream of ABL1 exon 2, creating the BCR::ABL1 fusion gene on the shortened chromosome 22, the Philadelphia chromosome. Present in ~95% of chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML), ~25% of adult and ~3% of paediatric B-ALL; rare ABL1 fusions with other partners (e.g. NUP214) in T-ALL and Ph-like ALL.
- History: the Philadelphia chromosome was described in 1960 by Peter Nowell and David Hungerford in Philadelphia – the first consistent chromosomal abnormality in a human cancer; Janet Rowley showed in 1973 that it results from a translocation.
- Drugs: imatinib (STI571; Brian Druker, Novartis; approved 2001) transformed CML into a chronic disease with near-normal life expectancy; second-generation nilotinib, dasatinib, bosutinib; ponatinib for the T315I gatekeeper mutation; asciminib, an allosteric inhibitor binding the myristoyl pocket.

attrs.mnemonic: Philadelphia 9;22 – '9 to 22, the CML commute': ABL from 9, BCR from 22; 'BCR in front, ABL behind'.
attrs.anecdote: Imatinib made the cover of TIME magazine in May 2001 as a 'magic bullet' after it was approved by the FDA in record time (less than 3 months).

items.gloss_md: A non-receptor tyrosine kinase involved in cytoskeletal remodelling and the DNA damage response, kept inactive by an autoinhibitory myristoyl clamp.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *ABL1*; isoform 1b has 1149 amino acids. Domains: N-terminal cap (myristoylated in 1b), SH3, SH2, tyrosine kinase domain, and a long C-terminal region with nuclear localisation and export signals and DNA- and F-actin-binding domains.

- Autoinhibition: the myristoyl group binds a hydrophobic pocket in the C-lobe of the kinase domain, and the SH3 and SH2 domains clamp the kinase in an inactive conformation (similar to SRC).
- Functions: shuttles between cytoplasm and nucleus; cytoplasmic ABL1 regulates actin dynamics, cell spreading and migration; nuclear ABL1 is activated by ATM after DNA damage and contributes to p73-mediated apoptosis.
- Paralog ABL2 (ARG).
- Kinase inhibitors bind the ATP site in specific conformations (imatinib binds the 'DFG-out' inactive state); asciminib occupies the myristoyl pocket and restores autoinhibition.

items.gloss_md: The breakpoint cluster region gene on chromosome 22 that fuses with ABL1 to form the BCR::ABL1 oncogene of the Philadelphia chromosome.
items.body_md:
Located on 22q11.23; the name *breakpoint cluster region* reflects the small region of chromosome 22 where translocation breakpoints in CML cluster.

- Normal function: encodes a multidomain protein with an N-terminal coiled-coil oligomerisation domain, a serine/threonine kinase activity, a Rho guanine nucleotide exchange factor (DH–PH) domain and a C-terminal GTPase-activating protein (GAP) domain for RAC.
- Breakpoints and fusion proteins: major breakpoint (M-bcr, exon 13 or 14 → e13a2/e14a2 transcripts) → p210 BCR::ABL1 in nearly all CML; minor breakpoint (m-bcr, after exon 1 → e1a2) → p190 in most Ph+ ALL; micro breakpoint (μ-bcr, e19a2) → p230 in rare neutrophilic CML.
- Clinic: quantitative RT-PCR of BCR::ABL1 transcripts normalised to the International Scale (IS) is the standard CML monitoring; major molecular response (MMR) = ≤0.1% IS; deep, durable responses allow attempts at treatment-free remission. FISH and karyotyping detect the translocation.

attrs.mnemonic: Fusion sizes: 'p210 for the Chronic patient (CML), p190 for the Acute one (ALL)' – the bigger one is the slower disease.
attrs.full_name: BCR activator of RhoGEF and GTPase

items.gloss_md: A constitutively active chimeric tyrosine kinase produced by the Philadelphia chromosome that drives chronic myeloid leukaemia and Ph-positive ALL.
items.body_md:
Product of the *BCR::ABL1* fusion gene from t(9;22)(q34;q11). Depending on the BCR breakpoint it is 190, 210 or 230 kDa (p190, p210, p230); all contain the ABL1 SH3, SH2 and kinase domains but lack the ABL1 myristoylated N-cap.

- Activation: the BCR coiled-coil domain drives oligomerisation and trans-autophosphorylation, while loss of the autoinhibitory N-cap keeps the kinase on. The fusion is cytoplasmic.
- Signalling: phosphorylated Tyr177 of BCR recruits GRB2–GAB2–SOS → RAS–MAPK and PI3K–AKT; also STAT5 (survival, proliferation), CRKL (adhesion). It confers growth-factor independence on haematopoietic progenitors.
- Inhibitors: imatinib, nilotinib, dasatinib, bosutinib (ATP site), ponatinib (also T315I), asciminib (allosteric, myristoyl pocket); combinations of ATP-site and allosteric inhibitors are under study.
- Resistance: kinase-domain mutations (T315I gatekeeper, P-loop mutations), BCR::ABL1 amplification.
- Phospho-CRKL is a pharmacodynamic readout of kinase activity.

attrs.anecdote: The Philadelphia chromosome (1960) was the first chromosomal abnormality consistently linked to a human cancer, and its product BCR::ABL1 became the first kinase successfully targeted by a rationally developed small molecule, imatinib (2001).

items.gloss_md: An oncogene encoding the receptor tyrosine kinase ALK; activated by fusions (EML4-ALK in lung cancer, NPM1-ALK in anaplastic large-cell lymphoma) and point mutations in neuroblastoma.
items.body_md:
Located on 2p23.2; name *anaplastic lymphoma kinase*.

- Alterations: fusions with an N-terminal partner providing an oligomerisation domain: NPM1::ALK from t(2;5)(p23;q35) in ~80% of ALK-positive anaplastic large-cell lymphoma (ALCL), where ALK was discovered in 1994 (Morris et al.); EML4::ALK from a small inversion inv(2)(p21p23) in ~3–7% of NSCLC (described 2007, Soda et al.), typically adenocarcinomas of younger never-smokers; fusions also in inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour and rarely in KRAS-wild-type PDAC. Activating kinase-domain point mutations (F1174L, R1275Q) in neuroblastoma, germline in familial neuroblastoma.
- Testing: IHC (clone D5F3 or 5A4), FISH break-apart probe, RNA-based NGS.
- Drugs: crizotinib (approved 2011, a MET inhibitor that turned out to hit ALK), ceritinib, alectinib, brigatinib, lorlatinib (active against the G1202R solvent-front resistance mutation and in the brain). ALK-positive NSCLC patients now often survive many years.

attrs.mnemonic: ALK partners: 'ELM-tree in the lung (EML4), NPM in the lymphoma (NPM1)'.
attrs.anecdote: Crizotinib was originally developed as a MET inhibitor; the 2007 discovery of EML4-ALK led to its approval for ALK-positive lung cancer only four years later.

items.gloss_md: A receptor tyrosine kinase of the insulin-receptor superfamily, normally expressed in the developing nervous system, that becomes a constitutively active oncoprotein when fused or mutated.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *ALK*; 1620 amino acids. Extracellular region with two MAM domains, an LDLa domain and a glycine-rich region; single transmembrane helix; intracellular tyrosine kinase domain related to LTK and the insulin receptor.

- Ligands: ALKAL1 and ALKAL2 (formerly FAM150A/B, 'augmentors'); its role in adults is limited, which partly explains the tolerability of ALK inhibitors.
- Oncogenic fusions: the partner (EML4 coiled-coil, NPM1 oligomerisation domain, and many others) causes ligand-independent dimerisation; the fusion is cytoplasmic (NPM1–ALK also nuclear, explaining nuclear plus cytoplasmic ALK IHC in ALCL).
- Downstream: STAT3 (especially in ALCL), PI3K–AKT, RAS–MAPK, PLCγ.
- ALK protein expression detected by IHC is a reliable surrogate for ALK rearrangement in lung adenocarcinoma.

items.gloss_md: A complex imprinted locus encoding the stimulatory G-protein α subunit Gsα; activating R201 mutations characterise IPMN of the pancreas and McCune–Albright syndrome.
items.body_md:
Located on 20q13.32. A complex, imprinted locus: alternative promoters and first exons produce Gsα (biallelically expressed in most tissues, maternally in some, e.g. renal proximal tubule), XLαs, NESP55 and non-coding transcripts.

- Activating mutations (the 'gsp oncogene') at codon R201 (R201H/C) and less often Q227 abolish GTP hydrolysis. Found in ~40–70% of intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMN) of the pancreas – together with KRAS the molecular hallmark of IPMN and IPMN-derived carcinoma, rare in conventional PDAC – and in low-grade appendiceal mucinous neoplasms (pseudomyxoma peritonei), GH-secreting pituitary adenomas (~40%), and fibrous dysplasia.
- Postzygotic mosaic R201 mutations cause McCune–Albright syndrome (polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, café-au-lait spots, precocious puberty).
- Inactivating germline mutations cause Albright hereditary osteodystrophy and pseudohypoparathyroidism, with parent-of-origin effects due to imprinting.
- Clinic: GNAS and KRAS testing of pancreatic cyst fluid (EUS-FNA) helps classify mucinous cysts.

attrs.mnemonic: (de) GNAS macht Schleim: eine GNAS-Mutation spricht für eine muzinöse Zyste (IPMN) bzw. eine muzinöse Appendixneoplasie.
attrs.anecdote: Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates exactly the same residue, Arg201 of Gsα, that is mutated in tumours – the toxin creates a 'chemical gsp mutation', flooding intestinal cells with cAMP.

items.gloss_md: The α subunit of the stimulatory heterotrimeric G protein that couples GPCRs to adenylyl cyclase and cAMP production.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *GNAS*; 394 amino acids (long form; a short form lacks exon 3 residues). Contains a Ras-like GTPase domain and an α-helical domain that buries the bound nucleotide.

- Cycle: an activated G-protein-coupled receptor (e.g. β-adrenergic, TSH, GHRH, PTH, glucagon receptors) acts as GEF and exchanges GDP for GTP; Gsα–GTP dissociates from Gβγ and activates adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → protein kinase A (PKA) and EPAC. Intrinsic GTPase activity (accelerated by RGS proteins) terminates the signal.
- R201 and Q227 are catalytic residues; their mutation keeps Gsα GTP-bound and cAMP permanently high.
- Toxins: cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates R201 (constitutive activation); pertussis toxin ADP-ribosylates Gαi (blocks inhibition).
- In IPMN, constitutive cAMP–PKA signalling promotes mucin production and papillary growth.

aliases: Guanine nucleotide-binding protein G(s) subunit alpha

items.gloss_md: A tumour suppressor encoding a transmembrane E3 ubiquitin ligase that removes Frizzled WNT receptors from the cell surface; mutated in pancreatic cystic neoplasms, some PDAC and MSI colorectal cancer.
items.body_md:
Located on 17q22; itself a WNT/β-catenin target gene (negative feedback), like its homologue *ZNRF3*.

- Alterations: truncating mutations in IPMN and mucinous cystic neoplasms of the pancreas, ~5–10% of PDAC, MSI-high colorectal, endometrial and gastric cancers (the frameshift G659fs in a mononucleotide repeat is common in MSI tumours), and serrated-pathway colorectal tumours. Rare germline variants are associated with serrated polyposis syndrome.
- Biology: RNF43-mutant cells have more Frizzled at the surface and become hypersensitive to WNT ligands, but – unlike APC- or CTNNB1-mutant cells – they still depend on WNT secretion.
- Clinic: this ligand dependence makes RNF43-mutant PDAC a candidate for porcupine inhibitors (which block WNT secretion, e.g. WNT974) and anti-Frizzled antibodies (trials). R-spondin (RSPO2/3) fusions in colorectal cancer have an equivalent effect.

attrs.mnemonic: RNF43 and ZNRF3 are the 'WNT receptor bouncers' – they throw Frizzled out; R-spondin (via LGR5) ties up the bouncers.

items.gloss_md: A transmembrane RING-type E3 ubiquitin ligase that ubiquitinates Frizzled and LRP6, triggering their endocytosis and degradation.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *RNF43*; 783 amino acids. Domains: extracellular protease-associated (PA) domain that binds Frizzled, single transmembrane helix, intracellular RING finger E3 ligase domain and a long C-terminal tail.

- Function: ubiquitinates the cytoplasmic loops of Frizzled receptors (and LRP6), leading to their internalisation and lysosomal degradation; this limits sensitivity to WNT ligands. In intestinal stem cells it restricts WNT signalling to the stem cell niche.
- Antagonism: R-spondins (RSPO1–4) bind both LGR4/5 and RNF43/ZNRF3 and induce clearance of the ligases from the membrane, thereby potentiating WNT signalling.
- Homologue: ZNRF3; double knockout in mouse intestine produces adenomas.
- Cancer mutants lose ligase activity or membrane function, raising surface Frizzled levels.

items.gloss_md: A hereditary breast and pancreatic cancer gene encoding PALB2, which bridges BRCA1 and BRCA2 in homologous recombination.
items.body_md:
Located on 16p12.2; also called *FANCN*.

- Germline: heterozygous loss-of-function variants confer a high breast cancer risk (estimated around 35% by age 70) and increased pancreatic and ovarian cancer risk; biallelic variants cause Fanconi anaemia complementation group N with early childhood cancers. PALB2 is part of all standard hereditary breast/pancreatic cancer gene panels.
- History: identified as a BRCA2-binding partner in 2006 (Xia et al., Livingston lab); in 2009 Jones et al. (Johns Hopkins) found truncating PALB2 variants by exome sequencing of a patient with familial pancreatic cancer – one of the first disease genes discovered by exome sequencing.
- Somatic: rare (~1%) in PDAC.
- Clinic: tumours with biallelic PALB2 loss are homologous-recombination deficient and sensitive to platinum and PARP inhibitors (evidence from phase II trials in pancreatic and breast cancer).

attrs.mnemonic: PALB2 = 'PAL of BRCA2' – BRCA2's best friend that brings it to BRCA1.

items.gloss_md: A scaffold protein that links BRCA1 to BRCA2 at DNA double-strand breaks, enabling RAD51 loading during homologous recombination.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *PALB2*; 1186 amino acids. N-terminal coiled-coil (binds BRCA1 coiled-coil; also self-oligomerises), a chromatin-association motif (ChAM) and a C-terminal WD40 β-propeller that binds BRCA2.

- Function: BRCA1 recruits PALB2 to resected double-strand breaks; PALB2 in turn brings BRCA2, which loads RAD51 onto ssDNA. The BRCA1–PALB2–BRCA2 axis is therefore a linear chain, and loss of any member produces a similar HRD phenotype.
- PALB2 also binds RAD51 directly, protects stalled replication forks and is regulated by KEAP1–CUL3-mediated ubiquitination in G1, which prevents BRCA1 binding outside S/G2.

items.gloss_md: A tumour suppressor encoding the ATM kinase, the master sensor of DNA double-strand breaks; biallelic loss causes ataxia-telangiectasia and heterozygous variants increase breast and pancreatic cancer risk.
items.body_md:
Located on 11q22.3; name from *ataxia-telangiectasia mutated*.

- Germline: biallelic mutations cause ataxia-telangiectasia (A-T): progressive cerebellar ataxia, oculocutaneous telangiectasias, immunodeficiency, extreme sensitivity to ionising radiation and a high risk of lymphoma and leukaemia. Heterozygous carriers (~1% of the population) have a moderately increased risk of breast cancer and of PDAC; germline ATM variants are found in ~1–3% of PDAC patients.
- Somatic: deletion of 11q22–23 or mutation in CLL (poor prognosis), mantle cell lymphoma, T-prolymphocytic leukaemia; mutations in ~5% of PDAC and in prostate, lung and colorectal cancer.
- History: cloned in 1995 by Yosef Shiloh's group (Savitsky et al.).
- Clinic: ATM loss is a candidate biomarker for PARP and ATR inhibitor sensitivity (synthetic lethality), studied in trials; A-T patients must avoid radiotherapy at standard doses.

attrs.mnemonic: ATM answers double-strand breaks, ATR answers Replication stress (RPA-coated single strands): ATM → CHK2, ATR → CHK1 ('M-2, R-1').

items.gloss_md: A large PI3K-like serine/threonine kinase that is activated by DNA double-strand breaks and phosphorylates hundreds of substrates to coordinate checkpoints and repair.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *ATM*; 3056 amino acids (~350 kDa). Member of the PIKK family (with ATR, DNA-PKcs, mTOR); N-terminal HEAT repeats, FAT, kinase and FATC domains; prefers Ser/Thr-Gln (S/TQ) motifs.

- Activation: the MRE11–RAD50–NBS1 (MRN) complex senses double-strand breaks and recruits ATM; inactive ATM dimers autophosphorylate (Ser1981) and dissociate into active monomers (Bakkenist and Kastan, 2003).
- Key substrates: histone H2AX (Ser139 → γH2AX, which spreads over megabases around the break), CHK2 (Thr68), p53 (Ser15), MDM2, BRCA1, KAP1 (chromatin relaxation), NBS1.
- Outcomes: G1/S arrest via CHK2–p53–p21, intra-S and G2/M checkpoints, DNA end resection, apoptosis or senescence.
- ATM also senses oxidative stress as a disulfide-linked dimer independently of DNA damage.

attrs.mnemonic: ATM is the 'cash machine' of the DNA damage response: insert a double-strand break and it pays out phosphates to p53, CHK2 and H2AX.

items.gloss_md: A tumour suppressor encoding ARID1A (BAF250a), a SWI/SNF chromatin-remodelling subunit; among the most frequently mutated epigenetic regulators in cancer, including PDAC, HCC and ovarian clear cell carcinoma.
items.body_md:
Located on 1p36.11; encodes ARID1A, also called BAF250a.

- Alterations: mostly truncating (nonsense, frameshift) mutations, leading to loss of protein. Frequencies: ~50% of ovarian clear cell carcinomas and ~30% of ovarian endometrioid carcinomas (both endometriosis-associated; reported in 2010), endometrial carcinoma, gastric cancer (MSI and EBV subtypes), urothelial carcinoma, ~5–10% of PDAC, ~5–15% of HCC and cholangiocarcinoma.
- SWI/SNF genes together (ARID1A, ARID1B, ARID2, PBRM1, SMARCA4, SMARCB1, …) are mutated in ~20% of all human cancers.
- Clinic: loss of ARID1A by IHC is a surrogate for mutation. Synthetic-lethal vulnerabilities under investigation include EZH2 inhibitors (tazemetostat), ATR inhibitors and dependence on the paralogue ARID1B. ARID1A loss has been linked to mismatch-repair defects and immunotherapy responsiveness, but this is not an established biomarker.

attrs.mnemonic: ARID1A defines canonical BAF, ARID2 defines PBAF: 'one for cBAF, two for PBAF'.

items.gloss_md: A large DNA-binding subunit of the canonical BAF (SWI/SNF) chromatin-remodelling complex that targets it to enhancers.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *ARID1A*; 2285 amino acids. Contains an AT-rich interaction domain (ARID, non-sequence-specific DNA binding) and a C-terminal domain that docks onto the SMARCA4/SMARCA2 ATPase core.

- Complex: the mammalian SWI/SNF family has three forms: canonical BAF (cBAF, with ARID1A or ARID1B), polybromo-associated PBAF (with ARID2, PBRM1, BRD7) and non-canonical ncBAF (GLTSCR1/BRD9). They use ATP hydrolysis to slide or evict nucleosomes, opening chromatin.
- ARID1A-containing cBAF maintains accessibility at enhancers, cooperating with lineage transcription factors and AP-1; ARID1A also participates in DNA damage repair and checkpoint control.
- Loss leaves ARID1B-containing complexes, creating a paralogue dependency.

items.gloss_md: An X-linked tumour suppressor encoding the H3K27 demethylase UTX; frequently mutated in bladder cancer and in PDAC, where loss is linked to the squamous subtype.
items.body_md:
Located on Xp11.3; encodes UTX ('ubiquitously transcribed tetratricopeptide repeat, X chromosome'). It escapes X inactivation, so females express two copies; the Y-linked paralogue *UTY* encodes a protein with weak demethylase activity that partly compensates in males.

- Alterations: truncating mutations or deletions in ~25% of urothelial carcinomas, ~5–10% of PDAC, T-ALL and multiple myeloma.
- PDAC: KDM6A loss has been associated with the aggressive squamous (basal-like) subtype; in mouse models its loss accelerated tumourigenesis especially in females (Andricovich et al., 2018).
- Germline: de novo variants cause Kabuki syndrome type 2 (type 1 is KMT2D – the two are partners in the same complex).
- Clinic: loss of UTX makes cells dependent on EZH2-mediated H3K27 methylation balance; EZH2 inhibitors are a proposed strategy.

attrs.mnemonic: UTX removes the K27 'silence' mark that EZH2 writes – 'EZH2 writes, UTX/JMJD3 erase'.

items.gloss_md: A Jumonji-C histone demethylase that removes di- and trimethyl marks from histone H3 lysine 27, counteracting Polycomb silencing.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *KDM6A*; 1401 amino acids. N-terminal tetratricopeptide repeats (TPR, protein interactions) and a C-terminal JmjC catalytic domain (Fe(II)- and 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase).

- Function: demethylates H3K27me3/me2, activating Polycomb (PRC2/EZH2)-repressed genes; KDM6B (JMJD3) is its paralogue.
- Complex: part of the COMPASS-like complex with KMT2C/KMT2D (MLL3/MLL4), which monomethylates H3K4 at enhancers; UTX also recruits p300 for H3K27 acetylation, so it activates enhancers partly independently of its catalytic activity.
- As a 2-oxoglutarate-dependent enzyme it can be inhibited by the oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate (IDH mutant tumours).

items.gloss_md: A frequently mutated epigenetic tumour suppressor encoding MLL3, an enhancer H3K4 monomethyltransferase, mutated in many carcinomas including PDAC.
items.body_md:
Located on 7q36.1; previously *MLL3*. Encodes MLL3 (KMT2C).

- Alterations: mostly truncating mutations across many carcinomas – breast, bladder, gastric, colorectal and ~5–10% of PDAC; also frequent in large sequencing studies partly because of its size (care with passenger mutations and a segmental duplication that causes alignment artefacts).
- Biology: as part of the COMPASS-like complex with KDM6A (UTX), KMT2C marks and activates enhancers; loss impairs enhancer activation of differentiation and tumour-suppressive programmes (e.g. in mouse models it cooperates with p53 loss).
- Nomenclature trap: the KMT2 family was renamed in 2013: KMT2A = MLL1, KMT2B = MLL2 (old MLL4), KMT2C = MLL3, KMT2D = MLL4 (old MLL2), KMT2E = MLL5.
- No targeted therapy.

attrs.mnemonic: KMT2 letters → MLL numbers: A=1, C=3 (easy), but B and D are swapped: B=2 and D=4 ('B-D are the troublemakers').

items.gloss_md: A very large SET-domain histone methyltransferase that monomethylates H3K4 at enhancers as part of the COMPASS-like complex.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *KMT2C*; 4911 amino acids. Contains multiple PHD fingers, an HMG box, FYR domains and a C-terminal SET domain with catalytic activity.

- Function: deposits H3K4me1 (and some H3K4me2), the characteristic mark of primed and active enhancers. Together with UTX (KDM6A), PTIP, PA1, NCOA6 and the WRAD core (WDR5, RBBP5, ASH2L, DPY30) it forms the COMPASS-like complex that recruits p300/CBP for H3K27 acetylation.
- MLL3 and MLL4 are partly redundant; double knockout prevents enhancer activation during differentiation (e.g. adipogenesis).

items.gloss_md: An epigenetic tumour suppressor encoding MLL4, an enhancer H3K4 methyltransferase; one of the most frequently mutated genes in lymphoma and many solid cancers, and the main Kabuki syndrome gene.
items.body_md:
Located on 12q13.12; previously *MLL2* (and also called *ALR*). Encodes MLL4 (KMT2D).

- Alterations: truncating mutations in ~80% of follicular lymphomas and ~30% of diffuse large B-cell lymphomas (early events in germinal centre B cells), medulloblastoma, and many carcinomas (oesophageal, lung squamous, bladder, PDAC ~5%).
- Germline: de novo heterozygous variants cause Kabuki syndrome type 1 (characteristic facial features with long palpebral fissures, intellectual disability), the most common cause of Kabuki syndrome; KDM6A causes type 2.
- Biology: loss impairs enhancer activation; in lymphoma it reduces expression of genes for immune signalling and differentiation in germinal centre B cells.
- No targeted therapy.

attrs.anecdote: Kabuki syndrome was named by Japanese physicians (Niikawa and Kuroki, 1981) because the facial features of affected children resemble the make-up of actors in Kabuki theatre.

items.gloss_md: A large SET-domain H3K4 monomethyltransferase that, with UTX, activates enhancers and is essential for cell-type-specific gene programmes.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *KMT2D*; 5537 amino acids, one of the largest human proteins. Multiple PHD fingers, an HMG box, FYR domains and a C-terminal SET domain.

- Function: catalyses H3K4 monomethylation at enhancers within the COMPASS-like complex (with UTX/KDM6A, PTIP, PA1, NCOA6 and WRAD core), enabling recruitment of p300/CBP and enhancer–promoter communication; partially redundant with MLL3.
- Required for differentiation of adipocytes, myocytes, B cells and others; loss blocks lineage-specific enhancer activation.

items.gloss_md: A tumour suppressor encoding the master kinase LKB1; germline mutations cause Peutz–Jeghers syndrome and somatic loss is common in lung adenocarcinoma.
items.body_md:
Located on 19p13.3; encodes LKB1 (liver kinase B1).

- Germline: Peutz–Jeghers syndrome (PJS), autosomal dominant: hamartomatous polyps throughout the GI tract, mucocutaneous pigmentation of lips and buccal mucosa, and a high lifetime risk of cancers of the GI tract, breast, ovary (sex-cord tumours), cervix (adenoma malignum) and pancreas. Gene identified in 1998 (Hemminki et al.; Jenne et al.).
- Somatic: loss in ~15–20% of lung adenocarcinomas, frequently together with KRAS mutations and KEAP1 loss; also in cervical cancer, and rarely in PDAC.
- Clinic: KRAS/STK11 co-mutant lung adenocarcinomas are typically immunologically 'cold' and respond poorly to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade (STK11/KEAP1 as negative predictors); PJS patients need intensive surveillance including pancreas screening.

attrs.mnemonic: Peutz–Jeghers: 'Pigmented Pouting lips with Polyps' – the LKB1 syndrome.
attrs.anecdote: The syndrome is named after the Dutch physician Jan Peutz (1921) and the American Harold Jeghers (1949), who described families with lip freckles and intestinal polyps.

items.gloss_md: A master serine/threonine kinase that activates AMPK and AMPK-related kinases, linking energy status to growth control and polarity.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *STK11*; 433 amino acids. Kinase domain flanked by N- and C-terminal regulatory regions (farnesylated CAAX at the C-terminus).

- Active complex: LKB1 is active only in a heterotrimer with the pseudokinase STRAD (STRADα/β) and the scaffold MO25 (CAB39), which also relocates it from nucleus to cytoplasm.
- Substrates: phosphorylates the activation loop (Thr172) of AMPKα and 12 AMPK-related kinases (MARK1–4, SIK1–3, NUAK1/2, BRSK1/2, SNRK).
- Effects: under energy stress (high AMP/ATP) AMPK inhibits mTORC1 (by phosphorylating TSC2 and Raptor) and anabolic pathways; MARKs control cell polarity (PAR-4 is the worm homologue).
- The antidiabetic drug metformin activates AMPK in an LKB1-dependent way in the liver.

items.gloss_md: A tumour suppressor encoding the TGF-β type II receptor; inactivated by frameshift in most MSI colorectal cancers and in a subset of PDAC.
items.body_md:
Located on 3p24.1.

- Alterations: the coding sequence contains a polyadenine tract (A10, 'BAT-RII'); in mismatch-repair-deficient tumours frameshift mutations in this repeat inactivate TGFBR2 in most MSI colorectal and gastric cancers (a classic example of an MSI target gene, Markowitz et al., 1995). In PDAC, TGFBR2 or TGFBR1 is mutated in a few percent of tumours, as an alternative to SMAD4 loss in disrupting TGF-β signalling. Also mutated in head and neck SCC.
- Germline: Loeys–Dietz syndrome (aortic aneurysms and dissection, arterial tortuosity, hypertelorism, bifid uvula) via TGFBR1/2 mutations.
- Biology: loss frees epithelial cells from TGF-β-induced cytostasis while the tumour stroma remains exposed to high TGF-β levels (fibrosis, immunosuppression).
- Clinic: TGF-β pathway inhibitors (galunisertib, bintrafusp alfa) have been disappointing in trials.

attrs.mnemonic: The type II receptor is the 'boss' that phosphorylates type I (ALK5); type I then phosphorylates the SMADs – 'II comes first, then I, then SMAD'.

items.gloss_md: A constitutively active transmembrane serine/threonine kinase that binds TGF-β and phosphorylates and activates the type I receptor ALK5.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *TGFBR2*; 567 amino acids. Small cysteine-rich extracellular domain, single transmembrane helix, intracellular serine/threonine kinase domain.

- Signalling: TGF-β1, -β2 or -β3 dimers first bind TβRII (TGF-β2 needs the co-receptor betaglycan/TGFBR3); TβRII then recruits TβRI (ALK5) and phosphorylates its glycine-serine-rich (GS) domain, releasing the inhibitor FKBP12. Activated TβRI phosphorylates SMAD2 and SMAD3, which bind SMAD4.
- Non-canonical outputs: TAK1–p38/JNK, PI3K–AKT, RHO GTPases, ERK; these partly mediate the pro-invasive effects of TGF-β.
- Antibodies and ligand traps directed at the TGF-β–TβRII interaction have been tested in cancer and fibrosis.

items.gloss_md: A tumour suppressor encoding Axin-1, the concentration-limiting scaffold of the β-catenin destruction complex; inactivated in ~5–10% of hepatocellular carcinomas.
items.body_md:
Located on 16p13.3.

- Alterations: truncating mutations and homozygous deletions in ~5–10% of HCC and in hepatoblastoma, mutually exclusive with CTNNB1 mutations; also in some colorectal and other cancers.
- HCC phenotype: unlike CTNNB1-mutant HCC, AXIN1-mutant tumours usually do not show the canonical β-catenin target signature (no diffuse glutamine synthetase staining), suggesting WNT-independent functions of Axin-1; they are often less differentiated.
- Paralogue *AXIN2* (conductin) is a WNT target gene used as a readout of pathway activity; its germline mutations cause oligodontia with colorectal cancer predisposition.
- Pharmacology: tankyrase inhibitors (e.g. XAV939) stabilise Axin by preventing its poly(ADP-ribosyl)ation and degradation – an experimental strategy to dampen WNT signalling.

attrs.anecdote: Axin was first identified as the mouse 'Fused' locus (Zeng et al., 1997): mutations caused axis duplication and kinked tails – hence the name 'Axis inhibitor'.

items.gloss_md: The scaffold protein of the β-catenin destruction complex that brings together APC, GSK3β, CK1α and β-catenin.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *AXIN1*; 862 amino acids. Domains: N-terminal RGS domain (binds APC SAMP repeats), GSK3β- and β-catenin-binding regions, PP2A-binding region and a C-terminal DIX domain that polymerises and binds Dishevelled.

- Function: present at much lower concentrations than other complex components, Axin is the rate-limiting factor of the destruction complex that phosphorylates β-catenin for β-TrCP-mediated degradation.
- Wnt signalling: activated LRP5/6 (phosphorylated PPPSPxS motifs) and Dishevelled recruit Axin to the membrane, inactivating the complex and stabilising β-catenin.
- Turnover: tankyrase PARylates Axin, leading to RNF146-mediated ubiquitination and degradation.

items.gloss_md: A tumour suppressor encoding ARID2 (BAF200), the defining subunit of the PBAF chromatin-remodelling complex; mutated in hepatocellular carcinoma and melanoma.
items.body_md:
Located on 12q12; encodes ARID2, also called BAF200.

- Alterations: inactivating mutations in ~5–10% of HCC (first reported in HCV-associated HCC in 2011), melanoma and NSCLC. In HCC, ARID1A, ARID2 and other SWI/SNF genes are collectively mutated in ~20% of tumours.
- Germline: de novo heterozygous loss-of-function variants cause a Coffin–Siris-like intellectual disability syndrome.
- Biology: ARID2 loss impairs PBAF function; in mouse liver it cooperates with oncogenes in HCC formation and affects DNA repair. PBAF (with PBRM1) is required for some interferon-stimulated genes, and PBAF loss has been linked to responsiveness to immune checkpoint blockade in some cancers.

items.gloss_md: The signature DNA-binding subunit of the polybromo-associated BAF (PBAF) SWI/SNF chromatin-remodelling complex.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *ARID2*; 1835 amino acids. N-terminal ARID DNA-binding domain, RFX-like domain and C-terminal C2H2 zinc fingers.

- Complex: PBAF contains ARID2, PBRM1 (polybromo, six bromodomains) and BRD7, plus the shared ATPase SMARCA4/SMARCA2 and core subunits; ARID2 incorporation is mutually exclusive with ARID1A/B (cBAF).
- Function: ATP-dependent nucleosome remodelling at promoters and enhancers; roles in interferon-γ responses, centromeric cohesion and DNA repair.

items.gloss_md: An oncogene encoding NRF2, the master transcription factor of the antioxidant response; activated by mutation in squamous cancers and some HCC.
items.body_md:
Located on 2q31.2; encodes NRF2 (nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2), cloned in 1994 (Moi et al.).

- Alterations: gain-of-function missense mutations or exon 2 skipping deletions that destroy the KEAP1-binding DLG and ETGE motifs in the Neh2 domain, so NRF2 escapes degradation. Frequent in lung squamous cell carcinoma (~15%), oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma, head and neck cancer, and ~5–6% of HCC; pathway activation also through KEAP1 or CUL3 loss.
