- Consequences: constitutive antioxidant and detoxification programme, metabolic rewiring (pentose phosphate pathway, glutamine use), resistance to chemotherapy and radiotherapy, poor prognosis.
- Physiology: protects liver and other organs from oxidative and electrophilic stress; Nrf2-knockout mice are highly sensitive to acetaminophen hepatotoxicity.
- Clinic: no approved NRF2 inhibitor; NRF2 activators (dimethyl fumarate, omaveloxolone for Friedreich ataxia) act via KEAP1.

attrs.mnemonic: KEAP1 'keeps' NRF2 on a leash: KEAP1 lost or NRF2 mutated → antioxidant programme always on.

items.gloss_md: A cap'n'collar bZIP transcription factor that binds antioxidant response elements and induces detoxification and antioxidant genes when released from KEAP1.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *NFE2L2*; 605 amino acids. Seven Neh domains: Neh2 contains the DLG (low-affinity) and ETGE (high-affinity) motifs for KEAP1 binding; Neh1 is the CNC-bZIP DNA-binding and dimerisation domain.

- Regulation: in unstressed cells KEAP1–CUL3 ubiquitinates NRF2 continuously (half-life ~15–20 min). Oxidants and electrophiles modify KEAP1 cysteines, NRF2 is stabilised, accumulates in the nucleus, heterodimerises with small MAF proteins and binds antioxidant response elements (ARE, TGACnnnGC).
- Targets: *NQO1*, *HMOX1*, *GCLC*/*GCLM* (glutathione synthesis), *TXNRD1*, *SRXN1*, *G6PD*, drug transporters (ABCC), *AKR1C*.
- KEAP1-independent degradation also occurs via GSK3β–β-TrCP.
- NQO1 or AKR1C expression is used as a readout of NRF2 pathway activation.

items.gloss_md: A tumour suppressor encoding KEAP1, the cysteine-rich stress sensor that targets NRF2 for degradation; lost in ~15–20% of lung adenocarcinomas.
items.body_md:
Located on 19p13.2; encodes KEAP1, identified as the NRF2 inhibitor in 1999 (Itoh et al., Yamamoto lab).

- Alterations: loss-of-function missense mutations (mainly in the Kelch domain), LOH and promoter methylation; ~15–20% of lung adenocarcinomas, often co-mutated with STK11 and KRAS, also in lung squamous cancer, HCC (rare) and papillary renal cancer. Somatic loss of the E3 ligase partner CUL3 has a similar effect.
- Clinic: KEAP1-mutant lung cancers are aggressive, radio- and chemoresistant and respond poorly to immunotherapy; they depend on glutaminolysis, making glutaminase inhibitors a tested (so far unsuccessful) strategy.
- Germline KEAP1 variants have been reported in familial multinodular goitre.

items.gloss_md: A substrate adaptor of the CUL3 E3 ubiquitin ligase that binds NRF2 and acts as a cysteine-based sensor of oxidative and electrophilic stress.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *KEAP1*; 624 amino acids. Domains: BTB (homodimerisation, CUL3 binding), intervening region (IVR) rich in reactive cysteines, and a C-terminal six-bladed Kelch β-propeller that binds the ETGE and DLG motifs of NRF2.

- Hinge-and-latch model: a KEAP1 dimer binds one NRF2 molecule via both motifs, positioning it for ubiquitination by CUL3–RBX1.
- Sensing: electrophiles and ROS modify cysteines (e.g. Cys151, Cys273, Cys288), changing the conformation so NRF2 is no longer ubiquitinated; newly synthesised NRF2 then accumulates.
- Other substrates: PALB2 (cell cycle-dependent), PGAM5; p62/SQSTM1 sequesters KEAP1 into autophagosomes (link between autophagy defects and NRF2 activation, seen in liver Mallory–Denk bodies).

items.gloss_md: A tumour suppressor encoding tuberin, the GTPase-activating protein that switches off RHEB and mTORC1; germline mutations cause tuberous sclerosis complex.
items.body_md:
Located on 16p13.3, directly adjacent to *PKD1* (contiguous TSC2–PKD1 deletions cause tuberous sclerosis with early severe polycystic kidney disease). Gene identified in 1993 (European Chromosome 16 Tuberous Sclerosis Consortium).

- Germline: tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), autosomal dominant, ~2/3 de novo; TSC2 mutations cause more severe disease than TSC1. Features: cortical tubers and epilepsy, subependymal giant cell astrocytoma (SEGA), facial angiofibromas, cardiac rhabdomyomas, renal angiomyolipomas, lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM), PEComas.
- Somatic: TSC1/TSC2 mutations in a few percent of HCC, PEComas, bladder cancer and some renal cancers.
- Clinic: mTOR inhibitors (everolimus, sirolimus) are approved for SEGA, renal angiomyolipoma, LAM and TSC-associated seizures; TSC1/2-mutant tumours can respond exceptionally to everolimus.

attrs.mnemonic: TSC1 = hamartin, TSC2 = tuberin – numerical and alphabetical order agree (1/H before 2/T).

items.gloss_md: The catalytic GTPase-activating subunit of the TSC complex that inactivates the small GTPase RHEB and thereby inhibits mTORC1.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *TSC2*; 1807 amino acids, with a C-terminal RAP-GAP domain.

- TSC complex: tuberin, hamartin (TSC1, stabilises tuberin) and TBC1D7. It converts RHEB-GTP to RHEB-GDP on lysosomes; RHEB-GTP is the direct activator of mTORC1.
- Integration hub: AKT phosphorylates tuberin (Ser939, Thr1462) and drives the TSC complex off the lysosome → mTORC1 on; ERK and RSK also inhibit it. AMPK (energy stress) and GSK3 phosphorylation activate it → mTORC1 off. Hypoxia acts via REDD1.
- Loss of tuberin leads to constitutive mTORC1 activity, increased cell size and protein synthesis, and feedback inhibition of PI3K–AKT (explaining the benign, hamartomatous nature of many TSC lesions).

items.gloss_md: An oncogene encoding cyclin D1, activated by t(11;14) in mantle cell lymphoma and by 11q13 amplification in breast, head and neck and liver cancer.
items.body_md:
Located on 11q13.3 in an amplicon that also contains *FGF19*, *FGF4*, *FGF3* and *ORAOV1*. Formerly *PRAD1* (parathyroid adenomatosis 1, rearranged with the PTH gene in parathyroid adenomas) and *BCL1*.

- Alterations: t(11;14)(q13;q32) IGH::CCND1 in nearly all mantle cell lymphomas and ~15–20% of multiple myelomas; 11q13 amplification in ~15% of breast cancers (luminal), head and neck and oesophageal SCC, and ~5% of HCC (co-amplified FGF19 drives FGFR4 signalling); overexpression without amplification is common.
- A common splice variant produces cyclin D1b, which lacks the Thr286 degradation signal and is constitutively nuclear.
- Clinic: cyclin D1 IHC (with SOX11) is diagnostic for mantle cell lymphoma; t(11;14) myeloma is particularly sensitive to venetoclax. Luminal breast cancers depend on cyclin D1–CDK4/6, the rationale for CDK4/6 inhibitors.

attrs.mnemonic: The three IGH (chr 14) lymphoma translocations in ascending order: t(8;14) MYC – Burkitt, t(11;14) CCND1 – Mantle cell, t(14;18) BCL2 – Follicular ('B-M-F').

items.gloss_md: A G1 cyclin that, induced by mitogenic signals, activates CDK4/6 to phosphorylate Rb and start cell-cycle entry.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *CCND1*; 295 amino acids. N-terminal LxCxE motif (binds Rb), cyclin box (binds CDK4/6), PEST sequence and Thr286 phosphodegron.

- Mitogen sensor: transcription is induced by RAS–ERK, WNT/β-catenin, NF-κB, STAT and oestrogen receptor signalling; its levels rise in G1 as long as mitogens are present.
- Function: binds CDK4 or CDK6 and is helped by p21/p27 (assembly factors) to form active complexes that phosphorylate Rb and sequester p21/p27 away from CDK2.
- Turnover: GSK3β phosphorylates Thr286 → nuclear export → ubiquitination by SCF ligases (FBXO31, FBX4, AMBRA1–CRL4, the latter identified in 2021) → proteasome; half-life ~30 min.
- CDK-independent roles: co-regulator of transcription factors such as oestrogen receptor.

attrs.mnemonic: Cyclin D = 'Decision' cyclin: it measures mitogen signalling and decides whether the cell commits to division (cyclin D → CDK4/6 → Rb).

items.gloss_md: An oncogene encoding the HGF receptor c-MET; activated by exon 14 skipping, amplification or germline mutation and targeted by MET inhibitors and cabozantinib.
items.body_md:
Located on 7q31.2.

- Alterations: MET exon 14 skipping mutations (splice-site mutations, ~3% of NSCLC, older patients, sarcomatoid histology) remove the juxtamembrane Tyr1003 docking site for the E3 ligase CBL, reducing receptor degradation; focal amplification (gastric, NSCLC, and a common mechanism of acquired resistance to EGFR TKIs); germline activating kinase mutations cause hereditary papillary renal carcinoma type 1 (1997); overexpression in HCC and many other cancers.
- History: identified in 1984 as the TPR::MET fusion oncogene in a chemically (MNNG) transformed osteosarcoma cell line (Cooper et al., Vande Woude lab).
- Physiology: HGF–MET signalling is essential for liver development and liver regeneration (HGF is the main hepatocyte mitogen).
- Drugs: capmatinib and tepotinib (METex14 NSCLC), crizotinib, amivantamab (EGFR–MET antibody), cabozantinib (MET/VEGFR2/AXL; approved for second-line HCC after the CELESTIAL trial). Tivantinib failed in MET-high HCC (METIV-HCC trial).

attrs.mnemonic: HGF alias 'scatter factor' makes epithelial cells scatter and invade via MET – and in the liver the same HGF–MET axis drives regeneration after hepatectomy.

items.gloss_md: A receptor tyrosine kinase for hepatocyte growth factor that drives invasive growth, scattering, survival and liver regeneration.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *MET*; synthesised as a 1390-amino-acid single-chain precursor that furin cleaves into a disulfide-linked extracellular α chain (~50 kDa) and transmembrane β chain (~145 kDa).

- Domains: SEMA domain (binds HGF), PSI domain, four IPT domains, transmembrane helix, juxtamembrane region with Tyr1003 (CBL binding, negative regulation), kinase domain with Tyr1234/1235, and a C-terminal multifunctional docking site Tyr1349/Tyr1356 that binds GAB1, GRB2, PI3K, SRC and STAT3.
- Ligand: HGF (scatter factor), secreted as inactive pro-HGF by mesenchymal cells (stellate cells in liver) and activated by proteolysis.
- Programme: 'invasive growth' – cell dissociation, migration, proliferation, survival, branching morphogenesis; essential for hepatocyte proliferation after partial hepatectomy.
- Cross-talk with EGFR, HER3 and integrins; MET IHC and gene copy number are used as biomarkers.

items.gloss_md: The gene of the master angiogenic factor VEGF-A, induced by hypoxia via HIF and targeted by bevacizumab, including in first-line HCC therapy.
items.body_md:
Located on 6p21.1. Alternative splicing of exons 6 and 7 produces isoforms with different heparin binding: VEGF121 (freely diffusible), VEGF165 (predominant, partly matrix-bound), VEGF189 and VEGF206 (matrix-bound).

- Regulation: strongly induced by hypoxia through HIF-1α/HIF-2α binding to a hypoxia response element; also by oncogenes (RAS, MYC), growth factors and loss of VHL (clear cell renal carcinoma is highly vascular).
- Alterations: focal 6p21 amplification of VEGFA in a subset of HCC (~5–10%).
- History: described as vascular permeability factor by Dvorak and colleagues (1983) and cloned as VEGF by Napoleone Ferrara (1989); Judah Folkman had proposed in 1971 that tumour growth depends on angiogenesis.
- Clinic: bevacizumab (anti-VEGF-A antibody; approved 2004 for colorectal cancer) is used in colorectal, lung, ovarian, cervical cancer and with atezolizumab as first-line therapy for advanced HCC (IMbrave150, 2020). Aflibercept (VEGF trap) and ranibizumab treat neovascular macular degeneration. Class side effects: hypertension, proteinuria, bleeding, impaired wound healing, GI perforation.

attrs.anecdote: Judah Folkman's 1971 hypothesis that tumours need to recruit their own blood vessels was ridiculed for years; bevacizumab's approval in 2004 vindicated him. Napoleone Ferrara cloned VEGF while working at Genentech.

items.gloss_md: A homodimeric secreted glycoprotein that binds VEGFR2 (and VEGFR1) on endothelial cells to drive angiogenesis and vascular permeability.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *VEGFA*; member of the cystine-knot growth factor superfamily (related to PDGF). Active as an antiparallel homodimer; the C-terminal heparin-binding domain (exons 6–7) determines matrix retention.

- Receptors: VEGFR2 (KDR) mediates most angiogenic signalling (proliferation, migration, survival, permeability); VEGFR1 (FLT1) binds with higher affinity but weak kinase activity and acts partly as a decoy (soluble sFLT1 is elevated in pre-eclampsia). Neuropilins NRP1/2 are co-receptors for VEGF165.
- Effects: endothelial sprouting via tip cells (with DLL4–Notch lateral inhibition of stalk cells), fenestration and increased permeability (hence 'vascular permeability factor' and its role in ascites and oedema).
- Family: VEGF-B, VEGF-C and VEGF-D (lymphangiogenesis via VEGFR3), PlGF.
- Measurable in serum/plasma, but not an established predictive biomarker.

attrs.mnemonic: VEGF-A isoforms are named by amino-acid length, and longer means stickier: 121 diffuses freely, 165 is partly matrix-bound, 189 and 206 stay in the matrix.

items.gloss_md: The gene of VEGFR2, the main endothelial VEGF receptor and a key target of the multikinase inhibitors used in HCC (sorafenib, lenvatinib, regorafenib, cabozantinib) and of ramucirumab.
items.body_md:
Located on 4q12 near *KIT* and *PDGFRA*. Mouse orthologue *Flk1*. The name refers to the kinase insert splitting its tyrosine kinase domain.

- Physiology: expressed on endothelial cells and their progenitors (haemangioblasts); Kdr knockout mice die at ~E8.5–9.5 without blood islands or vessels.
- Alterations: rare activating mutations in angiosarcoma; amplification in some gliomas; mostly relevant as a drug target in the tumour vasculature.
- Drugs for HCC: sorafenib (SHARP trial, 2007, the first systemic therapy to prolong survival in HCC), lenvatinib (REFLECT, non-inferior first line), regorafenib (RESORCE, after sorafenib), cabozantinib (CELESTIAL), ramucirumab (anti-VEGFR2 antibody, REACH-2, for HCC with AFP ≥400 ng/mL). Also sunitinib, pazopanib, axitinib (renal cancer). These drugs cause hypertension, hand–foot skin reaction and diarrhoea.

attrs.mnemonic: VEGFR1 = FLT1 (decoy), VEGFR2 = KDR (the real angiogenic engine), VEGFR3 = FLT4 (lymphatics) – the KDR in the middle does the work.

items.gloss_md: The receptor tyrosine kinase that transmits most angiogenic VEGF-A signals in endothelial cells.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *KDR*; 1356 amino acids. Seven extracellular immunoglobulin-like domains (VEGF binds domains 2–3), transmembrane helix, juxtamembrane region, split tyrosine kinase domain and C-terminal tail.

- Ligands: VEGF-A (all isoforms), processed VEGF-C and VEGF-D.
- Signalling: ligand-induced dimerisation and autophosphorylation; pTyr1175 binds PLCγ (→ PKC → RAF–MEK–ERK proliferation, the main mitogenic route in endothelium) and SHB (→ PI3K–AKT survival, FAK migration); pTyr951 binds TSAd (migration, permeability via SRC); pTyr1214 → p38 actin remodelling.
- Co-receptors: neuropilin-1, VE-cadherin, integrin αvβ3. Internalisation regulates signalling.

items.gloss_md: An oncogene encoding the receptor tyrosine kinase FGFR2; FGFR2 fusions occur in ~10–15% of intrahepatic cholangiocarcinomas and are treated with FGFR inhibitors.
items.body_md:
Located on 10q26.13. Alternative splicing of exon 8/9 produces the epithelial IIIb isoform (FGFR2b, KGFR, binds FGF7/FGF10) and the mesenchymal IIIc isoform.

- Alterations: in-frame fusions (FGFR2::BICC1 and many other partners) or rearrangements in ~10–15% of intrahepatic cholangiocarcinomas (iCCA; mutually exclusive with IDH1/2 and KRAS, rare in extrahepatic CCA); amplification in ~5–10% of gastric cancers (diffuse type); activating point mutations in ~10% of endometrial cancers.
- Germline gain-of-function mutations cause craniosynostosis syndromes: Crouzon, Apert (S252W, P253R) and Pfeiffer syndromes.
- Drugs: pemigatinib (approved 2020), futibatinib (covalent, 2022) for previously treated FGFR2-fusion iCCA (infigratinib was withdrawn); erdafitinib; bemarituzumab (anti-FGFR2b antibody) in gastric cancer trials. Class side effects: hyperphosphataemia (FGF23 signalling blocked in the kidney), nail and eye toxicity (central serous retinopathy).

attrs.mnemonic: Cholangiocarcinoma's two big actionable targets: 'F and I' – FGFR2 fusions and IDH1 mutations (both intrahepatic, mutually exclusive).

items.gloss_md: A receptor tyrosine kinase for fibroblast growth factors that signals via FRS2 to RAS–MAPK and PI3K and controls epithelial–mesenchymal communication.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *FGFR2*; 821 amino acids (IIIc isoform). Three extracellular immunoglobulin-like domains (D1–D3) with an acid box between D1 and D2, transmembrane helix, split tyrosine kinase domain.

- Activation: FGF ligand plus heparan sulfate proteoglycan form a 2:2:2 complex that dimerises the receptor; autophosphorylation recruits the docking protein FRS2α (constitutively bound to the juxtamembrane region) → GRB2–SOS → RAS–MAPK and GRB2–GAB1 → PI3K–AKT; pTyr769 binds PLCγ.
- Isoform specificity: the IIIb/IIIc alternative exon in D3 determines ligand choice, ensuring paracrine signalling between epithelium (IIIb) and mesenchyme (IIIc).
- Fusion proteins retain the kinase and replace the C-terminus by a dimerising partner (e.g. BICC1 SAM domain), giving ligand-independent activity.
- Family: FGFR1–4 (FGFR4 binds FGF19, the gut hormone regulating bile acid synthesis in the liver).

items.gloss_md: An oncogene encoding the small GTPase N-Ras, mutated mainly at Q61 in ~20–25% of melanomas and in AML and colorectal cancer.
items.body_md:
Located on 1p13.2. Named after its discovery in 1983 as a transforming gene in a human neuroblastoma cell line (hence 'N'), not via a retrovirus.

- Alterations: activating mutations at codons 12, 13 and 61 – in melanoma mainly Q61R/Q61K (~20–25% of cutaneous melanomas, mutually exclusive with BRAF V600), AML (~10–15%), multiple myeloma, thyroid cancer, ~3–5% of colorectal cancer. Germline variants cause rare Noonan-like RASopathies; somatic mosaic NRAS mutations cause giant congenital melanocytic naevi.
- Clinic: in colorectal cancer extended RAS testing (KRAS and NRAS exons 2, 3 and 4) is required before anti-EGFR antibody therapy – NRAS mutations predict non-response just like KRAS mutations. No approved direct NRAS inhibitor; MEK inhibitors (binimetinib) show modest activity in NRAS-mutant melanoma.

attrs.mnemonic: Which RAS where? 'K for the gut and lung (PDAC, CRC, NSCLC), N for melanoma and blood, H for head-neck and bladder.'

items.gloss_md: A small membrane-associated GTPase of the RAS family that relays receptor signals to RAF–MEK–ERK and PI3K.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *NRAS*; 189 amino acids. Shares the highly conserved G domain (residues 1–165) with KRAS and HRAS but differs in the hypervariable C-terminal region.

- Membrane anchoring: farnesylation of the CAAX cysteine plus palmitoylation of Cys181; cycles of palmitoylation/depalmitoylation shuttle N-Ras between plasma membrane and Golgi.
- Q61 mutations (dominant in NRAS-driven tumours) block intrinsic and GAP-stimulated GTP hydrolysis, keeping N-Ras active; codon 12/13 mutations dominate in KRAS instead – the reasons for these isoform-specific mutation patterns are not fully understood.
- Effectors: RAF kinases (preferentially CRAF in NRAS-mutant melanoma), PI3K, RalGDS.

items.gloss_md: The first human oncogene shown to carry an activating point mutation (G12V in bladder cancer, 1982); mutated in head and neck, bladder and thyroid cancers and in Costello syndrome.
items.body_md:
Located on 11p15.5. Named after the Harvey murine sarcoma virus (Jennifer Harvey, 1964), whose v-H-ras oncogene is its retroviral homologue.

- History: in 1982 the groups of Robert Weinberg, Mariano Barbacid and Michael Wigler showed that the transforming gene of the T24/EJ bladder carcinoma cell line is HRAS with a single G→T change converting Gly12 to Val – the first demonstration that a point mutation can create a human oncogene.
- Alterations: activating mutations in ~5% of head and neck SCC, bladder cancer, thyroid cancer, Spitz naevi and cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas arising under BRAF inhibitors; germline mutations (mostly G12S) cause Costello syndrome, a RASopathy with cancer predisposition (rhabdomyosarcoma, neuroblastoma).
- Clinic: tipifarnib, a farnesyltransferase inhibitor, shows activity in HRAS-mutant head and neck SCC because HRAS, unlike KRAS and NRAS, cannot be alternatively geranylgeranylated when farnesylation is blocked.

attrs.anecdote: The 1982 discovery that a single nucleotide change turns HRAS into an oncogene came from transfecting tumour DNA into NIH 3T3 mouse fibroblasts – the 'focus-forming assay' – and was published nearly simultaneously by three labs in Nature.

items.gloss_md: A small RAS-family GTPase anchored to the plasma membrane by farnesyl and palmitoyl groups, the best-studied model RAS protein.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *HRAS*; 189 amino acids. The first RAS protein crystallised (1980s–1990s), it served as the structural model for the GTP/GDP switch mechanism: switch I and switch II change conformation on GTP binding; Gln61 positions the catalytic water; the arginine finger of a GAP completes the active site.

- Membrane anchoring: farnesylation of the CAAX box (CVLS) plus palmitoylation of Cys181 and Cys184; traffics via the Golgi to cholesterol-rich microdomains.
- HRAS depends exclusively on farnesylation for membrane localisation – the basis for testing farnesyltransferase inhibitors (tipifarnib) in HRAS-mutant tumours.
- Effectors as for other RAS proteins: RAF, PI3K, RalGDS.

items.gloss_md: An oncogene encoding the orphan receptor tyrosine kinase ROS1, activated by fusions in ~1–2% of NSCLC and targeted by crizotinib, entrectinib and repotrectinib.
items.body_md:
Located on 6q22.1. Homologue of v-ros of the UR2 avian sarcoma virus; its Drosophila orthologue is *sevenless* (needed for photoreceptor R7 development).

- Alterations: fusions with an N-terminal partner – CD74::ROS1 (most common), SLC34A2, EZR, SDC4, GOPC (FIG) – in ~1–2% of NSCLC (mostly adenocarcinoma, young never-smokers, mutually exclusive with EGFR, KRAS and ALK), and in inflammatory myofibroblastic tumours, spitzoid neoplasms, glioblastoma and cholangiocarcinoma.
- Testing: ROS1 IHC (screening), FISH break-apart, RNA-based NGS.
- Drugs: crizotinib (ROS1 approval 2016), entrectinib, repotrectinib (2023, also against the G2032R solvent-front resistance mutation); lorlatinib active. The ROS1 kinase domain is closely related to ALK, explaining cross-sensitivity.

items.gloss_md: An orphan receptor tyrosine kinase related to ALK whose fusion proteins are constitutively active oncogenic drivers.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *ROS1*; 2347 amino acids with a very large extracellular region of fibronectin type III repeats and YWTD (β-propeller) domains, a transmembrane helix and a kinase domain closely related to ALK and LTK.

- No confirmed human ligand; normal expression is limited (epididymis, transient in lung and kidney development), and Ros1-knockout male mice are infertile.
- Fusions keep the ROS1 kinase and transmembrane region (depending on breakpoint) and gain dimerisation and localisation signals from the partner; signalling via SHP2, STAT3, PI3K–AKT, RAS–MAPK.

items.gloss_md: An oncogene encoding the RET receptor tyrosine kinase; germline activating mutations cause MEN2 and medullary thyroid cancer, somatic fusions drive papillary thyroid and lung cancers.
items.body_md:
Located on 10q11.21. Named 'REarranged during Transfection' – discovered in 1985 (Takahashi et al.) as an oncogene created by DNA rearrangement during transfection of lymphoma DNA into NIH 3T3 cells.

- Germline gain-of-function: multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A (MEN2A; most often codon C634: medullary thyroid carcinoma, phaeochromocytoma, primary hyperparathyroidism), MEN2B (M918T: medullary thyroid carcinoma, phaeochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas, marfanoid habitus) and familial medullary thyroid cancer. Prophylactic thyroidectomy is timed by codon risk class (ATA guidelines).
- Germline loss-of-function: Hirschsprung disease (aganglionic colon) – the same gene can cause cancer or a developmental defect.
- Somatic: M918T in ~40–50% of sporadic medullary thyroid cancers; RET fusions (CCDC6::RET = RET/PTC1, NCOA4::RET = RET/PTC3) in papillary thyroid carcinoma, frequent in radiation-associated cases after Chernobyl; KIF5B::RET in ~1–2% of NSCLC.
- Drugs: selective inhibitors selpercatinib and pralsetinib (2020); older multikinase inhibitors vandetanib, cabozantinib. Calcitonin and CEA are serum markers of medullary thyroid cancer.

attrs.mnemonic: MEN2A = 'MTC + Pheo + Parathyroid' (2 P's), MEN2B = 'MTC + Pheo + mucosal neuromas + marfanoid' (B for Bumpy lips) – both RET.

items.gloss_md: A receptor tyrosine kinase for GDNF-family ligands, required for enteric nervous system and kidney development.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *RET*; isoforms RET9 (1072 aa) and RET51 (1114 aa) differ in the C-terminal tail. Extracellular region with four cadherin-like domains (calcium-dependent) and a cysteine-rich domain, transmembrane helix and tyrosine kinase domain.

- Activation: GDNF-family ligands (GDNF, neurturin, artemin, persephin) first bind GPI-anchored GFRα co-receptors (GFRα1–4); the ligand–GFRα complex then recruits and dimerises RET. GDF15 signals via GFRAL–RET in the brainstem (appetite, cachexia).
- Signalling: pTyr1062 is the main docking site (SHC, FRS2, IRS → RAS–MAPK and PI3K–AKT).
- MEN2A cysteine mutations (e.g. C634) form disulfide-linked ligand-independent dimers; M918T alters substrate specificity and activity of monomers.

items.gloss_md: An oncogene encoding the stem cell factor receptor KIT (CD117); activating mutations drive most gastrointestinal stromal tumours and systemic mastocytosis.
items.body_md:
Located on 4q12 next to *PDGFRA* and *KDR*. Homologue of v-kit of the Hardy–Zuckerman 4 feline sarcoma virus.

- Alterations: gain-of-function mutations in ~75–80% of gastrointestinal stromal tumours (GIST; Hirota et al., 1998) – most often exon 11 (juxtamembrane), then exon 9 (extracellular, mainly small-intestinal GIST; needs a higher imatinib dose of 800 mg); secondary resistance mutations in exons 13, 14, 17, 18. D816V (exon 17, kinase activation loop) in >90% of systemic mastocytosis – imatinib-resistant. Also in acral and mucosal melanoma, seminoma and core-binding-factor AML.
- Germline loss-of-function: piebaldism (white forelock); familial GIST with gain-of-function mutations.
- Clinic: KIT (CD117) and DOG1 IHC establish GIST diagnosis; imatinib (approved for GIST in 2002) is used adjuvantly and in advanced disease, followed by sunitinib, regorafenib and ripretinib; avapritinib and midostaurin for advanced systemic mastocytosis.

attrs.mnemonic: GIST is 'KIT-ty': CD117 (KIT) and DOG1 – a cat and a dog for the diagnosis.
attrs.anecdote: Imatinib, developed for CML, proved dramatically effective in GIST: the first patient, treated in Helsinki in 2000, responded within weeks, leading to approval in 2002 – one of the fastest drug repurposings in oncology.

items.gloss_md: A type III receptor tyrosine kinase for stem cell factor, essential for haematopoietic stem cells, mast cells, melanocytes, germ cells and interstitial cells of Cajal.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *KIT*; 976 amino acids. Type III receptor tyrosine kinase family (with PDGFRα/β, FLT3, CSF1R): five extracellular immunoglobulin-like domains, transmembrane helix, autoinhibitory juxtamembrane domain, kinase domain split by a kinase insert.

- Ligand: stem cell factor (SCF, KIT ligand, 'Steel factor'); binding dimerises KIT and relieves juxtamembrane autoinhibition → autophosphorylation → PI3K–AKT, RAS–MAPK, SRC family, STAT.
- Expression: CD34+ haematopoietic progenitors (CD117 used in flow cytometry for AML blasts), mast cells, melanocytes, germ cells and interstitial cells of Cajal (the pacemaker cells from which GISTs arise).
- Mouse mutants: White spotting (W, Kit) and Steel (Sl, Kitl) loci show identical pigment, germ cell and blood defects.

aliases: Mast/stem cell growth factor receptor Kit
attrs.anecdote: The mouse coat-colour mutants Dominant white spotting (W) and Steel (Sl) were studied for decades before it turned out in 1988–1990 that W encodes the receptor KIT and Steel its ligand SCF – a receptor and ligand found as two separate pigment mutants.

items.gloss_md: An oncogene encoding PDGFRα; activating mutations cause ~5–10% of GISTs and FIP1L1::PDGFRA fusion causes imatinib-sensitive eosinophilic neoplasms.
items.body_md:
Located on 4q12, in the cluster with *KIT* and *KDR*.

- Alterations: activating mutations in ~5–10% of GISTs (often gastric, epithelioid, KIT-negative or weak); D842V (exon 18) is imatinib-resistant but sensitive to avapritinib (approved 2020). The FIP1L1::PDGFRA fusion, created by a cryptic interstitial 4q12 deletion (removing CHIC2), causes myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia (chronic eosinophilic leukaemia/hypereosinophilic syndrome), which respond to low-dose imatinib. Amplification in glioblastoma and paediatric high-grade glioma.
- Germline: familial GIST / inflammatory fibroid polyps.
- Clinic: KIT/PDGFRA genotyping guides GIST therapy (imatinib dose, resistance); FISH or PCR for FIP1L1::PDGFRA in hypereosinophilia work-up.

attrs.mnemonic: GIST genes: KIT (~80%), PDGFRA (~5–10%), the rest 'wild-type' (SDH-deficient, NF1) – 'K before P'.
attrs.full_name: Platelet derived growth factor receptor alpha

items.gloss_md: A type III receptor tyrosine kinase for platelet-derived growth factors that controls mesenchymal cell proliferation and migration.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *PDGFRA*; 1089 amino acids, CD140a. Five immunoglobulin-like extracellular domains, transmembrane helix, juxtamembrane domain and split kinase domain, like KIT.

- Ligands: PDGF dimers (AA, AB, BB, CC) built from PDGF-A, -B, -C, -D chains; PDGFRα binds A, B and C chains, PDGFRβ binds B and D. Receptor dimers αα, αβ or ββ.
- Signalling: PI3K, PLCγ, SRC, GRB2–SOS–RAS–MAPK, STATs.
- Physiology: development of lung alveoli, intestinal villi, oligodendrocyte precursors (glioma origin), mesenchymal and fibroblast lineages; PDGFRα marks fibro-adipogenic progenitors and activated fibroblasts.

items.gloss_md: An oncogene encoding FGFR1, amplified in squamous lung and luminal breast cancers and fused in 8p11 myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms.
items.body_md:
Located on 8p11.23.

- Alterations: focal amplification in ~10–20% of lung squamous cell carcinomas and ~10% of HR-positive breast cancers (associated with endocrine resistance); fusions (e.g. ZMYM2::FGFR1, BCR::FGFR1) define the 8p11 myeloproliferative syndrome / myeloid–lymphoid neoplasms with FGFR1 rearrangement; FGFR1 internal tandem duplications and mutations in low-grade gliomas (pilocytic astrocytoma, dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumour).
- Germline: gain-of-function P252R causes Pfeiffer syndrome; loss-of-function causes Kallmann syndrome (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with anosmia).
- Clinic: FGFR1 amplification turned out to be a weak predictor of FGFR inhibitor response in lung cancer; pemigatinib is approved for relapsed FGFR1-rearranged myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms (2022).

items.gloss_md: A receptor tyrosine kinase that binds fibroblast growth factors and, with Klotho co-receptors, endocrine FGF21 and FGF23.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *FGFR1*; 822 amino acids. Same architecture as other FGFRs: three immunoglobulin-like domains (IIIb/IIIc splice variants in D3), acid box, transmembrane helix, split kinase domain.

- Signalling via FRS2α → RAS–MAPK and PI3K, and PLCγ.
- Endocrine roles: FGFR1c with β-Klotho mediates FGF21 action in adipose tissue and brain; FGFR1 with α-Klotho mediates FGF23 effects on phosphate in the kidney (together with FGFR3/4).
- Roles in mesoderm formation, limb, craniofacial and GnRH neuron development.

items.gloss_md: An oncogene encoding FGFR3, activated by mutations or fusions in urothelial carcinoma and by t(4;14) in myeloma; germline G380R causes achondroplasia.
items.body_md:
Located on 4p16.3.

- Somatic: activating mutations (S249C most common, also R248C, Y375C) in ~60–70% of non-muscle-invasive papillary urothelial carcinomas and ~15% of muscle-invasive ones; FGFR3::TACC3 fusions in bladder cancer and glioblastoma; t(4;14)(p16;q32) in ~15% of multiple myelomas, which juxtaposes IGH to FGFR3 and NSD2 (MMSET) and indicates higher risk. Also in benign seborrhoeic keratoses.
- Germline: G380R in the transmembrane domain causes ~98% of achondroplasia (most common short-limbed dwarfism, mostly de novo, linked to advanced paternal age); K650E causes lethal thanatophoric dysplasia. FGFR3 activation restrains chondrocyte proliferation in the growth plate.
- Drugs: erdafitinib (approved 2019) for FGFR-altered metastatic urothelial carcinoma; vosoritide (a C-type natriuretic peptide analogue counteracting FGFR3 signalling) for achondroplasia.

attrs.mnemonic: FGFR3 is a growth brake in cartilage: too much FGFR3 (G380R) = too little bone growth (achondroplasia).

items.gloss_md: A fibroblast growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase that inhibits chondrocyte proliferation and promotes urothelial cell growth when activated.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *FGFR3*; 806 amino acids, with IIIb (epithelial) and IIIc (mesenchymal/chondrocyte) splice isoforms.

- Activation by FGF plus heparan sulfate; downstream FRS2 → RAS–MAPK, PI3K, PLCγ and, in chondrocytes, STAT1 and MAPK-mediated growth arrest.
- Extracellular cysteine mutations (S249C, R248C) create unpaired cysteines forming ligand-independent disulfide-linked dimers; transmembrane G380R stabilises dimers; kinase K650E directly activates the kinase.
- FGFR3::TACC3 fusions add a coiled-coil dimerisation domain and mislocalise the kinase.

items.gloss_md: An oncogene encoding the nerve growth factor receptor TrkA; NTRK1/2/3 fusions are rare tumour-agnostic targets of larotrectinib and entrectinib.
items.body_md:
Located on 1q23.1; paralogues *NTRK2* (TrkB) and *NTRK3* (TrkC).

- History: TRK was one of the first oncogenic fusions identified – TPM3::NTRK1 from a colon carcinoma (Martin-Zanca, Barbacid, 1986); TrkA was later identified as the high-affinity NGF receptor.
- Alterations: NTRK1/2/3 fusions occur in <1% of common cancers (lung, colorectal, PDAC – mainly KRAS-wild-type, MSI-high colorectal), but are very frequent in rare tumours: ETV6::NTRK3 in infantile fibrosarcoma, secretory breast carcinoma and secretory (mammary analogue) carcinoma of the salivary gland; NTRK1 fusions in papillary thyroid cancer.
- Germline loss-of-function of NTRK1: congenital insensitivity to pain with anhidrosis (CIPA, hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy type IV).
- Clinic: larotrectinib (2018) and entrectinib (2019) were approved for any solid tumour with an NTRK fusion – among the first tissue-agnostic approvals; repotrectinib for resistance. Pan-TRK IHC can screen, RNA-based NGS confirms.

attrs.mnemonic: Trk 'A-B-C' = NTRK '1-2-3' with ligands 'NGF-BDNF-NT3' (NT-4 also binds B).
attrs.anecdote: Rita Levi-Montalcini discovered nerve growth factor (NGF), the ligand of TrkA, in the 1950s – having started her research in a home laboratory in her bedroom during the Second World War; she shared the 1986 Nobel Prize with Stanley Cohen.

items.gloss_md: The high-affinity receptor tyrosine kinase for nerve growth factor that supports survival and differentiation of sensory and sympathetic neurons.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *NTRK1*; 796 amino acids. Extracellular leucine-rich repeats flanked by cysteine clusters and two immunoglobulin-like domains (Ig2 binds NGF), transmembrane helix, tyrosine kinase domain.

- Signalling: NGF-induced dimerisation; pTyr496 (SHC → RAS–MAPK and PI3K–AKT) and pTyr791 (PLCγ). The low-affinity neurotrophin receptor p75NTR (TNF receptor superfamily) modulates affinity and specificity.
- Physiology: nociceptor and sympathetic neuron development; NGF–TrkA mediates inflammatory pain (anti-NGF antibodies such as tanezumab were developed for osteoarthritis pain).
- Fusion oncoproteins lose the extracellular domain and dimerise through the partner (e.g. TPM3 coiled-coil).

aliases: High affinity nerve growth factor receptor

items.gloss_md: An oncogene encoding the receptor tyrosine kinase FLT3; internal tandem duplications (FLT3-ITD) occur in ~25% of AML and are targeted by midostaurin, gilteritinib and quizartinib.
items.body_md:
Located on 13q12.2.

- Alterations: internal tandem duplications in the juxtamembrane domain (FLT3-ITD, ~25% of AML, enriched in normal-karyotype AML and with NPM1 mutations; associated with high leukocyte counts and relapse risk) and point mutations in the tyrosine kinase domain (FLT3-TKD, mainly D835, ~7–10%). One of the most common mutations in AML.
- Prognosis: FLT3-ITD is an adverse factor; in ELN 2022 risk classification, FLT3-ITD AML is classified as intermediate risk regardless of allelic ratio (unless other markers apply), whereas earlier versions used the allelic ratio and NPM1 status.
- Drugs: midostaurin plus intensive chemotherapy for newly diagnosed FLT3-mutant AML (RATIFY trial, approved 2017); gilteritinib for relapsed/refractory (2018); quizartinib for FLT3-ITD (QuANTUM-First, 2023). Allogeneic stem cell transplantation is commonly used; FLT3 inhibitor maintenance after transplant (sorafenib, gilteritinib) is studied.

attrs.mnemonic: ITD = 'internal tandem duplication' in the juxtamembrane brake: the duplicated stretch jams the brake open.

items.gloss_md: A type III receptor tyrosine kinase for FLT3 ligand that supports survival and proliferation of haematopoietic progenitors and dendritic cell development.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *FLT3*; 993 amino acids, CD135. Type III receptor tyrosine kinase like KIT and PDGFR: five immunoglobulin-like domains, transmembrane helix, autoinhibitory juxtamembrane domain, split kinase domain.

- Ligand: FLT3 ligand (FLT3LG); essential for dendritic cell development (Flt3l-knockout mice lack most DCs).
- Expression: early haematopoietic progenitors (CD34+), DC precursors; expressed on the blasts of most AML and B-ALL.
- ITD duplications lengthen the juxtamembrane domain and destroy its autoinhibitory function → ligand-independent activation with strong STAT5 signalling (unlike wild-type FLT3), plus RAS–MAPK and PI3K–AKT. TKD mutations stabilise the active conformation of the activation loop.
- Type I inhibitors (midostaurin, gilteritinib) inhibit ITD and TKD mutants; type II inhibitors (quizartinib, sorafenib) only ITD.

items.gloss_md: An oncogene encoding CDK4, the cyclin D-dependent kinase that phosphorylates Rb in G1; amplified in liposarcoma and target of the CDK4/6 inhibitors palbociclib, ribociclib and abemaciclib.
items.body_md:
Located on 12q14.1, close to *MDM2* (12q15).

- Alterations: co-amplification with MDM2 in ~90% of well-differentiated and dedifferentiated liposarcomas; amplification in glioblastoma and some other cancers. Germline R24C/R24H mutations, which prevent binding of p16INK4a, cause familial melanoma – the same pathway as germline CDKN2A mutations.
- Clinic: CDK4/6 inhibitors palbociclib (approved 2015), ribociclib and abemaciclib combined with endocrine therapy are standard in HR-positive/HER2-negative advanced breast cancer (PALOMA, MONALEESA, MONARCH trials) and are used adjuvantly in high-risk early disease. They need intact Rb; resistance arises through RB1 loss, CCNE1 amplification or CDK6 amplification. Neutropenia is the typical toxicity of palbociclib/ribociclib (CDK6 dependency of haematopoiesis); abemaciclib (more CDK4-selective) causes more diarrhoea.

attrs.mnemonic: Cyclin D partners with CDK 4/6, cyclin E with CDK2, cyclin A with CDK2 then CDK1, cyclin B with CDK1: 'D-4/6, E-2, A-2/1, B-1' – the CDK numbers count down as the cycle progresses.

items.gloss_md: A serine/threonine kinase that, bound to a D-type cyclin, phosphorylates Rb in early G1.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *CDK4*; 303 amino acids, a typical CDK kinase fold with the PSTAIRE-like helix that cyclin binding repositions.

- Activation requires a D-type cyclin (D1, D2, D3), phosphorylation of Thr172 by the CDK-activating kinase (CAK = CDK7–cyclin H–MAT1), and assembly helped by p21/p27.
- Substrates: Rb (initial monophosphorylation), p107, p130, FOXM1, SMAD3.
- Inhibitors: INK4 proteins (p16, p15, p18, p19) bind CDK4/6 directly and block cyclin binding; drugs (palbociclib, ribociclib, abemaciclib) are ATP-competitive.
- CDK4/6 inhibition also has immune effects (enhanced antigen presentation, reduced Treg proliferation).

items.gloss_md: An oncogene encoding CDK6, the CDK4 paralogue that drives G1 progression and is particularly important in haematopoietic cells; target of CDK4/6 inhibitors.
items.body_md:
Located on 7q21.2.

- Alterations: overexpression or amplification in lymphoid leukaemias and lymphomas (including translocations to immunoglobulin loci in some splenic marginal zone lymphomas), medulloblastoma, gliomas; CDK6 amplification is a mechanism of resistance to CDK4/6 inhibitors in breast cancer.
- Physiology: Cdk4/Cdk6 double-knockout mice die from anaemia, while single knockouts are viable – the two kinases are partly redundant, CDK6 being dominant in haematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (explaining CDK4/6 inhibitor neutropenia).
- Kinase-independent functions: CDK6 acts as a transcriptional co-regulator together with STAT3, AP-1 or cyclin D, e.g. inducing VEGFA and p16INK4a in leukaemic cells.

items.gloss_md: A cyclin D-dependent kinase closely related to CDK4 that phosphorylates Rb and also acts as a transcriptional co-regulator.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *CDK6*; 326 amino acids, ~70% identical to CDK4 in the kinase domain.

- Partners: cyclins D1–D3 (also viral cyclins of Kaposi sarcoma herpesvirus, which resist inhibition by INK4 proteins).
- Activation by CAK phosphorylation (Thr177); inhibition by INK4 family proteins and by CDK4/6 inhibitors.
- Substrates: Rb family, FOXM1, and proteins of metabolism such as PFKP and PKM2 (CDK6 restrains glycolytic flux into the pentose phosphate pathway).
- Nuclear transcriptional complexes independent of kinase activity, relevant in haematopoietic and leukaemic stem cells.

items.gloss_md: The gene of p21 (WAF1/CIP1), the key p53 target that halts the cell cycle after DNA damage and enforces senescence.
items.body_md:
Located on 6p21.2. Discovered in 1993 nearly simultaneously by several groups and therefore known under several names: WAF1 ('wild-type p53-activated fragment 1', el-Deiry and Vogelstein), CIP1 ('CDK-interacting protein 1', Harper and Elledge), SDI1 ('senescent cell-derived inhibitor', Noda), and as p21 in CDK complexes (Xiong and Beach).

- Regulation: transcriptionally induced by p53 through two p53 response elements in its promoter, but also p53-independently by TGF-β/SMAD, KLF4, SP1 and others; repressed by MYC (via MIZ1).
- Alterations: rarely mutated (mainly urothelial carcinoma); its induction is lost when p53 is mutated, which is a major way that TP53 mutation removes the G1 checkpoint.
- Use: p21 expression is a standard readout of p53 activity and, together with p16, a marker of senescent cells in tissues (e.g. senescent hepatocytes in chronic liver disease).

attrs.mnemonic: The guardian p53 sends its deputy p21 to stop the cell cycle – 'p53 → p21' is the canonical G1 checkpoint axis.
attrs.anecdote: Four groups found the same protein in 1993 from four different angles (p53 target, CDK interactor, senescence inhibitor, CDK complex component) – which is why it still carries the names WAF1, CIP1 and SDI1.

items.gloss_md: A CIP/KIP cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor that stops the cell cycle in G1 and G2 by inhibiting CDK2 and CDK1 and blocks DNA replication by binding PCNA.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *CDKN1A*; 164 amino acids, intrinsically disordered. N-terminal region binds cyclins (Cy motif) and CDKs; C-terminal region binds PCNA and contains a nuclear localisation signal.

- Functions: inhibits cyclin E–CDK2 and cyclin A–CDK2 (G1/S arrest) and cyclin B–CDK1 (G2 arrest); paradoxically acts as an assembly factor for cyclin D–CDK4/6 complexes. Binding PCNA blocks replicative DNA synthesis but allows repair synthesis.
- Senescence: sustained p21 expression mediates the initial senescence arrest, later maintained by p16.
- Regulation: short half-life (<1 h); degraded by SCF-SKP2, CRL4-CDT2 (in S phase, PCNA-dependent) and APC/C-CDC20; cytoplasmic p21 (phosphorylated by AKT at Thr145) can be anti-apoptotic.
- CIP/KIP family: p21, p27 (CDKN1B), p57 (CDKN1C).

attrs.mnemonic: p21 is a handbrake with a clamp: it stops CDK2/CDK1 and grips PCNA so replication stops while repair can continue.

items.gloss_md: A haploinsufficient tumour suppressor encoding p27Kip1, a CDK2 inhibitor whose loss or mislocalisation is common in cancer; germline mutations cause MEN4.
items.body_md:
Located on 12p13.1.

- Alterations: rarely biallelically inactivated – CDKN1B is a classic haploinsufficient tumour suppressor (Cdkn1b+/− mice are tumour-prone). Truncating mutations in ~8% of small intestinal neuroendocrine tumours, a few percent of luminal breast cancers and in prostate cancer (12p deletions). Much more often the protein is reduced through increased SKP2-mediated degradation or relocated to the cytoplasm (AKT phosphorylation); low p27 protein is a well-known adverse prognostic marker in breast, colorectal, prostate and other cancers.
- Germline: multiple endocrine neoplasia type 4 (MEN4), a MEN1-like syndrome (parathyroid and pituitary tumours) without MEN1 mutation.
- Physiology: Cdkn1b-knockout mice are larger, with enlarged organs and pituitary tumours.

items.gloss_md: A CIP/KIP CDK inhibitor that keeps cyclin E/A–CDK2 inactive in quiescent and G1 cells and is degraded at the G1/S transition.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *CDKN1B*; 198 amino acids, intrinsically disordered, folding upon binding to cyclin–CDK complexes.

- Function: inhibits cyclin E–CDK2 and cyclin A–CDK2; like p21 it assembles and stabilises cyclin D–CDK4/6. High in quiescent (G0) cells; induced by TGF-β, contact inhibition, cAMP and serum withdrawal.
- Degradation: in late G1 cyclin E–CDK2 phosphorylates p27 on Thr187, creating a degron for SCF-SKP2 (with CKS1) – a feed-forward switch. In early G1, KPC ubiquitinates cytoplasmic p27.
- Switch to non-inhibitory form: phosphorylation of Tyr88/Tyr89 by SRC-family kinases or BCR-ABL1 ejects it from the CDK2 active site.
- AKT phosphorylates Thr157, retaining p27 in the cytoplasm where it promotes migration via RhoA inhibition.
- p27 IHC was widely studied as a prognostic marker.

items.gloss_md: An oncogene encoding cyclin E1; amplified in ~20% of high-grade serous ovarian cancers, typically in tumours without BRCA defects, conferring platinum resistance.
items.body_md:
Located on 19q12.

- Alterations: focal amplification in ~20% of high-grade serous ovarian carcinomas (mutually exclusive with BRCA1/2 inactivation and HRD; associated with primary platinum resistance and poor survival), uterine serous carcinoma, gastric, bladder and triple-negative breast cancers. Cyclin E protein is also stabilised by FBXW7 mutations.
- Consequences: premature S-phase entry, replication stress and genomic instability (oncogene-induced replication stress).
- Clinic: CCNE1-amplified tumours depend on CDK2 and on the G2/M checkpoint; CDK2 inhibitors and WEE1/PKMYT1 inhibitors (adavosertib, lunresertib) are in trials. CCNE1 amplification is also a mechanism of resistance to CDK4/6 inhibitors and to trastuzumab.

items.gloss_md: A G1/S cyclin that activates CDK2 to complete Rb phosphorylation and to license DNA replication origins.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *CCNE1*; 410 amino acids; paralogue cyclin E2.

- Function: transcribed in late G1 as an E2F target, forming cyclin E–CDK2, which hyperphosphorylates Rb (positive feedback on E2F), degrades p27 (Thr187 phosphorylation), phosphorylates NPAT (histone gene transcription) and promotes origin licensing (CDC6, CDT1) and centrosome duplication.
- Degradation: autophosphorylation on Thr380 and GSK3β phosphorylation on Thr384 create a phosphodegron for SCF-FBXW7; free cyclin E is also degraded by SCF-SKP2.
- Low-molecular-weight forms generated by elastase cleavage are hyperactive and were linked to poor prognosis in breast cancer.

items.gloss_md: The gene of CDK2, the kinase that partners with cyclins E and A to drive the G1/S transition and S phase; an emerging target in CCNE1-amplified cancers.
items.body_md:
Located on 12q13.2.

- Alterations: rarely mutated or amplified itself; its activity is raised by CCNE1 amplification, FBXW7 loss and loss of p21/p27.
- Surprise from knockout mice (Ortega et al. and Berthet et al., 2003): Cdk2-null mice are viable (though sterile), showing that CDK1 can compensate for CDK2 in the somatic cell cycle; this weakened enthusiasm for CDK2 as a general cancer target, until CCNE1-amplified tumours were found to be specifically CDK2-dependent.
- Clinic: selective CDK2 inhibitors are in early trials (CCNE1-amplified ovarian cancer, CDK4/6-inhibitor-resistant breast cancer). Older pan-CDK inhibitors (flavopiridol/alvocidib, roscovitine/seliciclib) were limited by toxicity.

items.gloss_md: A serine/threonine kinase activated by cyclin E at G1/S and by cyclin A during S phase that drives DNA replication and centrosome duplication.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *CDK2*; 298 amino acids; the best structurally characterised CDK (the classic model of cyclin-induced activation, with the PSTAIRE helix and T-loop).

- Activation: binding of cyclin E or A plus Thr160 phosphorylation by CAK (CDK7). Inhibition: Thr14/Tyr15 phosphorylation by WEE1/MYT1 (removed by CDC25A) and binding of p21/p27/p57.
- Substrates: Rb, p27 (Thr187), CDC6, NPAT, origin-firing factors, nucleophosmin (centrosome duplication), BRCA2.
- After DNA damage, CHK1-mediated degradation of CDC25A keeps CDK2 Tyr15-phosphorylated and blocks origin firing (intra-S checkpoint).

items.gloss_md: The gene of CDK1 (CDC2), the only cyclin-dependent kinase essential for mammalian cell division, which with cyclin B drives cells into mitosis.
items.body_md:
Located on 10q21.2; previous symbol *CDC2*.

- Essential: Cdk1 is the only CDK whose loss is incompatible with early embryonic development in mice (Santamaría et al., 2007) – CDK1 alone can drive all cell-cycle phases when other CDKs are missing.
- History: Paul Nurse identified *cdc2* as a key cell-cycle gene in fission yeast and in 1987 (Lee and Nurse) showed that human *CDC2* rescues the yeast mutant – proving that cell-cycle control is conserved from yeast to humans. Together with Lee Hartwell (budding yeast *CDC* genes) and Tim Hunt (cyclins) he received the 2001 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. CDK1–cyclin B is the 'maturation-promoting factor' (MPF) described in frog oocytes in 1971 (Masui and Markert).
- Cancer: not typically mutated; frequently overexpressed (proliferation marker). Targeted indirectly through WEE1, PKMYT1 and PLK1 inhibitors.

attrs.anecdote: Tim Hunt discovered cyclins in 1982 during a summer course at Woods Hole: a protein in sea urchin eggs that was destroyed at every division and resynthesised – hence 'cyclin'. He reportedly named it partly after his hobby, cycling.

items.gloss_md: The mitotic cyclin-dependent kinase that, bound to cyclin B, triggers nuclear envelope breakdown, chromosome condensation and spindle assembly.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *CDK1*; 297 amino acids, also p34cdc2.

- Partners: cyclin A (late S/G2) and cyclin B1 (G2/M).
- Switch-like activation: during G2 CDK1–cyclin B is kept inactive by WEE1 (Tyr15) and MYT1 (Thr14/Tyr15) phosphorylation; at the G2/M transition CDC25C (activated by PLK1 and Aurora A) removes the phosphates, and active CDK1 further activates CDC25 and inhibits WEE1 – positive feedback creates an all-or-none entry into mitosis.
- Substrates: lamins (nuclear envelope breakdown), condensin, histone H1, MAPs and many others (hundreds of phosphosites).
- Exit: the APC/C–CDC20 ubiquitin ligase degrades cyclin B at the metaphase–anaphase transition once the spindle assembly checkpoint is satisfied.

items.gloss_md: The gene of E2F1, the Rb-controlled transcription factor that activates S-phase genes and, when deregulated, can also trigger apoptosis.
items.body_md:
Located on 20q11.22.

- Discovery: E2F was identified in 1986 (Kovesdi, Reichel and Nevins) as a cellular factor binding the adenovirus E2 gene promoter, activated by the viral E1A protein – later shown to be the target released when E1A binds Rb.
- Dual role: E2F1 drives proliferation, but excess E2F1 induces apoptosis via p14ARF–p53 and p73; E2f1-knockout mice develop tumours, while overexpression is also oncogenic – so it behaves as both oncogene and tumour suppressor depending on context.
- Alterations: occasional amplification or overexpression (e.g. 20q gain in colorectal and other cancers); the pathway is deregulated in almost all cancers through Rb pathway lesions.
- E2F target gene signatures ('E2F targets' hallmark gene set) are standard proliferation readouts in transcriptomics.

attrs.mnemonic: E2F = 'E2 promoter Factor' (adenovirus E2 gene); E2F1–3a activate, E2F3b–8 repress – 'the first ones start, the later ones stop'.
attrs.role: cell-cycle transcription factor (oncogene and tumour suppressor)

items.gloss_md: A transcription factor that, with DP partners, activates genes required for S-phase entry and DNA replication once released from Rb.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *E2F1*; 437 amino acids. Domains: N-terminal cyclin A-binding region, winged-helix DNA-binding domain, DP dimerisation domain (heterodimer with TFDP1/2), and a C-terminal transactivation domain containing the Rb-binding pocket motif.

- Targets: genes for nucleotide synthesis and DNA replication (*CCNE1*, *CDC6*, *MCM2–7*, *DHFR*, *TK1*, *POLA1*, *PCNA*), mitotic genes and its own promoter (positive feedback). Binding site TTTSSCGC.
- Regulation: repressed by hypophosphorylated Rb; activated by CDK4/6 and CDK2 phosphorylation of Rb; inactivated in S/G2 by cyclin A–CDK2 phosphorylation of DP and by degradation (SCF-SKP2); after DNA damage, ATM/ATR and CHK2 stabilise E2F1 for apoptosis.
- Family: activators E2F1, E2F2, E2F3a; repressors E2F3b, E2F4, E2F5 (with p107/p130), atypical E2F6–8.

items.gloss_md: An oncogene encoding MDM2, the E3 ubiquitin ligase that degrades p53; amplified in liposarcomas and other cancers and targeted by MDM2–p53 inhibitors.
items.body_md:
Located on 12q15. Name from 'murine double minute 2': it was cloned from amplified extrachromosomal 'double minute' chromosomes of the spontaneously transformed mouse 3T3-DM cell line (Cahilly-Snyder et al., 1987).

- Alterations: amplification in ~7% of all cancers, most typically in well-differentiated and dedifferentiated liposarcoma (with CDK4), intimal sarcoma, osteosarcoma, glioblastoma; MDM2 amplification and TP53 mutation are largely mutually exclusive. The promoter SNP309 (T>G) increases MDM2 expression and has been associated with earlier tumour onset.
- Clinic: MDM2 FISH or IHC is the standard test to distinguish atypical lipomatous tumour/well-differentiated liposarcoma from lipoma. MDM2–p53 interaction inhibitors (nutlins, discovered at Roche in 2004; idasanutlin, milademetan, brigimadlin) reactivate p53 in TP53-wild-type tumours; on-target thrombocytopenia and neutropenia limit dosing.

attrs.mnemonic: MDM2 and p53 are a feedback loop: 'p53 makes its own executioner' – MDM2 is a p53 target gene that destroys p53.
attrs.anecdote: Mdm2-knockout mice die early in embryonic development, but double knockout of Mdm2 and Trp53 rescues them completely (Jones et al.; Montes de Oca Luna et al., 1995) – the clearest genetic proof that MDM2's essential job is to keep p53 in check.

items.gloss_md: A RING-finger E3 ubiquitin ligase that binds the p53 transactivation domain, blocks its activity and targets it for proteasomal degradation.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *MDM2*; 491 amino acids (HDM2 in human). Domains: N-terminal p53-binding pocket (binds p53 residues Phe19, Trp23 and Leu26 – the pocket mimicked by nutlins), central acidic domain, zinc finger, and C-terminal RING domain (E3 ligase, heterodimerises with MDMX/MDM4).

- Functions: ubiquitinates p53 (mono- for nuclear export, poly- for degradation) and conceals its transactivation domain; MDM2–MDMX heterodimers are the main p53 E3 ligase in vivo.
- Regulation: transcriptionally induced by p53 (negative feedback); inhibited by p14ARF (oncogenic stress), by ribosomal proteins RPL5/RPL11 (nucleolar/ribosomal stress) and by ATM/c-Abl phosphorylation after DNA damage; AKT phosphorylation promotes its nuclear entry and activity.
- Additional substrates: MDMX, Rb, FOXO, β-arrestin, itself (autoubiquitination).

attrs.mnemonic: Nutlins imitate the three 'fingers' of p53 that dip into the MDM2 pocket: Phe19, Trp23, Leu26 ('F-W-L').

items.gloss_md: An oncogene encoding Aurora kinase A, a mitotic kinase for centrosome maturation and spindle assembly; amplified on 20q13 in many cancers.
items.body_md:
Located on 20q13.2 (STK15/BTAK).

- Alterations: amplification and overexpression on 20q13 in colorectal, breast, gastric, bladder and ovarian cancer; overexpression causes centrosome amplification and aneuploidy and transforms rodent cells. A common polymorphism F31I has been associated with cancer risk.
- Neuroblastoma: Aurora A binds and stabilises N-Myc, protecting it from FBXW7-mediated degradation – a target in MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma.
- Clinic: Aurora A inhibitors (alisertib) showed activity in trials (e.g. peripheral T-cell lymphoma, small cell lung cancer) but are not approved; combinations with EGFR or other inhibitors are studied.

items.gloss_md: A serine/threonine kinase at centrosomes and spindle poles that controls centrosome maturation, mitotic entry and bipolar spindle assembly.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *AURKA*; 403 amino acids, catalytic domain at the C-terminus.

- Activation: by binding of TPX2 (on spindle microtubules), autophosphorylation of Thr288 and binding of BORA in G2.
- Functions: centrosome maturation and separation, mitotic entry (Aurora A–BORA phosphorylates and activates PLK1, which activates CDC25), bipolar spindle assembly; degraded by APC/C-CDH1 at mitotic exit.
- Family: Aurora B is the catalytic subunit of the chromosomal passenger complex (kinetochore–microtubule error correction, cytokinesis); Aurora C acts in meiosis.
- Non-mitotic roles: N-Myc stabilisation, ciliary disassembly.

items.gloss_md: The gene of Polo-like kinase 1, a master mitotic kinase overexpressed in many cancers and a target of experimental mitotic inhibitors.
items.body_md:
Located on 16p12.2. Named after the Drosophila gene *polo*, identified by Sunkel and Glover (1988) in mutants with abnormal spindle poles.

- Cancer: rarely mutated but widely overexpressed in proliferating tumours, correlating with poor prognosis. Cancer cells, especially those with KRAS mutations, were found in RNAi screens to be particularly dependent on PLK1 (Luo et al., 2009).
- Clinic: PLK1 inhibitors volasertib (failed a phase 3 trial in AML) and onvansertib (in trials, including KRAS-mutant colorectal cancer and PDAC) are not approved; toxicity to bone marrow is dose-limiting.

items.gloss_md: A mitotic serine/threonine kinase with a phosphopeptide-binding polo-box domain that coordinates mitotic entry, spindle assembly and cytokinesis.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *PLK1*; 603 amino acids. N-terminal kinase domain and a C-terminal polo-box domain (PBD) that binds phosphorylated S-pS/pT-P motifs created by CDK1 and other kinases ('self-priming' and 'non-self-priming' targeting to centrosomes, kinetochores, central spindle).

- Functions: mitotic entry (activates CDC25C, promotes WEE1 degradation), recovery from the G2 DNA damage checkpoint, centrosome maturation, kinetochore–microtubule attachment, cohesin removal from chromosome arms, cytokinesis (RhoGEF ECT2 recruitment).
- Activation by Aurora A–BORA phosphorylation of Thr210; degraded by APC/C-CDH1.
- Family: PLK1–5; PLK4 controls centriole duplication.

items.gloss_md: The gene of CHK1, the essential kinase downstream of ATR that enforces S and G2/M checkpoints after replication stress.
items.body_md:
Located on 11q24.2.

- Essential: Chek1-knockout mice die early in embryogenesis; heterozygous loss contributes to genome instability. Cancer cells rarely lose CHK1 and instead often depend on it heavily because of oncogene-induced replication stress and p53 loss (which removes the G1 checkpoint).
- Clinic: CHK1/CHK2 inhibitors (prexasertib, SRA737) showed activity in trials, e.g. in high-grade serous ovarian cancer, often combined with gemcitabine or PARP inhibitors; none approved. Rare germline CHEK1 variants cause female infertility (oocyte arrest).

attrs.mnemonic: Two pairs: ATR–CHK1 (both essential; replication stress) and ATM–CHK2 (both dispensable; double-strand breaks).

items.gloss_md: A serine/threonine checkpoint kinase activated by ATR that halts the cell cycle by inactivating CDC25 phosphatases.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *CHEK1*; 476 amino acids; N-terminal kinase domain and C-terminal regulatory region.

- Activation: ATR phosphorylates Ser317 and Ser345, with the mediator Claspin; this occurs at stalled replication forks and resected DNA ends coated with RPA.
- Targets: CDC25A (phosphorylation → β-TrCP-mediated degradation → CDK2 and CDK1 stay Tyr15-phosphorylated: intra-S and G2 arrest); CDC25C (phosphorylation of Ser216 → 14-3-3 binding and cytoplasmic sequestration); WEE1 (activation); RAD51 (homologous recombination); suppresses late origin firing.
- Also required in unperturbed cycles for replication fork progression and mitotic checkpoint control.

items.gloss_md: A moderate-penetrance cancer predisposition gene encoding the ATM-activated checkpoint kinase CHK2; the c.1100delC variant roughly doubles breast cancer risk.
items.body_md:
Located on 22q12.1.

- Germline: truncating variants, especially c.1100delC (frequent in Northern Europe, ~1% of the Dutch and Finnish population), confer a moderately increased breast cancer risk (~2–3-fold; higher with family history), plus prostate, colorectal and possibly kidney and thyroid cancer risk. The missense variant I157T confers a lower risk. CHEK2 is part of standard hereditary breast cancer gene panels; it was first reported in families with Li–Fraumeni-like syndrome (Bell et al., 1999).
- Somatic: occasional mutations in many tumours.
- Clinic: CHEK2 carriers follow intensified breast screening (e.g. MRI per national guidelines); evidence for PARP inhibitor benefit in CHEK2-mutant tumours is weak.

items.gloss_md: A serine/threonine checkpoint kinase activated by ATM after double-strand breaks that phosphorylates p53, CDC25A and BRCA1.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *CHEK2*; 543 amino acids. Domains: N-terminal SQ/TQ cluster domain (ATM phosphorylation of Thr68), forkhead-associated (FHA) domain and C-terminal kinase domain.

- Activation: ATM phosphorylates Thr68 → FHA-mediated dimerisation → trans-autophosphorylation of the activation loop → active monomers that spread the signal through the nucleus.
- Targets: p53 Ser20 (disrupts MDM2 binding), CDC25A (degradation), CDC25C (14-3-3 binding), BRCA1 (HR), E2F1 (stabilisation), PML (apoptosis), MDMX.
- Unlike CHK1, CHK2 is dispensable for viability (Chek2-null mice are viable and resistant to radiation-induced apoptosis).

items.gloss_md: The gene of ATR, the essential PIKK kinase that responds to single-stranded DNA and replication stress; ATR inhibitors are tested in ATM-deficient cancers.
items.body_md:
Located on 3q23; name from 'ataxia telangiectasia and Rad3-related'.

- Essential gene: complete loss is lethal in mouse embryos; hypomorphic germline mutations cause Seckel syndrome (microcephalic primordial dwarfism).
- Cancer: rarely inactivated (cancer cells need ATR to tolerate oncogene-induced replication stress); synthetic lethality with ATM loss, ARID1A loss, CCNE1 amplification and ALT (ATRX-deficient) telomere maintenance have been proposed.
- Clinic: ATR inhibitors (ceralasertib, berzosertib, camonsertib, elimusertib) are in clinical trials as monotherapy and with PARP inhibitors, chemotherapy or immunotherapy; none approved as of 2025.

items.gloss_md: A PI3K-like protein kinase that senses RPA-coated single-stranded DNA at stalled forks and resected breaks and activates CHK1.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *ATR*; 2644 amino acids; PIKK family (with ATM, DNA-PKcs, mTOR) with HEAT repeats, FAT, kinase and FATC domains.

- Recruitment: its obligate partner ATRIP binds RPA-coated ssDNA; activation requires TOPBP1 (brought by the RAD9–HUS1–RAD1 '9-1-1' clamp loaded by RAD17) or ETAA1.
- Substrates: CHK1 (Ser317/Ser345), RPA2, p53 Ser15, H2AX, SMARCAL1 and many others (S/TQ motifs).
- Outputs: stabilises stalled replication forks, suppresses new origin firing, prevents premature mitosis (CHK1–CDC25–CDK1), promotes fork restart and HR; also senses mechanical stress at the nuclear envelope.

items.gloss_md: The gene of the WEE1 kinase that inhibits CDK1 to hold cells in G2; WEE1 inhibitors exploit p53-deficient tumours' dependence on the G2 checkpoint.
items.body_md:
Located on 11p15.4.

- Concept: tumour cells with TP53 mutation lack a functional G1 checkpoint and rely on the G2/M checkpoint to repair DNA damage before mitosis; WEE1 inhibition forces them into mitosis with damaged DNA ('mitotic catastrophe').
- Clinic: adavosertib (AZD1775) showed activity in trials (e.g. uterine serous carcinoma, CCNE1-amplified ovarian cancer, combinations with gemcitabine in PDAC) but development was stopped; azenosertib and inhibitors of the related kinase PKMYT1 (lunresertib, for CCNE1-amplified tumours) are in trials.

attrs.anecdote: 'Wee' is Scottish for small: Paul Nurse named the fission yeast mutant wee1 (1975) because the cells divided prematurely at a small size – the first gene shown to control cell size at division.

items.gloss_md: A nuclear tyrosine kinase that phosphorylates CDK1 (and CDK2) on Tyr15 to inhibit mitotic entry until DNA replication and repair are complete.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *WEE1*; 646 amino acids; one of the few kinases phosphorylating tyrosine but structurally related to Ser/Thr kinases.

- Function: inhibitory Tyr15 phosphorylation of CDK1 (and CDK2), opposed by CDC25 phosphatases; the balance WEE1 versus CDC25 sets the timing of mitosis. Its relative PKMYT1 (MYT1) phosphorylates Thr14 and Tyr15 at the ER/Golgi.
- Regulation: activated by CHK1 after DNA damage; at mitotic entry phosphorylated by CDK1 and PLK1, then degraded by SCF-β-TrCP – part of the switch-like positive feedback of mitotic entry.
- Also limits CDK2 activity in S phase, preventing excessive origin firing and replication stress.

items.gloss_md: The gene of PARP1, the DNA damage sensor enzyme whose inhibition is synthetically lethal with BRCA1/2 deficiency – the basis of PARP inhibitor therapy.
items.body_md:
Located on 1q42.12.

- Synthetic lethality: in 2005 the groups of Alan Ashworth (Farmer et al.) and Thomas Helleday (Bryant et al.) showed in Nature that BRCA1- or BRCA2-deficient cells are exquisitely sensitive to PARP inhibitors – the first clinical application of the synthetic lethality concept.
- Drugs: olaparib (first approved 2014, ovarian cancer), niraparib, rucaparib, talazoparib; used in BRCA-mutated or HRD-positive ovarian cancer (maintenance after platinum), germline BRCA-mutated HER2-negative breast cancer, BRCA/HRR-mutated prostate cancer and germline BRCA-mutated metastatic PDAC (maintenance after platinum, POLO trial). The newer PARP1-selective saruparib (AZD5305) has better haematological tolerability.
- Mechanism of drug action: catalytic inhibition plus 'PARP trapping' on DNA, which blocks replication forks (talazoparib traps most strongly).
- Resistance: BRCA reversion mutations, loss of 53BP1/shieldin (restores resection), fork protection, drug efflux.

attrs.mnemonic: Synthetic lethality = two flat tyres: a car (cell) drives with one flat tyre (BRCA loss) but not with two (BRCA loss + PARP inhibitor).
attrs.anecdote: The 2005 synthetic-lethality papers were published back-to-back in Nature by two independent teams; olaparib went from that concept to first approval in under ten years.

items.gloss_md: A nuclear enzyme that detects DNA single-strand breaks and synthesises poly(ADP-ribose) chains from NAD+ to recruit repair factors.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *PARP1*; 1014 amino acids (~113 kDa). Domains: three N-terminal zinc fingers (DNA break recognition), BRCT domain (auto-modification), WGR domain, and the catalytic domain (helical subdomain plus ADP-ribosyltransferase fold).

- Function: binding to single-strand breaks (and other lesions) activates PARP1 up to 500-fold; it consumes NAD+ to attach branched poly(ADP-ribose) (PAR) to itself and to histones, recruiting XRCC1, DNA ligase III and polymerase β (base excision/single-strand break repair) and chromatin remodellers. Auto-PARylation releases PARP1 from DNA; PARG degrades PAR.
- Excessive activation depletes NAD+ and ATP and causes parthanatos (PAR-dependent cell death).
- Apoptosis marker: caspase-3/7 cleave PARP1 into 89 and 24 kDa fragments – 'cleaved PARP' on Western blots is a classic apoptosis readout.
- Inhibitors trap PARP1 on DNA, converting single-strand breaks into replication-associated double-strand breaks that HR-deficient cells cannot repair.

attrs.mnemonic: Cleaved PARP (89 kDa) on a Western blot = 'the cell is dying' – caspases cut PARP so it can't waste the last NAD+.

items.gloss_md: The gene of RAD51, the recombinase that performs homology search and strand invasion in homologous recombination.
items.body_md:
Located on 15q15.1; human homologue of yeast *RAD51* and bacterial *recA*.

- Cancer: RAD51 itself is rarely mutated (it is essential), but its loading depends on BRCA1/PALB2/BRCA2, and the paralogues *RAD51C* and *RAD51D* are moderate-risk ovarian cancer predisposition genes included in gene panels. RAD51 is often overexpressed in tumours, contributing to therapy resistance.
- Germline: dominant-negative RAD51 variants cause a Fanconi anaemia-like disorder (FANCR) and congenital mirror movements.
- Biomarker: nuclear RAD51 foci after DNA damage (immunofluorescence on biopsies, the 'RAD51 assay') are used experimentally as a functional readout of HR proficiency to predict PARP inhibitor response.

attrs.mnemonic: RAD51 is the 'RecA of humans' – it does the homology search; BRCA1/PALB2/BRCA2 are its loaders.

items.gloss_md: An ATP-dependent recombinase that forms helical filaments on single-stranded DNA and catalyses homology search and strand invasion.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *RAD51*; 339 amino acids, structurally related to bacterial RecA.

- Mechanism: after end resection, BRCA2 (with PALB2 and the RAD51 paralogues RAD51B/C/D, XRCC2/3) replaces RPA with RAD51 on 3' ssDNA tails, forming a right-handed nucleoprotein filament. The filament searches for the homologous sequence in the sister chromatid and invades it, forming a displacement loop (D-loop) that primes repair synthesis.
- Fork protection: RAD51 filaments also protect and remodel stalled replication forks.
- Regulation: inhibited by anti-recombinases (RTEL1, FBH1, BLM, RECQL5) to prevent toxic recombination; DMC1 is its meiosis-specific paralogue.

items.gloss_md: The gene of the histone variant H2AX, whose Ser139-phosphorylated form γH2AX is the standard marker of DNA double-strand breaks.
items.body_md:
Located on 11q23.3, a region often deleted in haematological and solid cancers; previous symbol *H2AFX*.

- Biology: H2AX makes up ~2–25% of cellular H2A; its C-terminal SQEY motif is phosphorylated at Ser139 by ATM, ATR and DNA-PK within minutes of DNA damage, spreading over ~1–2 Mb around a break.
- History: γH2AX was described in 1998 by Rogakou, Bonner and colleagues.
- Use: γH2AX foci counting by immunofluorescence or flow cytometry is the most widely used assay for double-strand breaks in radiobiology, genotoxicity testing and as a pharmacodynamic marker of DNA-damaging drugs; it also marks replication stress and apoptotic DNA fragmentation (pan-nuclear staining).
- H2ax-knockout mice show genomic instability, radiosensitivity and, on a p53-null background, lymphomas.

items.gloss_md: A histone H2A variant whose C-terminal Ser139 phosphorylation (γH2AX) around DNA double-strand breaks recruits and amplifies the damage response.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *H2AX*; 143 amino acids. Differs from canonical H2A mainly in its C-terminal tail with the SQ motif (Ser139) followed by Tyr142.

- Signalling cascade: γH2AX is bound by MDC1 via its BRCT domains; MDC1 recruits more MRN–ATM (amplification) and the E3 ligases RNF8 and RNF168, whose ubiquitination of H2A Lys15 (with H4K20me2) recruits 53BP1 and BRCA1.
- Tyr142 phosphorylation (by WSTF) is removed during the DNA damage response; persistence of pTyr142 favours apoptosis.
- Resolution: dephosphorylated by PP2A and WIP1 after repair; foci disappearance over hours reflects repair kinetics.

items.gloss_md: A tumour suppressor encoding the transcriptional kinase CDK12 that sustains expression of long DNA repair genes; biallelic loss defines a subtype of prostate cancer with tandem duplications.
items.body_md:
Located on 17q12 near *ERBB2* (often co-amplified in HER2-positive breast cancer).

- Alterations: biallelic inactivation in ~5–7% of metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancers, producing a distinctive genome with many focal tandem duplications, increased gene fusions and neoantigens (Wu et al., 2018); ~3% of high-grade serous ovarian cancers.
- Consequences: reduced expression of long genes with many polyadenylation sites, including HR genes (*BRCA1*, *ATR*, *FANCI*, *FANCD2*), leading to a partial HR defect.
- Clinic: CDK12 is in HRR gene panels for PARP inhibitor eligibility in prostate cancer, but responses are infrequent; CDK12-loss prostate cancers may respond to immune checkpoint blockade (under study).

items.gloss_md: A transcription-associated cyclin-dependent kinase that, with cyclin K, phosphorylates RNA polymerase II to support elongation of long genes.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *CDK12*; 1490 amino acids, with an N-terminal arginine/serine-rich (RS) domain and a central kinase domain; partner cyclin K (*CCNK*), paralogue CDK13.

- Function: phosphorylates Ser2 of the RNA polymerase II C-terminal domain heptad repeats, promoting productive elongation and suppressing premature intronic polyadenylation, which particularly matters for long DNA damage response genes.
- Also regulates splicing and translation of mRNAs.
- Inhibitors and molecular-glue degraders of cyclin K (e.g. CR8) are research tools.

items.gloss_md: The gene of DNA polymerase ε; exonuclease-domain mutations cause ultramutated tumours, especially in endometrial cancer, with excellent prognosis.
items.body_md:
Located on 12q24.33.

- Somatic: pathogenic mutations in the exonuclease (proofreading) domain, especially P286R and V411L, disable proofreading and cause an 'ultramutated' phenotype (often >100 mutations/Mb, signature SBS10a/b dominated by C>A in TCT and C>T in TCG contexts). Present in ~7–10% of endometrial carcinomas (defining the 'POLE-ultramutated' molecular subtype of TCGA 2013) and ~1% of colorectal cancers.
- Prognosis: POLE-mutant endometrial cancers have excellent prognosis despite often high-grade histology; FIGO 2023 staging incorporates molecular class (stage I–II POLE-mutated tumours are down-staged, 'IAmPOLEmut'), and adjuvant therapy can be de-escalated.
- Germline: polymerase proofreading-associated polyposis (PPAP; Palles et al., 2013) with colorectal adenomas and cancer, endometrial cancer.
- Immunotherapy: the high neoantigen load makes POLE-mutant tumours highly responsive to PD-1 blockade.

attrs.mnemonic: Endometrial cancer molecular classes (ProMisE/TCGA): 'POLE, MMRd, p53abn, NSMP' – POLE is the best prognosis, p53-abnormal the worst.

items.gloss_md: The catalytic subunit of DNA polymerase epsilon, the main leading-strand replicative polymerase with intrinsic 3'→5' proofreading exonuclease.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *POLE*; 2286 amino acids (~261 kDa, 'p261'). N-terminal half contains the polymerase and exonuclease domains; the inactive C-terminal half anchors the holoenzyme (with POLE2, POLE3, POLE4) to the CMG helicase.

- Division of labour: Pol ε synthesises the leading strand, Pol δ the lagging strand, Pol α–primase makes primers.
- Proofreading: the exonuclease removes misincorporated nucleotides, improving fidelity ~100-fold; cancer mutants such as P286R retain or even increase polymerase activity while losing proofreading, producing high mutation rates without impairing proliferation.
- Mismatch repair corrects remaining errors; combined POLE and MMR defects give the highest mutation burdens observed in human tumours.

aliases: DNA polymerase epsilon catalytic subunit A

items.gloss_md: A mismatch repair gene whose germline mutations cause Lynch syndrome and whose promoter hypermethylation causes most sporadic MSI colorectal and endometrial cancers.
items.body_md:
Located on 3p22.2. Cloned in 1994 (Papadopoulos et al.; Bronner et al.).

- Lynch syndrome (hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer, HNPCC): autosomal dominant germline variants in *MLH1*, *MSH2*, *MSH6*, *PMS2* (or *EPCAM* deletion); MLH1 and MSH2 carriers have the highest risks (colorectal ~40–50%, endometrial ~30–40%), plus ovarian, gastric, small bowel, upper urinary tract, biliary and pancreatic cancers, sebaceous tumours (Muir–Torre variant) and glioblastoma (Turcot variant).
- Sporadic: biallelic MLH1 promoter hypermethylation in ~12–15% of colorectal cancers (serrated pathway, CIMP-high, BRAF V600E) and in many endometrial cancers. Testing for BRAF V600E or MLH1 methylation separates these from Lynch.
- Diagnostics: universal tumour screening by MMR IHC (MLH1/PMS2 or MSH2/MSH6 loss) or MSI PCR; Amsterdam II criteria (3-2-1 rule) and revised Bethesda guidelines historically used. Biallelic germline MMR loss causes constitutional MMR deficiency (childhood cancers, café-au-lait spots).
- Clinic: dMMR/MSI-high tumours respond strongly to PD-1 blockade – pembrolizumab became the first tissue-agnostic approval (2017) for MSI-H/dMMR solid tumours, including the ~1% of PDAC that are MSI-H.

attrs.mnemonic: Amsterdam II '3-2-1' rule: ≥3 relatives with a Lynch cancer, ≥2 successive generations, ≥1 diagnosed before 50 (and FAP excluded).
attrs.anecdote: Aldred Warthin described 'Family G' in 1913 after his seamstress predicted she would die of cancer like her relatives; Henry Lynch revived and expanded the pedigree in the 1960s–70s – it is one of the longest-followed cancer families in history and turned out to carry an MSH2 mutation.

items.gloss_md: A MutL-homologue ATPase that forms the MutLα complex with PMS2 to execute DNA mismatch repair after mismatch recognition by MutS complexes.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *MLH1*; 756 amino acids; N-terminal GHKL-type ATPase domain and C-terminal dimerisation domain.

- Complexes: MutLα (MLH1–PMS2, the main complex), MutLβ (MLH1–PMS1) and MutLγ (MLH1–MLH3, meiotic crossover).
- Mechanism: after MutSα/β recognises a mismatch on the newly synthesised strand, MutLα is recruited; PCNA activates the PMS2 endonuclease to nick the nascent strand, EXO1 excises the error-containing stretch, Pol δ resynthesises and ligase I seals.
- Stability: MLH1 is the obligate partner – without MLH1, PMS2 is degraded. Hence MLH1 mutation or methylation causes loss of both MLH1 and PMS2 by IHC, whereas PMS2 mutation causes isolated PMS2 loss.
- MMR also signals apoptosis after certain DNA damage (e.g. O6-methylguanine from temozolomide), so dMMR causes alkylating-drug resistance.

attrs.mnemonic: IHC pairs: 'MLH1 takes PMS2 with it; MSH2 takes MSH6 with it' – the big partner (MLH1, MSH2) drags its little partner along when lost.
