items.gloss_md: A mismatch repair gene and the second major Lynch syndrome gene; EPCAM deletions upstream silence it epigenetically.
items.body_md:
Located on 2p21-p16.3. Cloned in 1993 (Fishel et al.; Leach et al.) as the human homologue of bacterial *mutS*, providing the first molecular link between MMR and hereditary colorectal cancer.

- Lynch syndrome: MSH2 carriers have high colorectal and endometrial cancer risk and the broadest tumour spectrum (urothelial, especially upper tract; ovarian; small bowel; sebaceous neoplasms in Muir–Torre syndrome are mainly MSH2-associated).
- EPCAM: germline deletions of the 3' end of the neighbouring *EPCAM* gene remove its polyadenylation signal; read-through transcription causes hypermethylation and silencing of the MSH2 promoter in EPCAM-expressing epithelia (constitutional epimutation) – ~1–3% of Lynch families.
- IHC: loss of MSH2 with concomitant loss of MSH6.
- Somatic biallelic MSH2/MSH6 inactivation also occurs, e.g. after temozolomide therapy in glioma (hypermutation).

attrs.mnemonic: MutS = Sensor (MSH2/MSH6 recognise the mismatch), MutL = Linker (MLH1/PMS2 recruit the excision machinery).

items.gloss_md: A MutS-homologue ATPase that, paired with MSH6 or MSH3, recognises base–base mismatches and insertion/deletion loops in newly replicated DNA.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *MSH2*; 934 amino acids.

- Complexes: MutSα (MSH2–MSH6) recognises single base–base mismatches and small 1–2 nucleotide insertion/deletion loops (IDLs); MutSβ (MSH2–MSH3) recognises larger IDLs. MSH2 is the common, obligate partner, so its loss destabilises MSH6 (and MSH3).
- Mechanism: the clamp scans DNA with PCNA; mismatch binding triggers ADP→ATP exchange converting MutS into a sliding clamp that recruits MutLα.
- Without MSH2, mononucleotide and dinucleotide repeats (microsatellites) accumulate length changes – the molecular basis of MSI testing.
- Also involved in signalling responses to alkylating and other DNA damage and in somatic hypermutation/class-switch recombination in B cells.

items.gloss_md: A mismatch repair gene causing a milder, later-onset form of Lynch syndrome with a high endometrial cancer risk.
items.body_md:
Located on 2p16.3, near *MSH2*.

- Lynch syndrome: MSH6 carriers have lower colorectal cancer risk than MLH1/MSH2 carriers, later onset, and relatively high endometrial cancer risk; tumours may show only low-level or no MSI by PCR (MSH3 partially compensates for repeats with larger loops), so IHC is more reliable.
- IHC: isolated MSH6 loss suggests MSH6 mutation (germline or somatic); patchy loss can follow neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy.
- Somatic: secondary MSH6 mutations after temozolomide treatment in glioblastoma cause therapy resistance and hypermutation.

items.gloss_md: The mismatch-binding partner of MSH2 in the MutSα complex that recognises single-base mismatches and small insertion/deletion loops.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *MSH6*; 1360 amino acids. N-terminal PWWP domain binds the histone mark H3K36me3 (deposited by SETD2), recruiting MutSα to actively transcribed chromatin before replication; a conserved Phe-X-Glu motif in its mismatch-binding domain inserts into the DNA at the mismatch.

- Function: MSH2–MSH6 (MutSα) accounts for most mismatch recognition in human cells; it also binds O6-methylguanine:T mispairs, triggering futile repair cycles and cell death after alkylating agents.
- Loss of SETD2 (H3K36me3) reduces MutSα recruitment, linking SETD2 mutations to a mutator phenotype.

items.gloss_md: The mismatch repair gene with the lowest-penetrance form of Lynch syndrome, encoding the MutLα endonuclease subunit; sequencing is complicated by pseudogenes.
items.body_md:
Located on 7p22.1. Name: 'postmeiotic segregation increased 2' (from the yeast PMS1 phenotype).

- Lynch syndrome: heterozygous PMS2 variants confer the lowest cancer risks among the MMR genes (colorectal lifetime risk roughly 10% or less), so many carriers lack a striking family history; biallelic PMS2 variants are the most common cause of constitutional MMR deficiency (CMMRD).
- Genetic testing pitfall: the 3' region of PMS2 is highly homologous to the pseudogene *PMS2CL* (and there are many other PMS2 pseudogenes), requiring long-range PCR or specialised NGS pipelines.
- IHC: isolated PMS2 loss indicates PMS2 alteration (or rarely MLH1 missense variants).

attrs.full_name: PMS1 homolog 2, mismatch repair system component

items.gloss_md: The endonuclease-containing subunit of MutLα that nicks the newly synthesised DNA strand to start excision during mismatch repair.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *PMS2*; 862 amino acids. N-terminal ATPase domain and a C-terminal domain containing the DQHA(X)2E(X)4E endonuclease motif and the MLH1-interaction region.

- Function: within MLH1–PMS2 (MutLα), the latent endonuclease is activated by PCNA loaded with the correct orientation, introducing nicks in the discontinuous (newly synthesised) strand, which serve as entry points for EXO1 or strand displacement by Pol δ.
- Stability: dependent on MLH1 binding; MLH1 loss leads to PMS2 degradation.

items.gloss_md: A base excision repair gene whose biallelic germline mutations cause MUTYH-associated polyposis (MAP), an autosomal recessive form of colorectal adenomatous polyposis.
items.body_md:
Located on 1p34.1.

- MUTYH-associated polyposis: autosomal recessive; typically tens to a few hundred colorectal adenomas and a high colorectal cancer risk, often without family history in the parents' generation. Two missense variants, Y179C and G396D (formerly Y165C and G382D), account for most cases in Europeans. Heterozygous carriers (~1–2% of Europeans) have at most a slightly increased risk.
- Mutational fingerprint: G:C→T:A transversions (signature SBS18/SBS36) in *APC* and *KRAS* – MAP tumours are enriched for KRAS G12C.
- History: discovered in 2002 by Al-Tassan, Sampson, Cheadle and colleagues (Cardiff) in a family with multiple adenomas and somatic APC transversions without germline APC mutation.
- Clinic: included in polyposis and hereditary colorectal cancer gene panels; colonoscopic surveillance and polypectomy, colectomy if polyps cannot be controlled.

attrs.mnemonic: MAP = MUTYH-Associated Polyposis = 'FAP's recessive cousin': fewer polyps, two hits inherited, and G→T transversions everywhere.

items.gloss_md: A base-excision-repair DNA glycosylase that removes adenine misincorporated opposite the oxidised base 8-oxoguanine.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *MUTYH*; 546 amino acids (several isoforms, nuclear and mitochondrial). Homologue of bacterial MutY.

- The 'GO system': 8-oxoguanine (8-oxoG), the most common oxidative DNA lesion, pairs with adenine during replication. OGG1 removes 8-oxoG from 8-oxoG:C pairs; MUTYH removes the A from 8-oxoG:A mispairs (giving polymerases a chance to insert C); MTH1 (NUDT1) sanitises the nucleotide pool.
- Without MUTYH, 8-oxoG:A pairs are replicated into T:A, so the original G:C becomes T:A – the characteristic G:C→T:A transversion.

items.gloss_md: The gene of the DNA repair enzyme MGMT; promoter methylation in glioblastoma silences it and predicts benefit from temozolomide.
items.body_md:
Located on 10q26.3.

- Epigenetic silencing: MGMT promoter CpG-island hypermethylation in ~40% of IDH-wild-type glioblastomas (and most IDH-mutant gliomas) and some colorectal cancers.
- Clinic: Hegi et al. (NEJM 2005) showed that MGMT-methylated glioblastoma patients benefit much more from temozolomide added to radiotherapy (Stupp protocol); MGMT methylation status (by methylation-specific PCR or pyrosequencing) is routinely tested and is used to withhold temozolomide in elderly patients with unmethylated tumours.
- Pitfall: temozolomide-induced lesions in MGMT-deficient tumours are processed by mismatch repair; MMR loss under treatment causes resistance and hypermutation.

attrs.mnemonic: 'Methylated MGMT = More Glioblastoma Medicine Time': promoter methylation silences repair, so temozolomide works.

items.gloss_md: A suicide DNA repair enzyme that transfers the methyl group from O6-methylguanine to its own cysteine, reversing alkylation damage in one step.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *MGMT*; 207 amino acids.

- Mechanism: direct reversal – the alkyl group from O6-alkylguanine (and O4-methylthymine) is transferred to the active-site Cys145; the alkylated enzyme is irreversibly inactivated, ubiquitinated and degraded. Repair capacity therefore depends on the amount of MGMT protein.
- Relevance: O6-methylguanine created by temozolomide, dacarbazine and procarbazine mispairs with thymine; if MGMT does not remove it, MMR-dependent futile cycles cause double-strand breaks and cell death. Nitrosoureas (carmustine, lomustine) are also counteracted by MGMT.
- O6-benzylguanine is a pseudosubstrate inhibitor tested to sensitise tumours.

items.gloss_md: A tumour suppressor encoding pVHL, the oxygen-dependent HIF-α degradation factor; germline loss causes von Hippel–Lindau disease and somatic loss drives most clear cell renal carcinomas.
items.body_md:
Located on 3p25.3. Cloned in 1993 (Latif et al.).

- Germline: von Hippel–Lindau disease, autosomal dominant: haemangioblastomas of the CNS and retina, clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC, often multiple), phaeochromocytoma/paraganglioma, pancreatic cysts and neuroendocrine tumours, endolymphatic sac tumours. Classified into type 1 and type 2 (with phaeochromocytoma).
- Somatic: biallelic inactivation (mutation, promoter methylation, 3p loss) in ~90% of sporadic ccRCC – the founding event in ccRCC evolution.
- Consequence: constitutive HIF-1α/HIF-2α activity even in normoxia → VEGF, PDGF-B, GLUT1, CA9 (carbonic anhydrase IX, a ccRCC IHC marker) and EPO expression – explaining the hypervascular tumours and occasional polycythaemia.
- Clinic: belzutifan, a HIF-2α inhibitor, was approved in 2021 for VHL disease-associated tumours and later for advanced ccRCC; VEGF-targeted TKIs (sunitinib, cabozantinib, axitinib) and immunotherapy for metastatic ccRCC.

attrs.mnemonic: Clear cell RCC = 3p loss: 'VHL lives at 3p – lose 3p, lose the oxygen sensor, the tumour thinks it is hypoxic'.
attrs.anecdote: William Kaelin, Peter Ratcliffe and Gregg Semenza received the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discovering how cells sense oxygen – Kaelin's starting point was the VHL tumour suppressor.

items.gloss_md: The substrate-recognition subunit of a cullin-2 E3 ubiquitin ligase that targets prolyl-hydroxylated HIF-α subunits for degradation in normoxia.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *VHL*; two main isoforms, pVHL30 (213 amino acids) and pVHL19 (from an internal start codon). Domains: β-domain (binds substrates) and α-domain (binds elongin C).

- Complex: pVHL–elongin B–elongin C–cullin-2–RBX1 (CRL2^VHL).
- Oxygen sensing: in normoxia, prolyl hydroxylases (PHD1–3/EGLN) use O2, 2-oxoglutarate and Fe(II) to hydroxylate HIF-1α Pro402 and Pro564 (and HIF-2α equivalents); pVHL binds hydroxyproline, HIF-α is ubiquitinated and degraded within minutes. In hypoxia (or with pVHL loss) HIF-α accumulates, dimerises with HIF-1β (ARNT) and activates hypoxia genes.
- Pharmacology: HIF-PH inhibitors (roxadustat, daprodustat) treat anaemia of chronic kidney disease; VHL ligands are used as E3 recruiters in PROTAC degraders.
- Additional roles: microtubule stability, primary cilium maintenance, extracellular matrix assembly.

items.gloss_md: A tumour suppressor encoding neurofibromin, a RAS GTPase-activating protein; germline loss causes neurofibromatosis type 1 and somatic loss activates RAS in melanoma, lung cancer and glioblastoma.
items.body_md:
Located on 17q11.2; a very large gene (~350 kb, 60 exons) with one of the highest germline mutation rates; ~50% of cases are de novo. Cloned in 1990 (Cawthon et al.; Viskochil et al.; Wallace et al.).

- Neurofibromatosis type 1 (von Recklinghausen disease; ~1 in 3000): café-au-lait macules, axillary/inguinal freckling, cutaneous and plexiform neurofibromas, Lisch nodules of the iris, optic pathway gliomas, skeletal dysplasias, learning difficulties; increased risk of malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumours (MPNST), GIST, juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia, phaeochromocytoma and breast cancer.
- Somatic: inactivation in ~10–15% of melanomas (BRAF/RAS-wild-type, especially desmoplastic and sun-exposed), lung adenocarcinoma, glioblastoma (mesenchymal subtype), MPNST; also a mechanism of resistance to BRAF and EGFR inhibitors.
- Clinic: the MEK inhibitor selumetinib was approved in 2020 for symptomatic inoperable plexiform neurofibromas in children with NF1 (mirdametinib in 2025 including adults).

attrs.mnemonic: NF1 sits on chromosome 17, NF2 on chromosome 22 – 'the 2 goes with 22'. NF1 is the skin disease (café-au-lait, neurofibromas), NF2 the ear disease (bilateral vestibular schwannomas).

items.gloss_md: A large cytoplasmic RAS GTPase-activating protein (RAS-GAP) that accelerates GTP hydrolysis by RAS and thereby turns RAS signalling off.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *NF1*; 2818 amino acids (~320 kDa). Contains a central GAP-related domain (GRD, homologous to yeast IRA proteins and p120GAP), a Sec14-like and pleckstrin homology (PH) lipid-binding module, and cysteine/serine-rich regions; forms dimers.

- Mechanism: inserts an arginine finger (Arg1276) into the RAS active site, accelerating GTP hydrolysis ~10^5-fold. Oncogenic RAS mutants (G12, G13, Q61) are insensitive to this GAP activity.
- Recruitment: SPRED1 (mutated in Legius syndrome, an NF1-like condition) brings neurofibromin to the membrane.
- Loss of neurofibromin increases RAS-GTP and downstream MEK–ERK and mTOR signalling; it also regulates cAMP levels in neurons (via adenylyl cyclase), relevant to learning deficits.

items.gloss_md: A tumour suppressor encoding merlin, an upstream activator of the Hippo pathway; germline loss causes NF2-related schwannomatosis and somatic loss is common in meningioma and mesothelioma.
items.body_md:
Located on 22q12.2. Cloned in 1993 (Trofatter et al.; Rouleau et al.).

- Germline: NF2-related schwannomatosis (formerly neurofibromatosis type 2), autosomal dominant: bilateral vestibular schwannomas (the hallmark; hearing loss, tinnitus), meningiomas, spinal ependymomas, juvenile cataracts. Despite the name, clinically distinct from NF1.
- Somatic: inactivation (often with 22q loss) in ~50–60% of sporadic meningiomas, most sporadic schwannomas, ~40% of malignant pleural mesotheliomas (with BAP1 and CDKN2A), and some renal cancers.
- Clinic: bevacizumab is used to slow vestibular schwannoma growth and preserve hearing in NF2; FAK inhibitors and TEAD inhibitors (exploiting Hippo pathway loss) are in trials for NF2-deficient tumours.

attrs.mnemonic: NF2 = 'two ears': bilateral vestibular schwannomas are the hallmark of NF2.

items.gloss_md: An ERM-related cytoskeleton-membrane linker protein that mediates contact inhibition and activates the Hippo kinase cascade.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *NF2*; 595 amino acids. Name: 'moesin–ezrin–radixin-like protein' (also schwannomin). N-terminal FERM domain, α-helical coiled-coil and C-terminal domain; folds into open and closed conformations regulated by phosphorylation (Ser518 by PAK and PKA inactivates it).

- Functions: at the plasma membrane and adherens junctions, merlin links cell–cell contact to growth arrest (contact inhibition), recruits LATS1/2 to the membrane for phosphorylation by MST1/2–SAV1, and thus inhibits YAP/TAZ; it also limits receptor tyrosine kinase signalling, RAC–PAK and mTORC1.
- In the nucleus, merlin inhibits the E3 ubiquitin ligase CRL4^DCAF1.

items.gloss_md: A gene encoding the zinc-finger transcription factor WT1; inactivated in a subset of Wilms tumours and syndromic kidney disorders, but overexpressed in AML and used as an IHC marker for mesothelioma and serous carcinoma.
items.body_md:
Located on 11p13. Cloned in 1990 (Call et al.; Gessler et al.) as the Wilms tumour gene.

- Wilms tumour (nephroblastoma): WT1 mutations in ~10–20% of cases, often with CTNNB1 mutation.
- Syndromes: WAGR (Wilms tumour, aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, range of developmental delay) from contiguous 11p13 deletion including *PAX6*; Denys–Drash syndrome (dominant-negative zinc-finger missense mutations: early nephropathy with diffuse mesangial sclerosis, disorders of sex development, high Wilms risk); Frasier syndrome (intron 9 splice-site mutations altering the +KTS/−KTS ratio: focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, gonadoblastoma).
- Oncogenic side: overexpressed in most AML and other leukaemias (WT1 transcript level is used as a minimal residual disease marker), mutated in ~10% of normal-karyotype AML; WT1 peptide vaccines and WT1-specific T-cell receptors are studied.
- Pathology: nuclear WT1 IHC is positive in mesothelioma, serous ovarian/peritoneal carcinoma (with PAX8), desmoplastic small round cell tumour (EWSR1::WT1 fusion, C-terminal antibody) and Wilms tumour.

attrs.mnemonic: WAGR = Wilms, Aniridia, Genitourinary anomalies, Range of developmental delay (formerly 'Retardation').

items.gloss_md: A zinc-finger transcription factor and RNA-binding protein essential for kidney, gonad, heart and mesothelium development.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *WT1*; ~449 amino acids for the main isoform, with numerous isoforms from alternative start codons and splicing. N-terminal proline/glutamine-rich regulatory domain (activation and repression, self-association) and four C-terminal C2H2 zinc fingers.

- Key isoforms: alternative splicing of exon 5 (±17 amino acids) and an alternative splice donor in exon 9 inserting three amino acids, lysine–threonine–serine (+KTS), between zinc fingers 3 and 4. −KTS isoforms bind DNA (e.g. GC-rich EGR1-like sites) and regulate genes such as *AMH*, *SRY*-pathway genes and podocyte genes; +KTS isoforms bind RNA and act in splicing/post-transcriptional regulation. The +KTS/−KTS balance is essential for podocyte and gonad function.
- Expression: podocytes (lifelong; WT1 is a podocyte marker), Sertoli and granulosa cells, mesothelium, haematopoietic progenitors.

items.gloss_md: An anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family gene that by alternative splicing produces the survival protein Bcl-xL and the pro-apoptotic Bcl-xS; amplified in several solid cancers.
items.body_md:
Located on 20q11.21; known as *BCL-X*. Cloned in 1993 by Boise and colleagues (Thompson lab), who described both splice forms in the same paper.

- Splicing: two competing 5' splice sites in exon 2 generate the long form Bcl-xL (anti-apoptotic) and the short form Bcl-xS, which lacks 63 amino acids including BH1 and BH2 and promotes apoptosis. Splice-switching oligonucleotides that shift splicing towards Bcl-xS are an experimental strategy.
- Alterations: 20q11 gain/amplification in colorectal, gastric, breast and other carcinomas; high Bcl-xL expression is a common cause of chemoresistance and of resistance to venetoclax.
- Physiology: Bcl-xL is essential for survival of platelets (it sets platelet lifespan), erythroid cells and neurons; Bcl-x-knockout mice die around E13 with neuronal and erythroid apoptosis.
- Clinic: navitoclax (ABT-263, inhibits BCL-2, BCL-xL and BCL-w) causes dose-limiting thrombocytopenia; Bcl-xL-targeting PROTAC degraders (e.g. DT2216, which spares platelets because they lack the recruited E3 ligase VHL) and antibody–drug conjugates are in development. Bcl-xL inhibitors are also senolytics.

attrs.mnemonic: Bcl-xL = Large = Lives (anti-apoptotic); Bcl-xS = Short = Suicide (pro-apoptotic).
attrs.anecdote: Navitoclax trials revealed that platelets have a 'molecular clock': Bcl-xL is slowly lost during their ~10-day life, and when it runs out platelets undergo apoptosis (Mason et al., 2007).

items.gloss_md: The long anti-apoptotic isoform of BCL2L1 that sequesters BH3-only proteins and BAX/BAK at the outer mitochondrial membrane.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *BCL2L1*; 233 amino acids. Contains BH1–BH4 domains forming the BH3-binding hydrophobic groove and a C-terminal transmembrane anchor.

- Function: binds and neutralises activator BH3-only proteins (BIM, tBID, PUMA), sensitisers (BAD, but not NOXA) and active BAX/BAK; also 'retrotranslocates' BAX from mitochondria to the cytosol, keeping BAX levels on mitochondria low.
- Selectivity: BAD and BIM bind Bcl-xL strongly; NOXA does not (NOXA prefers MCL-1). Hence cells relying on both Bcl-xL and MCL-1 need combined targeting.
- Other roles: regulates mitochondrial bioenergetics (ATP synthase), VDAC and IP3 receptor calcium flux.
- First anti-apoptotic protein whose structure was solved (1996, Muchmore et al.), revealing the groove that BH3 mimetics later targeted.

items.gloss_md: The short, pro-apoptotic splice isoform of BCL2L1 that lacks the BH1 and BH2 domains and antagonises Bcl-xL.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *BCL2L1* via the upstream (proximal) 5' splice site in exon 2, which removes 63 amino acids encompassing BH1 and BH2; 170 amino acids.

- Function: lacking the intact groove, Bcl-xS cannot sequester pro-apoptotic proteins; it promotes apoptosis, partly by binding and inhibiting Bcl-xL and other pro-survival proteins and in a BAK-dependent manner.
- Splicing regulation: splice factors (SRSF1, SAM68, hnRNP proteins, RBM25) and signalling (ceramide, PKC) shift the Bcl-xL/Bcl-xS ratio; cancers usually favour Bcl-xL.
- Experimental antisense oligonucleotides redirect splicing to Bcl-xS to sensitise tumour cells.

items.gloss_md: An anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family gene, among the most frequently amplified genes in human cancer; MCL-1 is a short-lived survival protein and a key venetoclax resistance factor.
items.body_md:
Located on 1q21.2; name from 'myeloid cell leukemia 1' – cloned in 1993 (Kozopas et al.) as a gene induced early during differentiation of the ML-1 myeloid leukaemia cell line.

- Alterations: 1q21 gain/amplification is one of the most common somatic copy-number gains across cancers (Beroukhim et al., 2010; breast, lung, HCC); 1q gain in multiple myeloma (high risk) increases MCL1 dosage.
- Physiology: required for embryo implantation, haematopoietic stem cells, lymphocytes, neutrophils, cardiomyocytes and hepatocytes (hepatocyte-specific Mcl1 deletion causes spontaneous apoptosis, liver damage and HCC in mice).
- Clinic: AML, myeloma and other tumours depend on MCL-1; upregulation of MCL-1 is a major mechanism of venetoclax resistance. MCL-1 inhibitors (tapotoclax/AMG 176, S64315, AZD5991) entered trials but cardiac toxicity (troponin rises) has slowed development; indirect strategies use CDK9 inhibitors that shut off MCL1 transcription.

attrs.mnemonic: MCL-1 is the 'mayfly' of the BCL-2 family: half-life well under an hour, so blocking transcription (CDK9) or translation removes it fast.
attrs.full_name: MCL1 apoptosis regulator, BCL2 family member

items.gloss_md: An anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family protein with a very short half-life that binds BIM, NOXA and BAK and is essential for survival of many normal and malignant cells.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *MCL1*; 350 amino acids. Unusual among pro-survival proteins: a long N-terminal PEST region (degradation, mitochondrial targeting) precedes the BH domains; C-terminal transmembrane anchor. Alternative splicing gives MCL-1L (anti-apoptotic) and MCL-1S (pro-apoptotic, lacking BH1/BH2/TM).

- Binding preferences: binds BIM, PUMA, NOXA (selectively, together with A1) and BAK; binds BAD and the drug venetoclax poorly.
- Turnover: half-life ~30–60 min; ubiquitinated by MULE/HUWE1, SCF-FBXW7 and SCF-β-TrCP (after GSK3β phosphorylation), deubiquitinated by USP9X; transcription and translation are rapidly regulated by growth factors (STAT3, PI3K–mTOR) and stress.
- In mitochondria, an N-terminally truncated form in the matrix supports cristae structure and oxidative phosphorylation.

aliases: Induced myeloid leukemia cell differentiation protein Mcl-1

items.gloss_md: The gene of BAX, one of the two pro-apoptotic effector proteins that permeabilise the mitochondrial outer membrane; a p53 target frequently frameshifted in MSI tumours.
items.body_md:
Located on 19q13.33. Discovered in 1993 by Oltvai, Milliman and Korsmeyer as a protein co-immunoprecipitating with BCL-2 that accelerates cell death.

- Regulation: transcriptionally induced by p53 (though p53-mediated apoptosis relies more on PUMA and NOXA).
- Alterations: frameshift mutations in a coding poly-guanine tract (G8) occur in ~50% of MSI colorectal and gastric cancers (Rampino et al., 1997), helping these tumours escape apoptosis; otherwise rarely mutated. BAX mutations also arise under venetoclax therapy in AML and CLL.
- Genetics: Bax/Bak double-knockout mice have extra cells in many tissues (persisting interdigital webs, excess neurons, lymphoid accumulation), and their cells resist almost all intrinsic apoptotic stimuli (Lindsten et al., 2000) – showing that BAX and BAK are the essential gateway of mitochondrial apoptosis.

attrs.mnemonic: BAX and BAK 'punch holes in the mitochondrion's back' – the two effectors of MOMP; no BAX/BAK, no intrinsic apoptosis.

items.gloss_md: A pro-apoptotic BCL-2 family effector that, once activated, oligomerises in the mitochondrial outer membrane to form pores releasing cytochrome c.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *BAX*; 192 amino acids, nine α-helices with BH1–BH3 domains and a C-terminal transmembrane helix α9 that, in the inactive cytosolic state, is tucked into its own groove.

- Activation: direct activator BH3-only proteins (BIM, tBID, possibly PUMA) bind a trigger site (α1/α6) or the groove; BAX undergoes conformational change (N-terminal 6A7 epitope exposure, α9 release), inserts into the outer mitochondrial membrane, forms BH3-in-groove homodimers and then larger oligomers creating lipidic pores (rings and arcs).
- Consequence: mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilisation (MOMP) releases cytochrome c, SMAC/DIABLO, HTRA2 and (via herniation) mtDNA, which can activate cGAS–STING when caspases are blocked.
- Constrained by anti-apoptotic BCL-2 proteins, which bind active BAX or retrotranslocate it to the cytosol.

items.gloss_md: The gene of BAK, the mitochondria-resident pro-apoptotic effector that acts redundantly with BAX to permeabilise the outer mitochondrial membrane.
items.body_md:
Located on 6p21.31. Cloned in 1995 by three groups (Chittenden et al.; Kiefer et al.; Farrow et al.).

- Physiology: Bak-knockout mice are normal, Bax-knockout mice have mild phenotypes (male infertility, lymphoid hyperplasia), but double knockouts show widespread defects in developmental cell death – the two proteins are functionally redundant.
- Cancer: rarely mutated; loss or reduced expression of BAK and BAX contributes to resistance to BH3-mimetic drugs. BAK is a key mediator of apoptosis triggered by navitoclax (via release from Bcl-xL and MCL-1).
- Note on naming: *BAK1* (the apoptosis gene) must not be confused with plant BAK1 (BRI1-associated receptor kinase).

items.gloss_md: A pro-apoptotic BCL-2 family effector constitutively anchored in the mitochondrial outer membrane that oligomerises into pores upon activation.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *BAK1*; 211 amino acids with BH1–BH3 domains and a C-terminal transmembrane anchor.

- Unlike BAX, BAK resides permanently in the outer mitochondrial membrane, held inactive by VDAC2 and by binding to MCL-1 and Bcl-xL (not BCL-2).
- Activation by BIM or tBID binding to its groove triggers dissociation of the BH3 domain, symmetric BH3-in-groove dimerisation and oligomerisation into pores; cytochrome c and SMAC are released.
- Because BAK is mainly restrained by MCL-1 and Bcl-xL, combined inhibition of these two potently kills cells via BAK.

items.gloss_md: The gene of BID, the BH3-only protein that links death-receptor signalling to mitochondria after cleavage by caspase-8 – crucial for Fas-induced hepatocyte apoptosis.
items.body_md:
Located on 22q11.21. Cloned in 1996 (Wang et al., Korsmeyer lab) as a BH3-domain protein interacting with BCL-2 and BAX.

- Type I versus type II cells: in type I cells (e.g. lymphocytes) caspase-8 activated at the death-inducing signalling complex directly activates enough caspase-3; in type II cells – notably hepatocytes – XIAP blocks this route, and death-receptor apoptosis needs mitochondrial amplification via caspase-8 cleavage of BID.
- Liver: Bid-knockout mice survive injection of agonistic anti-Fas antibody, which kills wild-type mice by fulminant hepatocyte apoptosis (Yin et al., Nature 1999). BID cleavage participates in hepatocyte death in viral, alcoholic, ischaemia–reperfusion and fatty liver injury models.
- Cancer: not commonly mutated; BID is also cleaved by granzyme B (cytotoxic T/NK killing), calpains and cathepsins.

attrs.mnemonic: BID = the 'bridge' between extrinsic and intrinsic apoptosis: caspase-8 cuts BID into tBID, which runs to the mitochondria.

items.gloss_md: A BH3-only protein that, after cleavage by caspase-8 into truncated tBID, translocates to mitochondria and directly activates BAX and BAK.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *BID*; 195 amino acids (~22 kDa). Unlike most BH3-only proteins it has a globular structure of eight α-helices resembling BAX.

- Activation: cleavage in an unstructured loop (after Asp60 for caspase-8) generates N-terminal p7 and C-terminal p15 fragments; the p15 tBID (often N-myristoylated) separates and targets mitochondria by binding the lipid cardiolipin and MTCH2.
- Action: tBID is a direct activator – its BH3 domain binds BAX/BAK and triggers their oligomerisation; it is also neutralised by Bcl-xL and MCL-1.
- Other proteases that cleave BID: granzyme B, calpains, cathepsins – connecting immune killing and lysosomal damage to mitochondrial apoptosis.

items.gloss_md: The gene of BAD, a 'sensitiser' BH3-only protein whose phosphorylation by AKT links growth-factor signalling to cell survival.
items.body_md:
Located on 11q13.1. Discovered in 1995 (Yang et al., Korsmeyer lab) as a BCL-2/Bcl-xL binding protein that promotes death.

- Survival signalling paradigm: growth factors (IL-3, IGF-1) activate AKT, which phosphorylates BAD (Ser136, human Ser99), causing its sequestration by 14-3-3 proteins; this was one of the first mechanisms shown to connect PI3K–AKT to apoptosis suppression (Datta et al.; del Peso et al., 1997).
- Drug design: the BH3 domain of BAD (which binds BCL-2, Bcl-xL and BCL-w but not MCL-1) was the template for the BH3 mimetic ABT-737 (Oltersdorf et al., 2005), the parent compound of navitoclax and venetoclax.
- Metabolism: BAD also regulates glucokinase activity and insulin secretion in β cells, and hepatic glucose metabolism.

attrs.full_name: BCL2 associated agonist of cell death

items.gloss_md: A BH3-only 'sensitiser' protein that displaces activators from BCL-2, Bcl-xL and BCL-w and is inactivated by survival-kinase phosphorylation.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *BAD*; 168 amino acids, largely unstructured outside its BH3 helix.

- Binding: high affinity for BCL-2, Bcl-xL and BCL-w, not MCL-1 or A1. It cannot directly activate BAX/BAK; instead it frees activators (BIM, tBID) and BAX/BAK from these pro-survival proteins.
- Regulation: phosphorylation at Ser75 (mouse Ser112; by RSK, PKA, PIM), Ser99 (mouse Ser136; by AKT, p70S6K) and Ser118 (mouse Ser155; within the BH3 domain, by PKA) causes 14-3-3 binding and loss of pro-apoptotic activity; dephosphorylation by calcineurin or PP2A releases it.
- BH3 profiling with BAD peptide indicates dependence on BCL-2/Bcl-xL; HRK peptide indicates Bcl-xL dependence and NOXA peptide MCL-1 dependence.

items.gloss_md: The gene of BIM, the most potent BH3-only activator of apoptosis; essential for lymphocyte deletion and for the efficacy of many targeted cancer drugs.
items.body_md:
Located on 2q13. Cloned in 1998 (O'Connor et al., Strasser and Huang labs) as a BCL-2-interacting mediator of cell death.

- Physiology: Bim-knockout mice accumulate lymphocytes, granulocytes and monocytes and develop autoimmune disease (Bouillet et al., 1999) – BIM is key for deletion of autoreactive thymocytes and for shutting down immune responses.
- Cancer: biallelic deletion in some mantle cell lymphomas and other B-cell malignancies; epigenetic silencing in Burkitt lymphoma. Many targeted drugs (EGFR, BCR::ABL1, BRAF/MEK inhibitors) kill tumour cells largely by inducing BIM.
- Polymorphism: a common 2.9-kb intron 2 deletion in ~12% of East Asians favours an isoform lacking the BH3 domain and was associated with reduced response to EGFR and BCR::ABL1 TKIs (Ng et al., 2012).

attrs.mnemonic: BIM binds 'em all: the activator that binds every anti-apoptotic protein and BAX/BAK directly.

items.gloss_md: The most potent BH3-only protein, binding all anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family members with high affinity and directly activating BAX and BAK.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *BCL2L11*; isoforms BIM-EL (198 amino acids), BIM-L and BIM-S from alternative splicing, with increasing pro-apoptotic potency (BIM-S most potent).

- Binding: BIM BH3 binds BCL-2, Bcl-xL, BCL-w, MCL-1 and A1 with nanomolar affinity and directly activates BAX/BAK.
- Regulation: transcription by FOXO3 (repressed by AKT), CHOP (ER stress), E2F1, MYC; microRNA repression (miR-17~92 cluster); BIM-EL and BIM-L are sequestered by dynein light chains on microtubules; ERK phosphorylation of BIM-EL (Ser69) targets it for β-TrCP-mediated proteasomal degradation – which is why MAPK pathway inhibitors raise BIM levels.
- In primed cancer cells BIM is pre-loaded onto BCL-2 or MCL-1; BH3 mimetics release it to trigger apoptosis.

items.gloss_md: The gene of PUMA, the BH3-only protein that is the principal mediator of p53-dependent apoptosis.
items.body_md:
Located on 19q13.32. Discovered in 2001 by two groups (Nakano and Vousden; Yu, Zhang and Vogelstein) as a gene strongly induced by p53, hence the name PUMA – 'p53 upregulated modulator of apoptosis'.

- Regulation: p53 (response elements near the promoter), and p53-independently by FOXO3 (growth factor withdrawal), CHOP and ATF4 (ER stress), NF-κB and p73.
- Genetics: Puma-knockout mice show strongly reduced apoptosis after γ-irradiation in thymocytes and intestinal crypt cells, making PUMA (with NOXA) the main effector of p53-induced apoptosis. Loss of PUMA does not on its own cause spontaneous tumours, but accelerates MYC-driven lymphomagenesis.
- Liver: PUMA is induced in hepatocytes by saturated free fatty acids (lipoapoptosis) and contributes to liver injury in experimental steatohepatitis.

attrs.mnemonic: PUMA and NOXA are p53's two 'hunting cats' for apoptosis: PUMA catches everyone, NOXA mainly MCL-1.

items.gloss_md: A strongly pro-apoptotic BH3-only protein that binds all anti-apoptotic BCL-2 proteins and is the main killer downstream of p53.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *BBC3*; the main isoform PUMA-α has 193 amino acids with a central BH3 domain and a C-terminal hydrophobic region targeting mitochondria.

- Binding: high affinity for BCL-2, Bcl-xL, BCL-w, MCL-1 and A1 (like BIM), so it efficiently neutralises all pro-survival proteins; whether it directly activates BAX remains debated.
- Mainly regulated at the transcriptional level (p53, FOXO3, CHOP/ATF4), so its protein level directly reflects stress signalling.
- Mediates apoptosis after DNA damage (chemotherapy, radiation), growth-factor deprivation, ER stress and glucocorticoids.

items.gloss_md: The gene of NOXA, a p53-induced BH3-only protein that selectively neutralises MCL-1 and A1.
items.body_md:
Located on 18q21.32. First described as a phorbol-ester (PMA)-responsive gene (APR) in 1990 and characterised in 2000 by Oda, Taniguchi and colleagues as a p53 target and BH3-only protein; they named it NOXA, Latin for 'damage'.

- Regulation: p53, p73, HIF-1α, ATF3/ATF4 (ER stress), MYC; strongly induced by proteasome inhibitors (bortezomib) – a mechanism of their activity in myeloma and lymphoma.
- Relevance: because NOXA binds only MCL-1 and A1, it marks MCL-1 dependence; tumours with high NOXA can be more sensitive to venetoclax plus agents that induce NOXA (e.g. azacitidine in AML).

attrs.anecdote: Noxa is Latin for 'damage', harm (as in 'noxious'); Oda and colleagues chose it for this damage-induced p53 target in 2000.

items.gloss_md: A small BH3-only protein that binds selectively to MCL-1 and A1, promoting MCL-1 degradation and sensitising cells to apoptosis.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *PMAIP1*; only 54 amino acids in humans, containing a BH3 domain and a C-terminal mitochondrial targeting domain.

- Selectivity: its BH3 helix binds MCL-1 and A1 (BFL-1) but not BCL-2, Bcl-xL or BCL-w. Binding to MCL-1 displaces BAK and BIM and triggers MCL-1 ubiquitination (by MULE) and degradation.
- Complementarity: NOXA (MCL-1/A1) and BAD (BCL-2/Bcl-xL/BCL-w) together neutralise all pro-survival proteins – the classic experiment showing that BH3-only proteins have different binding profiles (Chen et al., 2005).
- Functions as a weak killer on its own but strongly synergises with BH3 mimetics targeting BCL-2 or Bcl-xL.

items.gloss_md: The gene of caspase-3, the main executioner caspase of apoptosis; cleaved caspase-3 is the standard tissue marker of apoptotic cells.
items.body_md:
Located on 4q35.1. The caspase family was defined after the discovery that the C. elegans cell-death gene *ced-3* encodes a homologue of mammalian interleukin-1β-converting enzyme (ICE, caspase-1) (Yuan, Horvitz et al., 1993); caspase-3 (CPP32/Yama/apopain) was identified in 1994–95.

- Physiology: Casp3-knockout mice (on the 129 background) show brain overgrowth from defective neuronal apoptosis and perinatal death (Kuida et al., 1996); other strains survive, showing compensation by caspase-7.
- Cancer: rarely mutated; caspase-3 is required for apoptosis induced by most chemotherapies. Paradoxically, caspase-3 activity in dying cells can stimulate repopulation of surviving tumour cells via prostaglandin E2 ('Phoenix rising' effect).
- Use: cleaved (active) caspase-3 IHC/flow cytometry is the standard apoptosis readout; caspase-3/7 activity assays (DEVD substrates) in cell culture. In liver disease, caspase-cleaved cytokeratin-18 fragments (M30 assay) in serum reflect hepatocyte apoptosis and were studied as non-invasive markers of MASH.

attrs.mnemonic: Caspases: initiators 2, 8, 9, 10 ('2-8-9-10: the starters'), executioners 3, 6, 7 ('3-6-7: the killers'), inflammatory 1, 4, 5, (11, 12).
attrs.anecdote: The name 'caspase' was coined in 1996 (Alnemri et al.) from cysteine-dependent aspartate-specific protease – they cut their substrates after aspartate using an active-site cysteine.

items.gloss_md: The principal executioner cysteine protease of apoptosis that cleaves hundreds of cellular proteins after aspartate residues, dismantling the cell.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *CASP3*; synthesised as an inactive 32-kDa zymogen (procaspase-3, 277 amino acids) existing as a dimer. Cleavage by initiator caspases (caspase-8, caspase-9) or granzyme B at Asp175 separates large (p17/p20) and small (p12) subunits; the active enzyme is a heterotetramer.

- Specificity: prefers DEVD↓ motifs.
- Key substrates: ICAD/DFF45 (releasing the nuclease CAD → internucleosomal DNA fragmentation, the 'DNA ladder'), PARP1 (89 + 24 kDa fragments), ROCK1 (membrane blebbing), gelsolin, cytokeratin 18, XKR8 (phosphatidylserine exposure, the 'eat-me' signal), gasdermin E (switching to secondary pyroptosis), and caspase-6/-7 and -9 (feedback).
- Inhibited by XIAP (BIR2 domain); synthetic inhibitors such as Z-VAD-FMK (pan-caspase) or Z-DEVD-FMK.

attrs.mnemonic: DEVD = 'DEVil's Dagger': the tetrapeptide motif caspase-3 cuts after.

items.gloss_md: The gene of caspase-8, the initiator caspase of death-receptor apoptosis that also suppresses necroptosis; mutated in head and neck cancers.
items.body_md:
Located on 2q33.1 next to *CASP10* and *CFLAR* (c-FLIP). Cloned in 1996 as FLICE/MACH (Muzio et al., Boldin et al.) by its binding to FADD in the CD95 signalling complex.

- Necroptosis gatekeeper: Casp8-knockout mice die around E10.5, but additional deletion of Ripk3 or Mlkl rescues them (Oberst et al.; Kaiser et al., 2011) – caspase-8 prevents RIPK3-driven necroptosis by cleaving RIPK1, RIPK3 and CYLD.
- Cancer: inactivating mutations in ~10% of head and neck squamous cell carcinomas (often with HRAS), cervical, endometrial cancers; epigenetic silencing in neuroblastoma (MYCN-amplified) and small cell lung cancer. Loss impairs TRAIL- and cytotoxic-lymphocyte-mediated killing.
- Germline: biallelic CASP8 deficiency causes an ALPS-like immunodeficiency with defective lymphocyte activation, and very-early-onset inflammatory bowel disease.
- Liver: caspase-8 in hepatocytes is required for Fas/TNF-induced apoptosis; its deletion in mice shifts liver injury towards necroptosis in some models.

attrs.mnemonic: Caspase-8 at the DISC = 'eight at the gate': the first caspase activated at death receptors.

items.gloss_md: The initiator caspase of the extrinsic apoptosis pathway that is activated by dimerisation at death-receptor signalling complexes and cleaves BID, caspase-3 and RIPK1/3.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *CASP8*; procaspase-8 (~55 kDa) contains two N-terminal death effector domains (DEDs) and a C-terminal protease domain (large p18 and small p10 subunits).

- Activation: FasL or TRAIL engages its receptors → FADD binds via death domains → procaspase-8 binds FADD via DEDs and forms DED filaments → proximity-induced dimerisation and autocleavage → active p18/p10 heterotetramer released into the cytosol. This complex is the death-inducing signalling complex (DISC); for TNFR1 it forms in the cytosol as complex II.
- Substrates: caspase-3 and -7 (type I cells), BID (type II cells such as hepatocytes), RIPK1, RIPK3, CYLD (necroptosis suppression), gasdermin D (in some contexts).
- Regulation: c-FLIP isoforms form heterodimers with caspase-8 that either block (c-FLIP-S) or limit activity locally (c-FLIP-L, anti-necroptotic).

items.gloss_md: The gene of caspase-9, the initiator caspase of the mitochondrial (intrinsic) apoptosis pathway activated on the apoptosome.
items.body_md:
Located on 1p36.21, a region frequently deleted in neuroblastoma and other tumours.

- Discovery: identified in 1996–97 as ICE-LAP6/MCH6; Xiaodong Wang's lab showed it is 'Apaf-3', the third factor needed with cytochrome c ('Apaf-2') and Apaf-1 to activate caspase-3 in cell-free extracts (Li et al., 1997).
- Physiology: Casp9-knockout mice, like Apaf1-knockouts, die perinatally with forebrain overgrowth (exencephaly) from reduced neuronal apoptosis (Kuida et al.; Hakem et al., 1998).
- Regulation: phosphorylation by AKT (human Ser196) and ERK (Thr125) inhibits it – one link between survival signalling and intrinsic apoptosis.
- Therapy tool: inducible caspase-9 (iCasp9, activated by the dimeriser rimiducid) is used as a 'safety switch' in CAR-T and other cell therapies.

attrs.mnemonic: Caspase-9 is 'number nine on the wheel': the apoptosome (seven-spoked APAF1 wheel) activates caspase-9.

items.gloss_md: The initiator caspase of intrinsic apoptosis, activated by dimerisation on the cytochrome c–APAF1 apoptosome, which then cleaves caspase-3 and -7.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *CASP9*; procaspase-9 (46 kDa, 416 amino acids) has an N-terminal caspase recruitment domain (CARD) and a protease domain (p35/p10 after processing).

- Activation: after MOMP, cytochrome c binds APAF1, which assembles with dATP/ATP into the heptameric apoptosome; procaspase-9 binds through CARD–CARD interactions and is activated by dimerisation on this platform (the apoptosome acts as a holoenzyme; autoprocessing at Asp315 modulates activity).
- Substrates: procaspase-3 and -7.
- Inhibition: XIAP BIR3 binds the processed small subunit (exposed N-terminal ATPF motif) and blocks dimerisation; SMAC/DIABLO released from mitochondria competes with this interaction (AVPI motif).
- A splice variant, caspase-9b, lacks the catalytic domain and acts dominant-negatively.

items.gloss_md: The gene of XIAP, the most potent caspase-inhibiting IAP protein and a target of SMAC-mimetic drugs; germline loss causes X-linked lymphoproliferative syndrome type 2.
items.body_md:
Located on Xq25; also *BIRC4*.

- Germline: hemizygous loss-of-function mutations cause X-linked lymphoproliferative syndrome type 2 (XLP-2): haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (often triggered by EBV), splenomegaly and Crohn-like inflammatory bowel disease – reflecting XIAP's role in NOD2 signalling and preventing RIPK3/caspase-8-driven inflammatory cell death rather than in apoptosis inhibition per se.
- Cancer: overexpressed in many cancers and associated with chemoresistance; XIAP is the reason hepatocytes are 'type II cells' needing BID for Fas-induced apoptosis.
- Clinic: SMAC mimetics (birinapant, LCL161, xevinapant/Debio 1143, tolinapant) antagonise XIAP and cIAP1/2 (inducing cIAP auto-degradation and TNF-dependent death); xevinapant failed in phase 3 head and neck cancer trials (2024). Antisense oligonucleotides against XIAP were also tested.

attrs.mnemonic: IAPs carry BIR domains ('Baculovirus IAP Repeats') – IAPs were first found in baculoviruses that keep infected insect cells alive.

items.gloss_md: An inhibitor-of-apoptosis protein that directly binds and inhibits caspases-3, -7 and -9 and acts as a RING E3 ubiquitin ligase.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *XIAP*; 497 amino acids. Three baculovirus IAP repeat (BIR) domains, a UBA domain and a C-terminal RING domain.

- Caspase inhibition: the linker preceding BIR2 blocks the active sites of caspase-3 and -7, while BIR2 binds an exposed IBM groove; BIR3 binds processed caspase-9 and prevents its dimerisation. XIAP is the only mammalian IAP with strong direct caspase inhibition (cIAP1/2 bind but inhibit weakly).
- Antagonists: SMAC/DIABLO and HTRA2/OMI released from mitochondria bind BIR2/BIR3 via an N-terminal AVPI motif, freeing caspases; SMAC mimetics copy this motif.
- Other functions: E3 ligase for caspases and itself, NOD1/NOD2 signalling (RIPK2 ubiquitination for NF-κB activation), copper homeostasis, TAB1–TAK1 binding.

items.gloss_md: The gene of survivin, the smallest IAP protein, highly expressed in most cancers but absent from most differentiated adult tissues; a mitotic chromosomal passenger protein.
items.body_md:
Located on 17q25.3. Described in 1997 by Ambrosini, Adida and Altieri as a novel anti-apoptosis gene expressed in cancer and in fetal tissues but not in most normal adult tissues.

- Expression: cell-cycle regulated, peaking in G2/M; among the most consistently overexpressed genes in cancer transcriptomes (proliferation signatures), high expression associated with poor prognosis in many tumour types.
- Function: its essential role is in mitosis as part of the chromosomal passenger complex; its direct anti-apoptotic function is weaker and partly indirect (stabilising XIAP, mitochondrial pools).
- Clinic: transcriptional suppressor YM155 (sepantronium), antisense oligonucleotides and survivin peptide vaccines (survivin is a tumour-associated antigen recognised by T cells) were tested without approval.

attrs.mnemonic: Survivin = 'survival in mitosis': it guides Aurora B to the centromere – a passenger that helps cells survive division.

items.gloss_md: A small single-BIR IAP protein that is a subunit of the chromosomal passenger complex and supports mitosis and cell survival in cancer.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *BIRC5*; 142 amino acids (~16.5 kDa), one BIR domain and a long C-terminal α-helix; forms homodimers. Splice variants (survivin-ΔEx3, survivin-2B) have distinct localisations.

- Chromosomal passenger complex (CPC): survivin, borealin and INCENP target the kinase Aurora B to centromeres (survivin binds histone H3 phosphorylated at Thr3) to correct erroneous kinetochore–microtubule attachments and later to the central spindle for cytokinesis.
- Apoptosis: does not efficiently inhibit caspases directly; cooperates with XIAP (stabilising it) and is regulated by SMAC binding; a mitochondrial pool is released upon stress.
- Regulation: transcription repressed by p53 and Rb–E2F, activated by STAT3, β-catenin/TCF, NF-κB; degraded via XIAP/ubiquitin pathways.

items.gloss_md: The gene of the death receptor Fas (CD95/APO-1); germline mutations cause autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome and Fas signalling drives hepatocyte apoptosis in liver injury.
items.body_md:
Located on 10q23.31 (also known as *TNFRSF6*, *APO-1*, *CD95*). Discovered in 1989 independently by Shin Yonehara (antibody 'anti-Fas') and by Peter Krammer's group at the DKFZ in Heidelberg (antibody 'anti-APO-1'), both inducing apoptosis of cells; the receptor was cloned in 1991 (Itoh et al.).

- Germline: heterozygous dominant-negative mutations (mostly in the death domain) cause autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome (ALPS-FAS): chronic lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, autoimmune cytopenias, accumulation of TCRαβ+ CD4−CD8− 'double-negative' T cells, elevated serum FasL and IL-10, increased lymphoma risk. The lpr mouse carries a Fas defect (Watanabe-Fukunaga et al., 1992).
- Somatic: inactivating mutations in some lymphomas (germinal centre-derived), loss of expression in many carcinomas.
- Liver: hepatocytes express high Fas; injection of the agonistic anti-Fas antibody Jo2 causes fulminant hepatic failure in mice (Ogasawara et al., 1993). Fas–FasL-mediated apoptosis contributes to viral hepatitis, alcoholic liver disease, MASH and acute liver failure.
- Splicing: exon 6 skipping produces soluble Fas, which blocks FasL.

attrs.mnemonic: CD95 = Fas = APO-1: three names, one death receptor. 'FasL kills fast.'
attrs.anecdote: One of the two founding labs was Peter Krammer's at the German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ) in Heidelberg; his anti-APO-1 antibody made tumour cells die by apoptosis in 1989.

items.gloss_md: A death receptor of the TNF receptor superfamily that, engaged by Fas ligand, assembles the DISC and triggers caspase-8-dependent apoptosis.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *FAS*; 335 amino acids, type I transmembrane protein. Three extracellular cysteine-rich domains (pre-ligand assembly domain mediates trimerisation before ligand binding), a transmembrane helix and a cytoplasmic death domain (DD).

- Signalling: trimeric Fas ligand (FasL, CD178, on activated T and NK cells) clusters Fas → the DD recruits FADD → FADD recruits procaspase-8/-10 and c-FLIP → death-inducing signalling complex (DISC). Type I cells activate caspase-3 directly; type II cells (hepatocytes, β cells) need amplification via BID cleavage and MOMP because XIAP restrains caspase-3.
- Functions: activation-induced cell death of T cells (immune homeostasis), cytotoxic killing, immune privilege (FasL in eye, testis), and non-apoptotic signalling (NF-κB, MAPK, migration).
- Expression is induced by p53, interferons and TNF; the soluble form and decoy receptor DcR3 antagonise FasL.

aliases: Tumor necrosis factor receptor superfamily member 6

items.gloss_md: The gene of TRAIL receptor 1 (DR4), a death receptor for the cytokine TRAIL that preferentially kills tumour cells.
items.body_md:
Located on 8p21.3, clustered with *TNFRSF10B* (DR5) and the decoy receptor genes *TNFRSF10C* (DcR1) and *TNFRSF10D* (DcR2); 8p21–22 is frequently deleted in carcinomas (e.g. prostate, HCC, head and neck), which can remove DR4/DR5.

- History: identified in 1997 (Pan et al., Dixit lab) shortly after its ligand TRAIL (TNF-related apoptosis-inducing ligand) was cloned (Wiley et al., 1995). Mice have only one TRAIL death receptor (orthologue of DR5), so DR4 is human-specific.
- Therapy: the observation that TRAIL kills many tumour cell lines but spares normal cells (Ashkenazi et al.; Walczak et al., 1999) led to recombinant TRAIL (dulanermin) and agonistic DR4 antibodies (mapatumumab) – these failed in clinical trials because of low potency and tumour resistance.
- Polymorphisms in DR4 were associated with various cancer risks in small studies (not established).

attrs.mnemonic: TRAIL receptors: R1 = DR4, R2 = DR5 (killers); R3 = DcR1, R4 = DcR2 (decoys) – 'the first two kill, the next two catch'.

items.gloss_md: A TNF receptor superfamily death receptor that binds TRAIL and initiates caspase-8-dependent apoptosis.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *TNFRSF10A*; 468 amino acids; extracellular cysteine-rich domains, transmembrane helix and cytoplasmic death domain.

- Signalling: TRAIL trimers cluster DR4 (and DR5) → FADD and procaspase-8/-10 recruitment → DISC → apoptosis; also non-apoptotic NF-κB and MAPK signalling via a secondary complex (RIPK1, TRAF2), which can promote invasion in resistant tumour cells.
- Regulation: O-glycosylation of DR4/DR5 enhances clustering and sensitivity; decoy receptors DcR1 (GPI-anchored, no death domain) and DcR2 (truncated death domain) and osteoprotegerin sequester TRAIL; c-FLIP blocks caspase-8 activation.
- TRAIL is expressed by NK cells, activated T cells and some myeloid cells and contributes to tumour immunosurveillance.

aliases: Tumor necrosis factor receptor superfamily member 10A

items.gloss_md: The gene of TRAIL receptor 2 (DR5), a p53-inducible death receptor implicated in hepatocyte lipoapoptosis and targeted by agonist antibodies in trials.
items.body_md:
Located on 8p21.3 next to *TNFRSF10A*. Cloned in 1997 by several groups (also as KILLER/DR5, induced by p53 after DNA damage; Wu et al., 1997).

- Regulation: induced by p53 and by ER stress via CHOP – a link between unfolded protein response and death receptor apoptosis.
- Liver: in MASH (NASH) models, saturated free fatty acids (palmitate) upregulate DR5 via CHOP and cause ligand-independent DR5 clustering and hepatocyte lipoapoptosis (Cazanave et al., 2011, Gores lab); DR5 deletion or TRAIL deficiency reduces steatohepatitis in mice.
- Cancer: inactivating mutations in a small subset of head and neck cancers and non-Hodgkin lymphomas; 8p deletions.
- Therapy: DR5 agonist antibodies (conatumumab, lexatumumab, drozitumab, tigatuzumab) failed to show efficacy; a highly potent tetravalent DR5 nanobody (TAS266) caused severe hepatotoxicity in phase 1 – underlining hepatocyte sensitivity to strong DR5 clustering. Multivalent next-generation agonists are in trials.

attrs.mnemonic: DR5 = the ER-stress death receptor: 'CHOP chops' – CHOP induces DR5 and hepatocytes die from fat (lipoapoptosis).

items.gloss_md: A TNF receptor superfamily death receptor for TRAIL, inducible by p53 and ER stress, that triggers caspase-8-mediated apoptosis.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *TNFRSF10B*; two splice isoforms, a long form (440 amino acids, with an extra 29-residue extracellular stalk) and a short form, both with a cytoplasmic death domain.

- Signalling: like DR4, forms a DISC with FADD and caspase-8/-10 upon TRAIL binding, and can also cluster ligand-independently when unfolded proteins accumulate (misfolded proteins bind its ectodomain in the ER/Golgi) or when membranes are loaded with saturated fatty acids.
- DR5 is the more potent TRAIL receptor in many cells; it is the only TRAIL death receptor in mice (Tnfrsf10b, 'MK').
- Its upregulation by chemotherapy (via p53) and ER-stress drugs (bortezomib) sensitises tumour cells to TRAIL.

aliases: Tumor necrosis factor receptor superfamily member 10B

items.gloss_md: The gene of cytochrome c, the mitochondrial electron carrier whose release into the cytosol activates the apoptosome and caspase-9.
items.body_md:
Located on 7p15.3; many processed pseudogenes exist in the human genome.

- Germline: rare missense variants (e.g. G41S) cause autosomal dominant thrombocytopenia 4, due to increased apoptotic activity in megakaryocytes and premature platelet release – a mild disorder.
- Discovery of its apoptotic role: Xiaodong Wang's lab (Liu et al., Cell 1996) purified a factor from HeLa cytosol that activated caspase-3 together with dATP and found it was cytochrome c – a famous surprise that an essential respiratory protein is also an apoptosis trigger.
- Use: cytochrome c release (cytosolic fraction western blot, immunofluorescence) is a classic readout of MOMP; cytochrome c in serum has been studied as a marker of cell death after chemotherapy or in liver injury.

items.gloss_md: A small haem protein of the mitochondrial intermembrane space that shuttles electrons from complex III to complex IV and, when released into the cytosol, triggers apoptosome assembly.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *CYCS*; 104 amino acids (after removal of the initiator methionine, ~12 kDa); haem c is covalently attached via thioether bonds to two cysteines in a CXXCH motif (attachment by holocytochrome c synthase).

- Respiration: carries single electrons between complex III (cytochrome bc1) and complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) in the intermembrane space.
- Apoptosis: after BAX/BAK-mediated MOMP, cytochrome c is released (helped by cristae remodelling and its detachment from cardiolipin) and binds the WD40 repeats of APAF1, triggering dATP/ATP-dependent heptamerisation into the apoptosome that activates caspase-9.
- Peroxidase activity: bound to cardiolipin, cytochrome c oxidises cardiolipin, which facilitates its own release.
- Highly conserved in evolution – historically used to build some of the first molecular phylogenetic trees (Fitch and Margoliash, 1967).

attrs.mnemonic: Cytochrome c has two lives: 'C for Current' inside mitochondria (electron transport) and 'C for Corpse' in the cytosol (apoptosome).

items.gloss_md: The gene of APAF1, the scaffold protein that, bound to cytochrome c, assembles the apoptosome and activates caspase-9.
items.body_md:
Located on 12q23.1. Cloned in 1997 by Zou, Wang and colleagues as 'Apaf-1', the mammalian homologue of the C. elegans cell death gene *ced-4*.

- Evolutionary parallel: the worm pathway EGL-1 (BH3-only) ⟶ CED-9 (BCL-2) ⟶ CED-4 (APAF1) ⟶ CED-3 (caspase) maps onto mammalian intrinsic apoptosis; the genetics of programmed cell death in C. elegans earned Robert Horvitz, Sydney Brenner and John Sulston the 2002 Nobel Prize.
- Physiology: Apaf1-knockout mice die perinatally with forebrain overgrowth, facial clefts and persistent interdigital webs.
- Cancer: loss or silencing (LOH, promoter methylation) in metastatic melanoma (Soengas et al., Nature 2001) and some leukaemias, making cells resistant to chemotherapy-induced apoptosis.

attrs.anecdote: In C. elegans exactly 131 of the 1090 somatic cells generated during hermaphrodite development die by programmed cell death; mapping their fate led Horvitz to the ced genes, including ced-4, the ancestor of APAF1.

items.gloss_md: A cytosolic scaffold protein that binds cytochrome c and dATP/ATP to form the heptameric apoptosome, the activation platform of caspase-9.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *APAF1*; 1248 amino acids. Domains: N-terminal caspase recruitment domain (CARD), a nucleotide-binding oligomerisation domain (NB-ARC/NOD, related to NLR proteins such as the inflammasome sensors) and C-terminal WD40 repeats that bind cytochrome c.

- Activation: in its inactive state the WD40 repeats fold back and keep the NOD in an ADP-bound, closed form; cytochrome c binding plus dADP→dATP exchange opens APAF1, which assembles into a seven-spoked wheel (~1 MDa) – the apoptosome. Its central CARD disc recruits procaspase-9.
- Inhibitors: heat shock proteins (HSP70, HSP90), prothymosin-α; low cytosolic nucleotide or cytochrome c levels in neurons and cardiomyocytes limit apoptosome formation.

attrs.mnemonic: The apoptosome is the 'wheel of death': seven APAF1 spokes, cytochrome c on the rims, caspase-9 at the hub.

items.gloss_md: The gene of MEK1, the dual-specificity kinase between RAF and ERK; target of the MEK inhibitors trametinib, cobimetinib, binimetinib and selumetinib.
items.body_md:
Located on 15q22.31; paralogue *MAP2K2* (MEK2) on 19p13.3.

- Alterations: activating mutations or in-frame deletions are uncommon but occur in Langerhans cell histiocytosis and Erdheim–Chester disease (in many BRAF-wild-type cases), melanoma (often as resistance to BRAF inhibitors), lung adenocarcinoma and colorectal cancer. Germline mutations cause cardio-facio-cutaneous syndrome, a RASopathy.
- Drugs: MEK inhibitors trametinib (approved 2013), cobimetinib, binimetinib (all combined with BRAF inhibitors in BRAF V600 tumours), selumetinib and mirdametinib (NF1 plexiform neurofibromas); trametinib is also used in BRAF/MEK-altered histiocytoses and low-grade gliomas. Typical toxicities: acneiform rash, diarrhoea, serous retinopathy, reduced cardiac ejection fraction, CK elevation.
- MEK inhibitors failed in KRAS-mutant pancreatic and lung cancer because of feedback reactivation of RAS–RAF signalling.

attrs.mnemonic: MEK is the only substrate gatekeeper: RAF → MEK → ERK, and MEK's only known substrates are ERK1/2 – that makes MEK inhibitors very clean.

items.gloss_md: A dual-specificity protein kinase that phosphorylates ERK1/2 on both threonine and tyrosine in their TEY activation motif.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *MAP2K1*; 393 amino acids. N-terminal negative regulatory helix and docking site for ERK, kinase domain with a proline-rich insert, C-terminal domain.

- Activation: RAF kinases phosphorylate Ser218 and Ser222 in the activation loop; MEK1/2 exist in complexes with RAF and scaffolds (KSR).
- Substrates: essentially only ERK1 and ERK2 (Thr202/Tyr204 in ERK1, Thr185/Tyr187 in ERK2) – an unusually narrow specificity that makes MEK a clean pharmacological node.
- Pharmacology: most MEK inhibitors are allosteric, non-ATP-competitive compounds binding a pocket adjacent to ATP, which explains their high selectivity; some (e.g. trametinib) also prevent RAF-mediated MEK phosphorylation through binding to the KSR–MEK complex.

aliases: Dual specificity mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase 1

items.gloss_md: The gene of ERK2, the terminal kinase of the RAS–RAF–MEK–ERK pathway; with ERK1 (MAPK3) it relays mitogenic signals to transcription factors.
items.body_md:
Located on 22q11.22; ERK1 is encoded by *MAPK3* on 16p11.2.

- Alterations: rarely mutated; recurrent E322K in the common docking domain in cervical and head and neck squamous carcinomas; ERK2 amplification as a rare resistance mechanism to EGFR or BRAF inhibitors.
- Functional redundancy: Erk2-knockout mice die early in embryogenesis, whereas Erk1-knockout mice are viable – ERK2 can largely compensate for ERK1 but not vice versa (expression level differences).
- Clinic: ERK inhibitors (ulixertinib, temuterkib) are in trials for MAPK-driven tumours with resistance to upstream inhibitors. Phospho-ERK IHC and the expression of ERK target genes (*DUSP6*, *SPRY2/4*, *ETV4/5*, *FOSL1*; 'MAPK pathway activity score', MPAS) are used to assess pathway activity in tissue and transcriptomes.

attrs.mnemonic: ERK1 = MAPK3 (p44), ERK2 = MAPK1 (p42): the numbers are 'crossed' – remember 'ERK2 is MAPK1 and the lighter one (42 kDa)'.

items.gloss_md: A proline-directed serine/threonine MAP kinase activated by MEK that phosphorylates hundreds of substrates controlling proliferation, differentiation and survival.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *MAPK1*; 360 amino acids, p42 MAPK (ERK1 is p44). Activation loop TEY motif doubly phosphorylated by MEK1/2.

- Substrates (P-x-S/T-P motifs): cytoplasmic RSK, MNK1/2 (eIF4E), cPLA2, and negative feedback targets SOS1, RAF, EGFR; nuclear ELK1 (ternary complex factor → FOS), ETS factors, c-Fos (stabilisation), MYC (Ser62), FRA1.
- Docking: D-domain (common docking site) and DEF-site interactions determine substrate specificity.
- Termination: dual-specificity phosphatases (DUSP/MKP, e.g. DUSP6 cytoplasmic, DUSP1/4/5 nuclear), many of which are ERK target genes – a rapid negative feedback.
- Signal dynamics (transient vs sustained ERK activity, pulses) encode different cellular outcomes (e.g. proliferation vs differentiation in PC12 cells).

items.gloss_md: An oncogene encoding the kinase AKT1 (PKBα), the central effector of PI3K signalling; the E17K hotspot occurs in breast cancer and, as a mosaic mutation, causes Proteus syndrome.
items.body_md:
Located on 14q32.33. Named after the AKT8 retrovirus, isolated from a spontaneous thymoma of the AKR mouse strain (Staal, 1977); the cellular gene was cloned in 1991 (also as protein kinase B, PKB, and RAC-PK). Paralogues *AKT2* (insulin action, glucose homeostasis; germline mutations cause diabetes or hypoglycaemia) and *AKT3* (brain size).

- Alterations: the E17K mutation in the PH domain (Carpten et al., 2007) increases membrane binding; present in ~3% of breast cancers (mostly HR-positive), and in endometrial cancer and meningiomas.
- Mosaic E17K causes Proteus syndrome, with asymmetric progressive overgrowth (Lindhurst et al., 2011); Joseph Merrick, the 'Elephant Man', is thought to have had Proteus syndrome.
- Clinic: the AKT inhibitor capivasertib plus fulvestrant was approved in 2023 for HR+/HER2− breast cancer with PIK3CA, AKT1 or PTEN alterations (CAPItello-291). Hyperglycaemia, rash and diarrhoea are class effects.

attrs.mnemonic: AKT activation needs two phosphates: T308 by PDK1 and S473 by mTORC2 – 'three-oh-eight first, four-seven-three to finish'.

items.gloss_md: A serine/threonine kinase recruited to PIP3 at the membrane that phosphorylates many substrates to promote growth, survival, glucose uptake and metabolism.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *AKT1*; 480 amino acids, AGC kinase family. N-terminal pleckstrin homology (PH) domain binding PI(3,4,5)P3 and PI(3,4)P2, central kinase domain, C-terminal regulatory tail with the hydrophobic motif.

- Activation: PIP3 recruits AKT and PDK1 to the plasma membrane; PDK1 phosphorylates Thr308 (activation loop) and mTORC2 phosphorylates Ser473 (hydrophobic motif) for full activity. Dephosphorylation by PP2A and PHLPP terminates signalling.
- Key substrates (R-x-R-x-x-S/T motif): TSC2 and PRAS40 (→ mTORC1 activation), GSK3α/β (inhibition → glycogen synthesis, β-catenin/MYC/cyclin D stability), FOXO1/3 (nuclear exclusion → survival, reduced gluconeogenesis), BAD and caspase-9 (anti-apoptotic), MDM2 (p53 degradation), AS160/TBC1D4 (GLUT4 translocation), p27 and p21 (cytoplasmic retention).
- Allosteric (MK-2206) and ATP-competitive (capivasertib, ipatasertib) inhibitors exist.

items.gloss_md: The gene of mTOR, the kinase hub of mTORC1 and mTORC2 that integrates growth factors, nutrients and energy; target of the rapalogs sirolimus and everolimus used in transplantation and oncology.
items.body_md:
Located on 1p36.22 (formerly *FRAP1*).

- Alterations: activating point mutations in a few percent of clear cell renal carcinomas and other cancers; somatic mosaic mutations cause focal cortical dysplasia type II and hemimegalencephaly (epilepsy); germline variants cause Smith–Kingsmore syndrome. More often mTORC1 is activated indirectly (PIK3CA, PTEN, TSC1/2, STK11 alterations).
- History: rapamycin was isolated from Streptomyces hygroscopicus in a soil sample collected on Easter Island (Rapa Nui) in 1964–65 and described in 1975 (Sehgal, Ayerst); its yeast targets TOR1/TOR2 were identified in 1991 (Heitman, Movva and Hall) and mammalian mTOR in 1994 (Sabatini, Snyder; Brown, Schreiber; Chiu).
- Clinic: sirolimus (rapamycin) and everolimus are immunosuppressants after kidney and liver transplantation (calcineurin-inhibitor-sparing; antiproliferative properties studied for HCC recurrence after liver transplantation, e.g. SiLVER trial), and are used for lymphangioleiomyomatosis and TSC lesions. Everolimus and temsirolimus are approved in renal cancer, everolimus also in HR+ breast cancer (with exemestane) and neuroendocrine tumours. Side effects: stomatitis, hyperlipidaemia, hyperglycaemia, pneumonitis, impaired wound healing.

attrs.mnemonic: mTORC1 = Raptor = Rapamycin-sensitive (all R's); mTORC2 = Rictor = Rapamycin-insensitive (phosphorylates AKT S473).
attrs.anecdote: Rapamycin is named after Rapa Nui (Easter Island), where the soil sample containing the producing bacterium was collected by a Canadian expedition in the 1960s; it was first developed as an antifungal.

items.gloss_md: A PI3K-related serine/threonine kinase that forms two complexes, mTORC1 (growth, protein synthesis, autophagy suppression) and mTORC2 (AKT activation, cytoskeleton).
items.body_md:
Encoded by *MTOR*; 2549 amino acids; PIKK family with HEAT repeats, FAT, FRB (FKBP12–rapamycin-binding), kinase and FATC domains.

- mTORC1 (mTOR, Raptor, mLST8, PRAS40, DEPTOR): activated on the lysosomal surface when amino acids activate the Rag GTPases (via Ragulator, GATOR, sensors such as Sestrin2 for leucine and CASTOR1 for arginine) and growth factors activate RHEB (by inhibiting TSC2). Substrates: S6K1 and 4E-BP1 (cap-dependent translation, ribosome biogenesis), SREBP and lipogenesis, ULK1 and TFEB (inhibition of autophagy and lysosome biogenesis). S6K1 feedback inhibits IRS1.
- mTORC2 (mTOR, Rictor, mSIN1, mLST8): phosphorylates AKT Ser473, SGK1 and PKCα; regulates cytoskeleton and ion transport.
- Pharmacology: rapamycin–FKBP12 binds the FRB domain and allosterically inhibits mTORC1 (incompletely for 4E-BP1); chronic exposure also disrupts mTORC2 assembly. ATP-competitive TORKi (torin, sapanisertib) inhibit both complexes; RapaLink combines both mechanisms.

attrs.mnemonic: mTORC1 is a lysosomal AND gate: it fires only when amino acids (Rag GTPases) AND growth factors (RHEB) say go.

items.gloss_md: The gene of p85α, the regulatory subunit of class IA PI3K; its mutations release p110 inhibition in endometrial cancer and glioblastoma.
items.body_md:
Located on 5q13.1; encodes p85α and the shorter isoforms p55α and p50α (alternative promoters).

- Somatic: mutations (often in-frame deletions in the iSH2/nSH2 region) in ~20–30% of endometrial carcinomas, ~10% of glioblastomas and in colorectal and breast cancers; they disrupt the inhibitory contacts with p110 while keeping it stabilised, thereby activating PI3K. Because p85α is also required for PTEN stability and for PI3K signalling restraint, it is classed as a tumour suppressor.
- Germline: loss-of-function variants cause SHORT syndrome (Short stature, Hyperextensibility, Ocular depression, Rieger anomaly, Teething delay) with insulin resistance; gain-of-function splice variants (exon 11 skipping) cause activated PI3Kδ syndrome 2 (APDS2), a primary immunodeficiency treated with the PI3Kδ inhibitor leniolisib.

items.gloss_md: The regulatory subunit of class IA PI3K that stabilises, inhibits and recruits the p110 catalytic subunit to phosphorylated tyrosine motifs.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *PIK3R1*; 724 amino acids. Domains: SH3, BCR-homology (BH, RhoGAP-like) domain, N-terminal SH2 (nSH2), inter-SH2 coiled-coil (iSH2, binds the p110 adaptor-binding domain) and C-terminal SH2 (cSH2).

- Function: the iSH2 tightly binds p110α/β/δ; the nSH2 contacts the p110 helical and C2 domains and inhibits catalysis. Binding of the SH2 domains to pYXXM motifs on activated receptors or IRS1/2 relieves inhibition and brings p110 to the membrane.
- Free p85 monomers (in excess of p110) compete for docking sites and can bind PTEN and XBP1, modulating insulin sensitivity.
- Isoforms p55α and p50α lack the SH3 and BH domains; paralogues p85β (PIK3R2) and p55γ (PIK3R3).

items.gloss_md: A tumour suppressor encoding hamartin, the partner of tuberin in the TSC complex; germline mutations cause tuberous sclerosis complex and somatic loss occurs in bladder cancer.
items.body_md:
Located on 9q34.13. Identified in 1997 (van Slegtenhorst et al.).

- Germline: tuberous sclerosis complex, generally with a milder phenotype than TSC2 mutations (fewer seizures and intellectual disability, fewer renal lesions); TSC1 mutations account for ~20–25% of TSC cases with an identified mutation.
- Somatic: loss in ~6–8% of urothelial carcinomas and in some HCC, PEComas and other tumours.
- Exceptional responder: a patient with metastatic bladder cancer had a durable complete response to everolimus; tumour sequencing revealed TSC1 loss (Iyer et al., Science 2012) – a landmark of 'exceptional responder' genomics.

attrs.anecdote: Hamartin and tuberin are named after the lesions of tuberous sclerosis: hamartomas and cortical 'tubers' – potato-like hard nodules in the brain that gave the disease its name.

items.gloss_md: The scaffolding subunit of the TSC complex that stabilises tuberin and is required for its RHEB-GAP activity toward mTORC1.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *TSC1*; 1164 amino acids, with an N-terminal transmembrane-like region and a C-terminal coiled-coil that binds tuberin.

- Function: protects tuberin from ubiquitin-mediated degradation; with TBC1D7 completes the TSC complex that is recruited to lysosomes and inactivates RHEB.
- Also acts as a co-chaperone of HSP90, influencing kinase client folding.
- Loss of either hamartin or tuberin gives the same molecular phenotype: constitutive mTORC1 activity.

items.gloss_md: The first proto-oncogene discovered, encoding the non-receptor tyrosine kinase SRC; its viral version v-src from Rous sarcoma virus founded the oncogene concept.
items.body_md:
Located on 20q11.23.

- History: in 1911 Peyton Rous showed that a cell-free filtrate transmits chicken sarcoma (Rous sarcoma virus; Nobel Prize 1966). In 1976 Dominique Stehelin, Harold Varmus, Michael Bishop and Peter Vogt showed that the viral oncogene v-src has a normal cellular counterpart, c-src, in uninfected chicken DNA – the discovery of proto-oncogenes (Nobel Prize 1989 for Bishop and Varmus). In 1980, Tony Hunter and Bart Sefton found that v-Src phosphorylates tyrosine – the discovery of tyrosine phosphorylation.
- Cancer: rarely mutated in human tumours (a truncating mutation at codon 531 in a minority of advanced colon cancers was reported), but often overexpressed or activated downstream of receptor tyrosine kinases and integrins in colon, breast, pancreatic and other cancers, promoting invasion and metastasis.
- Drugs: dasatinib and bosutinib (approved as BCR::ABL1 inhibitors) also inhibit SRC-family kinases; SRC inhibitors have shown little single-agent activity in solid tumours.

attrs.mnemonic: SRC autoinhibition = 'the tail bites the SH2': phosphorylated Tyr530 (Tyr527 in chicken) folds back onto its own SH2 domain.
attrs.anecdote: Rous's 1911 discovery of a cancer-causing virus in chickens was largely ignored for decades; he received the Nobel Prize in 1966, 55 years after the discovery, at the age of 87.

items.gloss_md: A membrane-associated non-receptor tyrosine kinase that relays signals from integrins, receptor tyrosine kinases and GPCRs to control adhesion, migration and proliferation.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *SRC*; 536 amino acids (pp60c-src). Domains: N-terminal SH4 (myristoylated, membrane anchor), unique region, SH3, SH2, kinase (SH1) and a short C-terminal regulatory tail.

- Autoinhibition: CSK phosphorylates Tyr530 (Tyr527 in chicken), which binds the SH2 domain, while the SH3 domain binds the SH2–kinase linker – a closed inactive state. Dephosphorylation of Tyr530 (by PTP1B, SHP2, RPTPα) or ligand binding to SH2/SH3 opens SRC, followed by autophosphorylation of Tyr419 (Tyr416 in chicken) in the activation loop.
- v-Src lacks the C-terminal tail including Tyr527 and is therefore constitutively active.
- Partners/substrates: FAK (focal adhesions), p130Cas, cortactin, STAT3, EGFR, β-catenin and E-cadherin complexes (junction disassembly).
- Family: SRC, YES, FYN, FGR, LCK, HCK, LYN, BLK, (FRK).

items.gloss_md: An oncogene encoding N-Myc; MYCN amplification occurs in ~20–25% of neuroblastomas and is the strongest genetic marker of high-risk disease.
items.body_md:
Located on 2p24.3.

- Discovery: identified in 1983 as an amplified MYC-related gene in neuroblastoma cell lines (Schwab et al.; Kohl et al.); Brodeur et al. (Science 1984) showed that amplification correlates with advanced stage – the first oncogene amplification used for clinical risk stratification.
- Neuroblastoma: amplification (often >10 copies, in double minutes or homogeneously staining regions) in ~20–25% of cases, ~40% of high-risk cases; MYCN status is a core criterion of the International Neuroblastoma Risk Group (INRG) classification. Also amplified in medulloblastoma (SHH and group 3/4), small cell lung cancer, a subset of retinoblastoma without RB1 mutation, and neuroendocrine prostate cancer; overexpressed in Wilms tumour and some AML.
- Germline loss of function: Feingold syndrome (microcephaly, digital anomalies, oesophageal/duodenal atresia).
- Clinic: no direct inhibitor; strategies target N-Myc stabilisation by Aurora A (alisertib), BET bromodomains and synthetic-lethal partners. The ALK inhibitor lorlatinib is used in ALK-mutant neuroblastoma.

attrs.mnemonic: N-Myc = Neuroblastoma Myc: the 'N' tells you the tumour.

items.gloss_md: A MYC-family bHLH-leucine-zipper transcription factor expressed in the developing nervous system that heterodimerises with MAX and drives proliferation.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *MYCN*; 464 amino acids, with MYC boxes I–IV, a central region and a C-terminal bHLH-LZ.

- Function: like c-Myc it binds E-boxes as a MYCN–MAX heterodimer, amplifies transcription of genes for ribosome biogenesis, nucleotide and lipid metabolism and cell-cycle progression, and represses differentiation genes. Normally expressed in neural crest and neural progenitors, kidney and lung during development; switched off in most adult tissues.
- Turnover: phosphorylation of Ser62 (CDK1) and Thr58 (GSK3β) creates the FBXW7 degron; Aurora A binding protects N-Myc from FBXW7-mediated degradation in neuroblastoma; PI3K–AKT inhibition destabilises N-Myc by activating GSK3β.
- Paralogue redundancy: N-Myc can replace c-Myc in mouse development when knocked into the Myc locus.

items.gloss_md: The gene of GSK3β, a constitutively active kinase in the β-catenin destruction complex that also controls glycogen synthesis, MYC, cyclin D1 and MCL-1 stability.
items.body_md:
Located on 3q13.33; paralogue *GSK3A* on 19q13.2.

- History: first purified as the kinase that phosphorylates and inactivates glycogen synthase (Embi, Rylatt and Cohen, 1980); later recognised as the Drosophila *shaggy/zeste-white 3* gene in Wingless (WNT) signalling.
- Cancer: not commonly mutated. Its role is context-dependent – it suppresses WNT, MYC and cyclin D1 (tumour-suppressive) but promotes NF-κB activity and survival in some cancers (e.g. PDAC models), so GSK3 inhibitors have been tested in trials (e.g. elraglusib in PDAC).
- Neurology and psychiatry: lithium inhibits GSK3 directly (Klein and Melton, 1996), a candidate mechanism of its mood-stabilising action; GSK3β phosphorylates tau in Alzheimer disease.

attrs.mnemonic: GSK3 is the unusual kinase that is 'ON by default' and switched OFF by signalling (AKT phosphorylation of Ser9, or WNT).

items.gloss_md: A constitutively active serine/threonine kinase that phosphorylates primed substrates, marking many for degradation, and is inhibited by insulin/AKT and WNT signalling.
items.body_md:
Encoded by *GSK3B*; 420 amino acids (a neuronal splice variant GSK3β2 has 13 extra residues).

- Priming: GSK3 prefers substrates already phosphorylated four residues C-terminal (S/T-x-x-x-pS/T), e.g. β-catenin primed by CK1α at Ser45, glycogen synthase primed by CK2.
- Inhibition: AKT, p90RSK and PKA phosphorylate Ser9, turning the N-terminus into a pseudosubstrate that blocks the priming pocket (insulin → glycogen synthesis). In WNT signalling, GSK3 is sequestered at the LRP6 signalosome and in multivesicular bodies, independent of Ser9.
- Substrates creating degrons: β-catenin (Ser33/Ser37/Thr41), MYC (Thr58), cyclin D1 (Thr286), cyclin E (Thr384), MCL-1, NRF2, SNAIL, c-Jun, Notch ICD; plus glycogen synthase, tau, CRMP2.

items.gloss_md: A WNT target gene encoding the R-spondin receptor LGR5, the defining marker of intestinal stem cells and the basis of organoid technology.
items.body_md:
Located on 12q21.1 (formerly *GPR49*).
